> **The fifth row is the counterpart advantage: a small project with a spectacular ratio may add less value than a large one with a modest ratio, and NPV says so directly while a ratio does not.**

**ITS LIMITATIONS DESERVE HONEST STATEMENT SINCE NO SINGLE CRITERION SUFFICES:**

| Limitation | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is highly sensitive to the DISCOUNT RATE** ← | **Which is itself a judgement** ← |
| **It requires all benefits to be VALUED in money** ← | **Which many are not — lives, landscape, cultural heritage** ← |
| **It gives no indication of the SCALE of investment needed** ← | **A large NPV may require a large and unavailable capital sum** ← |
| **It says nothing about the DISTRIBUTION of costs and benefits** ← | **Who gains and who loses is invisible in a single number** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT LIMITATION FOR PUBLIC INFRASTRUCTURE AND IT IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: NPV aggregates everyone's gains and losses into one figure.**

> **A project with a large positive NPV may impose severe losses on a few people while benefiting many slightly, and the arithmetic does not distinguish that from a project whose benefits are widely shared.**

> **The resettlement question in a hydropower scheme is exactly this situation, and no NPV can resolve it.**

> **So the economic appraisal establishes whether a project is worth doing in aggregate, and a separate distributional analysis establishes whether it is acceptable in its effects on particular people — and a decision made on the first alone has answered only half the question.**
tags: positive NPV beats the discount rate

examTip.trick: **All cash flows discounted to the present; positive means accept** — it earns more than the discount rate.
examTip.trap: **NPV = 0 is acceptable, not a failure** — the project earns exactly the required return.
examTip.mnemonic: **NPVs ADD across projects; ratios and IRRs do not** — which is why NPV is the criterion for selecting a programme.

questions.stem: The INTERNAL RATE OF RETURN (IRR) of a project is:
options: The interest rate charged by the lender financing the project
The ratio of annual profit to capital employed
The rate at which the project's costs increase each year
The DISCOUNT RATE at which the project's NPV equals ZERO
questions.solution:
**The DISCOUNT RATE at which the project's NPV equals ZERO** — so it is the return the project itself earns, and it is compared against the required rate to decide acceptability.

**The definition and the decision rule:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **IRR is the value of i for which Σ [Bt − Ct] / (1 + i)ᵗ = 0** ← | ← |
| **It cannot generally be solved algebraically** ← | **It is found by trial and interpolation, or numerically** ← |
| **IRR > required rate** ← | **ACCEPT** ← |
| **IRR < required rate** ← | **REJECT** ← |
| **It is expressed as a percentage, which makes it intuitive** ← | **Its main appeal** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW EXPLAINS IRR'S POPULARITY AND IT IS A PRESENTATIONAL ADVANTAGE RATHER THAN A TECHNICAL ONE: 'this project returns 14 per cent' is immediately meaningful to a decision-maker in a way that 'this project has an NPV of Rs 340 million' is not.**

> **A percentage can be compared directly against a borrowing rate, a required return or another project without knowing anything about scale.**

> **So IRR communicates well, and it is reported alongside NPV in almost every appraisal for that reason.**

> **Its technical defects, however, are real and they are worth knowing because they bite in specific and recognisable circumstances.**

**THE THREE DEFECTS OF IRR:**

| Defect | Note |
|---|---|
| **MULTIPLE IRRs** ← | **A cash flow changing sign more than once can satisfy the equation at several rates** ← |
| **No IRR at all** ← | **Some cash flow patterns have no real solution** ← |
| **Wrong RANKING between mutually exclusive projects** ← | **IRR favours small early-returning projects over large valuable ones** ← |
| **An implicit REINVESTMENT assumption** ← | **It assumes intermediate cash flows are reinvested at the IRR itself, which may be unrealistic** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DEFECT MOST LIKELY TO PRODUCE A WRONG DECISION IN PRACTICE AND IT IS WORTH AN EXAMPLE: a small project costing 1 million and returning 2 million has an IRR far higher than a large project costing 100 million and returning 150 million.**

> **But the second adds 50 million of value and the first adds 1 million.**

> **If the two are mutually exclusive and the capital is available, the large project is plainly the better choice, and IRR ranks it second.**

> **So for mutually exclusive alternatives, NPV governs and IRR must not be used to rank — the correct procedure being to compute the incremental IRR on the DIFFERENCE between the two projects, which recovers the right answer but is more easily done by simply comparing NPVs.**

> **THE FIRST ROW'S MULTIPLE-IRR PROBLEM ARISES IN A SITUATION THAT INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS GENUINELY ENCOUNTER: a project with a large cost at the END of its life — decommissioning a plant, closing a landfill, restoring a mine — has a cash flow that goes negative, then positive, then negative again.**

> **Descartes' rule tells us that such a pattern can have as many IRRs as it has sign changes.**

> **Two IRRs are then mathematically valid and neither is meaningful as 'the return'.**

> **So for any project with significant end-of-life costs, IRR should be treated with suspicion and NPV relied upon — and noticing the sign changes in the cash flow before computing an IRR is the check that tells you whether the figure you are about to produce means anything.**
tags: wrong ranking of mutually exclusive projects

examTip.trick: **The discount rate at which NPV = 0** — the project's own return, compared against the required rate.
examTip.trap: **IRR ranks mutually exclusive projects WRONGLY** — it favours small early returns over large value. Use NPV to rank.
examTip.mnemonic: **Count the SIGN CHANGES in the cash flow** — more than one and multiple IRRs are possible, which end-of-life costs routinely cause.

questions.stem: A machine costs Rs 800,000, has a salvage value of Rs 80,000 and a useful life of 6 years. Using the STRAIGHT LINE method, the annual depreciation is:
questions.solution:
**Rs 120,000 per year.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Depreciable amount** | **Cost − salvage value = 800,000 − 80,000 = 720,000** ← |
| **Annual depreciation** | **720,000 ÷ 6 = 120,000** ← |

> **THE DISTRACTOR AT 133,333 IS 800,000 DIVIDED BY 6 WITH THE SALVAGE VALUE NOT DEDUCTED, and it is the error the question is built around.**

> **The asset is not written down to zero — it is written down to its salvage value, so only the difference is depreciated.**

> **Depreciating the full cost would write the asset off entirely while it still had Rs 80,000 of value, which overstates the expense and understates the asset.**

> **The check is that the book value after six years should equal the salvage value: 800,000 − 6 × 120,000 = 800,000 − 720,000 = 80,000 ✓.**

**THE PRINCIPAL DEPRECIATION METHODS COMPARED:**

| Method | Formula | Character |
|---|---|---|
| **STRAIGHT LINE** ← | **(C − S) / n** ← | **Equal each year — simple and most common** ← |
| **DECLINING BALANCE** ← | **A fixed percentage of the REMAINING book value** ← | **Accelerated — larger charges early** ← |
| **SUM OF YEARS' DIGITS** ← | **(C − S) × remaining life ÷ sum of the digits** ← | **Accelerated, but reaching the salvage value exactly** ← |
| **SINKING FUND** ← | **A uniform annual deposit that accumulates with interest to (C − S)** ← | **The charge RISES over time; recognises the time value of money** ← |
| **PRODUCTION / service output** ← | **Per unit produced or hour operated** ← | **Matches the charge to actual use** ← |

> **THE ACCELERATED METHODS IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS EXIST FOR A REASON WORTH UNDERSTANDING: most assets lose value fastest when new, and most also require increasing maintenance as they age.**

> **So a high depreciation charge early and a low one late, combined with low maintenance early and high maintenance late, gives a more nearly CONSTANT total annual cost of ownership.**

> **Straight-line depreciation combined with rising maintenance gives a total cost that climbs steadily, which misrepresents the economics.**

> **That is the economic argument for accelerated depreciation, quite separate from the tax argument, which is simply that deferring tax is worth money.**

**THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST APPROPRIATE METHOD FOR CONSTRUCTION PLANT AND IT IS WORTH NOTING WHY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An excavator's value depends on HOURS RUN, not years elapsed** ← | ← |
| **A machine idle for a year has depreciated much less than one worked continuously** ← | ← |
| **So depreciating per operating hour matches the charge to the consumption of the asset** ← | ← |
| **And it gives a proper hourly OWNING cost for estimating** ← | ← |

> **The fourth row is the practical reason a contractor cares about this: plant hire rates and cost estimates are built up per hour, and the owning cost per hour is depreciation plus interest, insurance, tax and storage.**

> **Adding the operating cost per hour — fuel, lubricants, tyres, repairs, the operator — gives the total hourly cost, which is the number an estimator needs.**

> **So depreciation is not merely an accounting entry for a contractor; it is an input to every rate they quote.**

> **And a contractor who depreciates on a calendar basis while their plant utilisation varies widely will misprice work systematically — over-recovering on busy plant and under-recovering on idle plant, which distorts every comparison between the two.**
tags: declining balance and sum of years digits

examTip.trap: **133,333 omits the salvage value** — the asset is written down to its salvage value, not to zero. Check: book value at year 6 = salvage.
examTip.mnemonic: **For plant, depreciate per OPERATING HOUR** — value follows hours run, not years elapsed, and the hourly owning cost feeds every rate quoted.

questions.stem: The BENEFIT-COST RATIO (BCR) of a project is used in public sector appraisal. A project is considered economically justified when its BCR is:
options: GREATER THAN 1.0
Less than 1.0
Exactly equal to zero
Greater than the project's internal rate of return
questions.solution:
**GREATER THAN 1.0 — meaning the present value of its benefits exceeds the present value of its costs.**

**The definition and its relationship to NPV:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **BCR = PV of benefits ÷ PV of costs** ← | **Both discounted at the same rate** ← |
| **BCR > 1 is equivalent to NPV > 0** ← | **The same test expressed as a ratio rather than a difference** ← |
| **BCR = 1 corresponds to NPV = 0** ← | ← |
| **So the two criteria always AGREE on whether to accept a single project** ← | ← |
| **But they can DISAGREE on ranking between projects** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER ARE THE POINT WORTH HOLDING: BCR and NPV never disagree about whether a project passes, and they frequently disagree about which project is best.**

> **A small project with a BCR of 3.0 and an NPV of Rs 10 million ranks above a large one with a BCR of 1.4 and an NPV of Rs 200 million, on the ratio criterion.**

> **On the NPV criterion the large project is far better, and where capital is available it plainly is.**

> **So BCR is the right criterion when CAPITAL IS RATIONED — when the constraint is the budget rather than the availability of good projects — because it measures value per unit of scarce capital, and NPV is right when the constraint is finding worthwhile projects at all.**

**THE DEFINITION OF THE RATIO IS ITSELF AMBIGUOUS AND THAT IS A REAL PRACTICAL PROBLEM:**

| Treatment | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Operating costs deducted from BENEFITS (numerator)** ← | **Gives a HIGHER ratio** ← |
| **Operating costs added to COSTS (denominator)** ← | **Gives a LOWER ratio** ← |
| **The NPV is identical either way** ← | **Since the difference is unchanged** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE OBSERVATION THAT EXPOSES THE RATIO'S WEAKNESS AND IT IS WORTH DEMONSTRATING: consider benefits of 100, capital cost 40 and operating cost 20.**

> **Netting operating costs off benefits gives (100 − 20)/40 = 2.00.**

> **Adding them to costs gives 100/(40 + 20) = 1.67.**

> **Both are 'the benefit-cost ratio' and they differ by 20 per cent, while the NPV is 40 either way.**

> **So a BCR is meaningless without a statement of how it was computed, and comparing BCRs from different studies is unsafe unless both used the same convention — which is a strong practical argument for reporting NPV as the primary figure and BCR as a supplement.**

> **THE ECONOMIC VERSUS FINANCIAL DISTINCTION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE SINCE IT IS WHERE PUBLIC APPRAISAL DIFFERS FROM PRIVATE: a FINANCIAL analysis counts money actually paid and received by the project entity, at market prices including taxes and subsidies.**

> **An ECONOMIC analysis counts resources consumed and benefits produced by society, at shadow prices that strip out transfers.**

> **So taxes and duties are a cost financially and merely a transfer economically; unskilled labour in an area of unemployment costs its wage financially and much less economically; and benefits to users who pay nothing count economically and not financially.**

> **A road project may have a strong economic case and no financial case at all, which is precisely why it is built by the government rather than by a private developer — and confusing the two analyses is the commonest error in appraising public infrastructure.**
tags: BCR greater than 1 equals NPV positive
ratio and NPV disagree on ranking

examTip.trick: **BCR > 1.0** — present value of benefits exceeds present value of costs. Equivalent to NPV > 0.
examTip.trap: **BCR depends on whether operating costs are netted off benefits or added to costs** — the same project can show 2.00 or 1.67, while NPV is unchanged.
examTip.mnemonic: **BCR when capital is RATIONED; NPV when projects are scarce** — ratio measures value per unit of scarce capital.

questions.stem: A sum of Rs 500,000 is invested at 8 per cent compound interest for 10 years. Its value at the end of that period is approximately:
questions.solution:
**About Rs 1,079,500.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **F = P (1 + i)ⁿ** | ← |
| **Compute the factor** | **1.08¹⁰** ← |
| ** ** | **1.08² = 1.1664** ← |
| ** ** | **1.08⁴ = 1.1664² = 1.3605** ← |
| ** ** | **1.08⁸ = 1.3605² = 1.8509** ← |
| ** ** | **1.08¹⁰ = 1.8509 × 1.1664 = 2.1589** ← |
| **So** | **F = 500,000 × 2.1589 = 1,079,450 ≈ Rs 1,079,500** ← |

> **THE SUCCESSIVE-SQUARING METHOD IN THE MIDDLE ROWS IS THE PRACTICAL WAY TO RAISE A NUMBER TO A POWER WITHOUT A CALCULATOR, and it is worth having: square to get the 2nd power, square again for the 4th, again for the 8th, then multiply by the 2nd to reach the 10th.**

> **Four multiplications rather than nine.**

> **The RULE OF 72 gives a faster check: at 8 per cent, money doubles in about 72/8 = 9 years.**

> **So after 10 years it has slightly more than doubled, giving a little over Rs 1,000,000 — which identifies the answer immediately and eliminates every distractor.**

**THE DISTRACTORS ARE EACH A NAMED ERROR:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **Rs 900,000** | **SIMPLE interest: 500,000 × (1 + 0.08 × 10) = 900,000** ← |
| **Rs 540,000** | **One year's compound interest only** ← |
| **Rs 1,250,000** | **An over-estimate, roughly 2.5× the principal** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST INSTRUCTIVE AND THE GAP IT REVEALS IS THE WHOLE POINT OF COMPOUNDING: simple interest gives Rs 900,000 and compound gives Rs 1,079,450.**

> **The difference of Rs 179,450 is interest earned ON interest, over just ten years at a modest rate.**

> **Over longer periods or at higher rates the divergence becomes dramatic — at 8 per cent over 30 years, simple interest triples the money and compound interest multiplies it by ten.**

> **So the distinction is not a technicality, and almost all engineering economics uses compound interest because that is how money actually behaves when it is reinvested.**

**A NOTE ON COMPOUNDING FREQUENCY DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD SINCE IT IS A COMMON EXAMINATION POINT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The NOMINAL rate is the quoted annual rate** ← | **8 per cent in this question** ← |
| **The EFFECTIVE rate accounts for compounding more often than annually** ← | ← |
| **Effective = (1 + r/m)^m − 1, with m the compounding periods per year** ← | ← |
| **At 8 per cent compounded quarterly, effective = (1.02)⁴ − 1 = 8.24 per cent** ← | ← |
| **Compounded monthly, 8.30 per cent; continuously, e^0.08 − 1 = 8.33 per cent** ← | ← |

> **The last row shows that the effective rate converges as compounding becomes more frequent, approaching the continuous limit rather than growing without bound — which is worth knowing because it bounds the effect and shows that monthly compounding is already close to the maximum.**

> **The practical significance is in comparing quoted rates: a loan at 8 per cent compounded monthly costs more than one at 8.2 per cent compounded annually, despite the lower quoted figure.**

> **So rates must be converted to a common effective basis before they are compared, and a quoted nominal rate without its compounding frequency is an incomplete statement.**

> **That is why regulations in many countries require an annual effective rate to be disclosed alongside any quoted rate, precisely so that comparison is possible.**

examTip.trap: **Rs 900,000 is SIMPLE interest** — the Rs 179,450 difference is interest earned on interest in only ten years.
examTip.mnemonic: **Rule of 72: at 8% money doubles in 9 years** — so after 10 it is just over double, which picks the answer instantly.

questions.stem: In comparing two alternatives with DIFFERENT service lives — say a pump lasting 6 years and another lasting 9 years — the correct approach is to:
options: Compare their total costs directly, ignoring the difference in life
Choose the one with the longer life automatically
Compare them over a COMMON basis
Compare only their initial purchase prices
questions.solution:
**Compare them over a COMMON basis — either the least common multiple of their lives, with repeated replacements, or by converting each to an EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST.**

**Why a common basis is essential:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Comparing a 6-year asset with a 9-year asset directly compares different things** ← | ← |
| **The 6-year option leaves the buyer without a pump after 6 years** ← | ← |
| **So the comparison must account for what happens then** ← | ← |
| **Either by extending both to a common horizon** ← | **The LCM of 6 and 9 is 18 years: three of the first, two of the second** ← |
| **Or by expressing each as a cost PER YEAR of service** ← | **The equivalent annual cost** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS ALMOST ALWAYS THE EASIER ROUTE AND IT IS THE ONE TO REACH FOR: the equivalent annual cost converts each option's whole life-cycle cost into a uniform annual amount.**

> **Since both are then expressed as a cost per year, they compare directly regardless of their lives.**

> **The conversion uses the capital recovery factor: EAC = PV of all costs × [i(1+i)ⁿ] / [(1+i)ⁿ − 1], with each option using its own n.**

> **So the different lives are handled automatically by the formula rather than by constructing an eighteen-year cash flow, which is why the EAC method is standard for equipment comparison.**

**A WORKED ILLUSTRATION MAKES THE METHOD CONCRETE:**

| Step | Pump A | Pump B |
|---|---|---|
| **Initial cost** | **Rs 400,000** ← | **Rs 550,000** ← |
| **Life** | **6 years** ← | **9 years** ← |
| **Capital recovery factor at 10 per cent** | **0.22961** ← | **0.17364** ← |
| **Annualised capital cost** | **400,000 × 0.22961 = 91,844** ← | **550,000 × 0.17364 = 95,502** ← |
| **Annual operating cost, say** | **Rs 30,000** ← | **Rs 24,000** ← |
| **EQUIVALENT ANNUAL COST** | **Rs 121,844** ← | **Rs 119,502** ← |

> **PUMP B IS CHEAPER ON THIS BASIS DESPITE ITS HIGHER PURCHASE PRICE, AND THAT IS THE KIND OF CONCLUSION THE METHOD EXISTS TO REACH: comparing purchase prices alone would have chosen Pump A, and comparing total undiscounted costs would have been distorted by the different lives.**

> **The margin here is small — about 2 per cent — which is itself a useful observation: where two options are this close, the decision should turn on factors the arithmetic does not capture, such as reliability, spare parts availability, or the supplier's local support.**

> **A 2 per cent difference is well within the uncertainty of the input estimates, so treating it as decisive would be false precision.**

> **So the calculation's honest conclusion is 'these are equivalent, decide on other grounds', and reporting it as 'Pump B is cheaper' overstates what the analysis has shown.**

**THE ASSUMPTION UNDERLYING BOTH METHODS DESERVES STATING BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN UNEXAMINED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Both methods assume the asset is REPLACED with an identical one at the end of its life** ← | ← |
| **So costs and performance repeat indefinitely** ← | ← |
| **That is reasonable for a pump or a vehicle** ← | ← |
| **And unreasonable where technology is changing fast** ← | **A control system, or anything with rapid obsolescence** ← |
| **Or where the need itself will end** ← | **A pump for a construction site that closes in 7 years** ← |

> **The fifth row describes a common situation in which both standard methods mislead, and the remedy is straightforward once the assumption is recognised: analyse the actual horizon.**

> **If the need lasts seven years, compare the options over seven years, with the 6-year pump requiring something at year six and the 9-year pump having a residual value at year seven.**

> **That is more work than an EAC calculation and it gives the right answer, whereas the EAC gives a clean answer to a question nobody asked.**

> **So the first step in any life-cycle comparison is to establish how long the need actually lasts — and only where that is indefinite do the standard methods apply directly.**
tags: least common multiple or equivalent annual cost

examTip.trick: **A common basis — LCM of the lives, or equivalent annual cost** — which handles unequal lives automatically.
examTip.trap: **EAC assumes indefinite identical replacement** — wrong where technology changes fast or the need itself ends. Check the actual horizon first.
examTip.mnemonic: **A 2% margin is inside the input uncertainty** — report 'equivalent, decide on other grounds', not 'B is cheaper'.

questions.stem: In cost estimating, a SUNK COST is:
options: A cost that has ALREADY BEEN INCURRED and cannot be recovered by any future decision
A cost incurred on foundations and other below-ground work
The lowest cost at which the work can be carried out
A cost that is deferred to a later financial year
questions.solution:
**A cost that has ALREADY BEEN INCURRED and cannot be recovered by any future decision** — and which should therefore be EXCLUDED entirely from the analysis of what to do next.

**Why sunk costs must be excluded:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A decision can only affect the FUTURE** ← | ← |
| **Money already spent is spent whichever option is chosen** ← | ← |
| **So it is identical across all options and cannot distinguish between them** ← | ← |
| **Including it in every option changes every total equally** ← | ← |
| **And therefore cannot change the ranking** ← | **Though it can change whether an option appears worthwhile in absolute terms, misleadingly** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS WHERE THE REAL DAMAGE OCCURS AND IT IS WORTH SPELLING OUT: including a sunk cost does not change which option is best, and it can make all of them look bad enough to reject.**

> **A project on which Rs 500 million has been spent, requiring Rs 200 million more to complete and delivering Rs 400 million of benefit, should be completed — the remaining Rs 200 million buys Rs 400 million.**

> **Counting the Rs 500 million makes the project look like a Rs 700 million cost for Rs 400 million of benefit, and invites abandonment.**

> **Abandoning it wastes the Rs 400 million that Rs 200 million would have secured, so the sunk cost's inclusion causes a genuinely wrong decision — which is the opposite of the intuition that counting all the money is the prudent course.**

**THE OPPOSITE ERROR IS EQUALLY COMMON AND IS WORTH NAMING:**

| Error | Note |
|---|---|
| **The SUNK COST FALLACY — continuing a failing project BECAUSE of what has been spent** ← | ← |
| **'We have invested too much to stop now'** ← | **A statement that is always economically irrelevant** ← |
| **The correct question is whether the REMAINING cost is justified by the REMAINING benefit** ← | ← |
| **If it is not, the project should stop regardless of what has been spent** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND FOURTH ROWS TOGETHER SHOW THAT THE PRINCIPLE CUTS BOTH WAYS AND THAT IS WHAT MAKES IT POWERFUL: the sunk cost is neither a reason to continue nor a reason to stop.**

> **It is simply irrelevant.**

> **So a project should be continued if finishing it is worthwhile from today, and abandoned if it is not, and the amount already spent enters neither judgement.**

> **That is a psychologically difficult discipline — abandoning a project feels like wasting what was spent, when in fact the waste already occurred and abandoning merely stops adding to it — and recognising the feeling as a bias rather than as prudence is what allows the right decision to be taken.**

**THE RELATED COST CONCEPTS DESERVE LISTING SINCE THEY ARE ROUTINELY CONFUSED:**

| Concept | Definition |
|---|---|
| **SUNK cost** ← | **Already incurred, unrecoverable, irrelevant to future decisions** ← |
| **OPPORTUNITY cost** ← | **The value of the best alternative forgone — a real cost even though no money changes hands** ← |
| **MARGINAL (incremental) cost** ← | **The cost of one more unit, or of the difference between two options** ← |
| **FIXED cost** ← | **Does not vary with output in the short run** ← |
| **VARIABLE cost** ← | **Varies directly with output** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MIRROR IMAGE OF THE FIRST AND IT IS EQUALLY COUNTER-INTUITIVE: an opportunity cost involves no payment and is nonetheless real, while a sunk cost involved a payment and is nonetheless irrelevant.**

> **So the money that changed hands is a poor guide to what counts as a cost in a decision.**

> **Using land the organisation already owns 'for free' ignores its opportunity cost — it could have been sold or used otherwise — and that omission makes the project look cheaper than it is.**

> **Both errors flow from the same mistake of equating cost with expenditure, and correcting it is the central discipline of economic as opposed to financial thinking.**
tags: sunk cost fallacy cuts both ways
opportunity cost is real without payment
cost is not the same as expenditure

examTip.trick: **Already incurred and unrecoverable — so exclude it entirely** from any decision about what to do next.
examTip.trap: **It is neither a reason to continue nor a reason to stop** — only the remaining cost against the remaining benefit matters.
examTip.mnemonic: **Sunk cost: money paid, irrelevant. Opportunity cost: no money paid, real.** Cost is not the same thing as expenditure.

questions.stem: In the economic appraisal of a public infrastructure project, a SHADOW PRICE is used because:
options: Market prices are always deliberately falsified by suppliers
Shadow prices are simply prices estimated when no market data is available
The MARKET PRICE of a resource may not reflect its true value to SOCIETY
Shadow prices are required for accounting purposes by the tax authorities
questions.solution:
**The MARKET PRICE of a resource may not reflect its true value to SOCIETY — because of taxes, subsidies, tariffs, unemployment or externalities** — so an adjusted price is used to measure the real economic cost or benefit.

**The main distortions and their adjustments:**

| Distortion | Adjustment |
|---|---|
| **TAXES and DUTIES** ← | **Removed — they are a TRANSFER within society, not a resource cost** ← |
| **SUBSIDIES** ← | **Added back — the resource cost is higher than the price paid** ← |
| **Import TARIFFS and an overvalued exchange rate** ← | **Traded goods valued at BORDER prices** ← |
| **UNEMPLOYED or underemployed labour** ← | **Shadow wage below the market wage — the opportunity cost of labour with no alternative use is low** ← |
| **EXTERNALITIES — pollution, congestion, noise** ← | **Valued and included, though no market price exists** ← |
| **Monopoly pricing** ← | **Adjusted toward the competitive price** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE ADJUSTMENT MADE MOST OFTEN AND THE REASONING IS WORTH GRASPING BECAUSE IT IS THE MODEL FOR THE REST: a tax paid by a project to the government is money moving from one part of society to another.**

> **No resource is consumed by the transfer itself.**

> **So from society's point of view the tax is not a cost, even though it is unambiguously a cost to the project entity.**

> **That is the clearest illustration of why financial and economic analyses differ, and it means a project's economic cost is typically LOWER than its financial cost, sometimes substantially so in a country with high import duties on equipment.**

**THE SHADOW WAGE IN THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL ADJUSTMENT FOR LABOUR-INTENSIVE WORK:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The economic cost of employing someone is what they would otherwise have produced** ← | **Their opportunity cost** ← |
| **A skilled engineer in demand has a high opportunity cost** ← | **Close to their market wage** ← |
| **An unemployed rural labourer in the slack agricultural season has a LOW one** ← | ← |
| **So the shadow wage for unskilled seasonal labour may be well below the market wage** ← | **Sometimes a half or less** ← |
| **Which makes LABOUR-BASED methods look considerably better economically than financially** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS A CONCLUSION WITH REAL POLICY WEIGHT AND IT CONNECTS DIRECTLY TO THE GREEN ROAD APPROACH: a labour-based construction method may cost more in financial terms than an equipment-based one and less in economic terms.**

> **The financial comparison counts wages at their market rate and equipment at its import cost including duty.**

> **The economic comparison counts labour at its lower opportunity cost and equipment at its border price without duty, and adds the foreign exchange implications.**

> **Whether labour-based methods win depends on the actual numbers, and the point is that the two analyses can reach opposite conclusions from the same facts — so the choice of analysis is not neutral, and a public agency using a purely financial comparison to choose a construction method is answering the wrong question.**

> **THE FIFTH ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE — EXTERNALITIES — DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS THE HARDEST AND THE MOST IMPORTANT: pollution, noise, congestion, accident risk and ecological damage are real costs borne by society and paid for by nobody.**

> **Omitting them because they have no market price does not make them zero; it makes the appraisal wrong in a known direction.**

> **So valuation techniques exist — willingness to pay, hedonic pricing, travel cost, contingent valuation — and all are imperfect and contested.**

> **The honest position is that an approximate value is better than an implicit zero, and that where a value cannot be defended, the effect should be described and quantified in physical terms alongside the monetary analysis rather than dropped from it — because a decision-maker shown 'NPV Rs 2 billion, plus 40 hectares of forest lost' can weigh the trade, and one shown only the NPV cannot.**
tags: taxes are transfers not resource costs

examTip.trick: **Market price may not reflect value to society** — taxes, subsidies, tariffs, unemployment and externalities all distort it.
examTip.trap: **Taxes are TRANSFERS, not resource costs** — so economic cost is typically lower than financial cost, especially with high import duties.
examTip.mnemonic: **A low shadow wage can make labour-based methods win economically while losing financially** — the two analyses can reach opposite conclusions.

questions.stem: The BREAK-EVEN POINT of an operation is the level of output at which:
options: TOTAL REVENUE exactly equals TOTAL COST
Profit is at its maximum
Variable cost equals fixed cost
The average cost per unit is at its lowest
questions.solution:
**TOTAL REVENUE exactly equals TOTAL COST** — so the operation makes neither profit nor loss, and it is found where the fixed cost is exactly covered by the contribution from each unit sold.

**The derivation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Total cost = Fixed cost + (variable cost per unit × quantity)** | **TC = F + vQ** ← |
| **Total revenue = price per unit × quantity** | **TR = pQ** ← |
| **At break-even, TR = TC** | **pQ = F + vQ** ← |
| **Rearranging** | **Q(p − v) = F** ← |
| **So** | **Q = F / (p − v)** ← |
| **Where (p − v) is the CONTRIBUTION per unit** | ← |

> **THE CONTRIBUTION CONCEPT IN THE LAST ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE FORMULA INTUITIVE RATHER THAN ALGEBRAIC: each unit sold contributes (price minus variable cost) toward covering the fixed cost.**

> **So the break-even quantity is simply the fixed cost divided by the contribution per unit — how many units it takes to pay off the fixed burden.**

> **Beyond that point every further unit's contribution is profit, which is why profitability rises so steeply once break-even is passed.**

> **And below it, every unit short of break-even leaves that much of the fixed cost unrecovered, which is why operating below break-even loses money at a rate that does not depend on how far below.**

**THE APPLICATIONS IN CONSTRUCTION ARE SEVERAL AND WORTH LISTING:**

| Application | Note |
|---|---|
| **Deciding whether to BUY or HIRE plant** ← | **Buying has a high fixed cost and a low hourly cost; hiring the reverse** ← |
| **Deciding whether to set up a batching plant or buy ready-mixed concrete** ← | **The same structure** ← |
| **Deciding whether to open a quarry or purchase aggregate** ← | ← |
| **Determining the minimum turnover a contracting business needs** ← | **To cover its overheads** ← |
| **Assessing a toll road's traffic requirement** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE CLASSIC APPLICATION AND THE BREAK-EVEN IS EXPRESSED IN HOURS RATHER THAN UNITS: buying a machine costs a large sum up front and then a modest amount per hour; hiring costs nothing up front and a larger amount per hour.**

> **The break-even is the number of hours at which the two are equal.**

> **Below it, hire; above it, buy.**

> **So the decision turns entirely on the expected UTILISATION, and a contractor who buys plant they will use for fewer hours than the break-even has made a loss that no amount of good operation will recover — which is why plant purchase decisions rest on the forward workload forecast rather than on the machine's merits.**

**THE ANALYSIS'S ASSUMPTIONS ARE STRONG AND DESERVE STATING:**

| Assumption | Reality |
|---|---|
| **Fixed costs are constant over the whole range** ← | **They step up at capacity thresholds — another machine, another supervisor** ← |
| **Variable cost per unit is constant** ← | **It often falls with volume through discounts and learning** ← |
| **Price per unit is constant** ← | **Selling more may require lowering the price** ← |
| **Everything produced is sold** ← | ← |
| **A single product, or a constant mix** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION IN A CONSTRUCTION CONTEXT AND IT PRODUCES A STEPPED RATHER THAN A STRAIGHT COST LINE: a batching plant has a capacity, and exceeding it requires a second plant.**

> **So the fixed cost jumps, and there is a second break-even beyond the step.**

> **A simple linear break-even analysis extrapolated across such a step gives a confidently wrong answer.**

> **So the valid range of the analysis must be stated along with its result, and the result applied only within it — which is the general discipline for any linear model of a system that is only piecewise linear.**

examTip.trick: **Total revenue = total cost** — so Q = Fixed cost ÷ contribution per unit, where contribution = price − variable cost.
examTip.trap: **It is not the point of maximum profit or lowest average cost** — it is simply where profit is zero.
examTip.mnemonic: **Buy above the break-even hours, hire below** — so the decision rests entirely on the forward utilisation forecast.

questions.stem: The PAYBACK PERIOD of an investment is:
options: The time taken for the cumulative cash inflows to recover the initial investment
The period over which the asset is depreciated
The time until the project's IRR exceeds the discount rate
The duration of the loan used to finance the project
questions.solution:
**The time taken for the cumulative cash inflows to recover the initial investment** — a simple measure of liquidity and risk exposure, which in its basic form ignores the time value of money and everything that happens after payback.

**Its two serious defects:**

| Defect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It IGNORES the time value of money** ← | **A rupee in year four counts the same as one in year one** ← |
| **It IGNORES everything after the payback point** ← | **A project paying back in 3 years and then stopping ranks equal to one paying back in 3 years and running profitably for 30** ← |
| **It gives no measure of profitability at all** ← | ← |
| **And the acceptable payback period is arbitrary** ← | **Why three years and not four?** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MORE SERIOUS OF THE TWO AND IT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: the DISCOUNTED payback period fixes the first defect by discounting the inflows before accumulating them.**

> **It does nothing whatever about the second.**

> **So even a discounted payback period is blind to the entire post-payback life of the project, which for long-lived infrastructure is where most of the value lies.**

> **A hydropower scheme paying back in twelve years and running for fifty is barely distinguishable, on this measure, from one paying back in twelve years and running for thirteen.**

**DESPITE THAT, PAYBACK IS WIDELY USED AND THE REASONS ARE WORTH TAKING SERIOUSLY:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is IMMEDIATELY understood by anyone** ← | **No training required** ← |
| **It measures LIQUIDITY — how long the money is tied up** ← | **Which matters greatly to a business with limited cash** ← |
| **It is a crude proxy for RISK** ← | **Later cash flows are more uncertain, so a short payback is less exposed** ← |
| **It is useful where the future is genuinely unforecastable** ← | **Rapid technological change, political instability** ← |
| **And it is a quick SCREENING device before fuller analysis** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST DEFENSIBLE JUSTIFICATION AND IT IS WORTH STATING PROPERLY: payback is a risk measure disguised as a profitability measure.**

> **Its implicit logic is that cash flows beyond the payback point are too uncertain to count, which is a crude but not unreasonable position in a genuinely unstable environment.**

> **Where that instability is real — a short concession, an uncertain political situation, a technology likely to be superseded — a short required payback is a rational response to uncertainty rather than a failure of analysis.**

> **The error is using payback as the criterion in a STABLE environment for a long-lived asset, where it systematically rejects exactly the projects with the greatest long-term value.**

**THE CORRECT ROLE FOR PAYBACK IN AN APPRAISAL DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Use NPV as the primary criterion** ← | ← |
| **Report IRR alongside, for communication** ← | ← |
| **Report payback as an indicator of LIQUIDITY and exposure** ← | ← |
| **Never use payback alone to accept or reject a long-lived project** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE HONEST USE AND IT IS GENUINELY INFORMATIVE ALONGSIDE THE OTHERS: two projects with identical NPVs, one paying back in four years and one in twelve, are not equally attractive to an organisation with limited cash or facing uncertainty.**

> **NPV cannot distinguish them and payback can.**

> **So the measures are complementary, each answering a different question — how much value, at what rate of return, and how long exposed.**

> **Reporting all three costs almost nothing once the cash flow is built, and it gives a decision-maker the three things they actually want to know, which is a better outcome than an argument about which single measure is correct.**
tags: ignores time value and post-payback life
discounted payback fixes only one defect

examTip.trick: **Time for cumulative inflows to recover the investment** — simple, and blind to the time value of money.
examTip.trap: **Discounted payback fixes the discounting and NOT the blindness to post-payback life** — which is where a long-lived asset's value sits.
examTip.mnemonic: **Payback is a RISK measure wearing a profitability costume** — legitimate where the future is genuinely unforecastable, wrong as a sole criterion otherwise.

questions.stem: A project's cash flow shows an initial cost of Rs 2,000,000 and net annual benefits of Rs 400,000 for 8 years. At a discount rate of 10 per cent, the present value of the benefits is approximately (the present worth factor for a uniform series at 10 per cent over 8 years is 5.335):
questions.solution:
**About Rs 2,134,000.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **PV of a uniform series = A × (P/A, i, n)** | ← |
| **Substituting** | **400,000 × 5.335** ← |
| ** ** | **= Rs 2,134,000** ← |

> **THE FACTOR 5.335 IS SUPPLIED, SO THE ARITHMETIC IS ONE MULTIPLICATION — AND THE INTERPRETATION IS WHERE THE VALUE LIES: the factor means that eight annual payments of 1 are worth 5.335 today at 10 per cent.**

> **Undiscounted they would be worth 8.**

> **So discounting has reduced their value by a third, which is the time value of money made visible.**

> **The distractor at Rs 3,200,000 is the UNDISCOUNTED total, 400,000 × 8, which is the error of ignoring discounting altogether — and comparing it with the correct answer shows exactly what the discounting has done.**

**THE PROJECT'S NPV FOLLOWS IMMEDIATELY AND IS THE REAL QUESTION BEHIND THIS ONE:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **PV of benefits** | **Rs 2,134,000** ← |
| **Less the initial cost** | **Rs 2,000,000** ← |
| **NPV** | **+ Rs 134,000** ← |
| **BCR** | **2,134,000 ÷ 2,000,000 = 1.07** ← |

> **A POSITIVE BUT SMALL NPV IS THE CONCLUSION AND IT DESERVES A CAREFUL INTERPRETATION RATHER THAN A SIMPLE ACCEPT: the project earns slightly more than 10 per cent, so on the criterion it passes.**

> **But the margin is under 7 per cent of the investment, which is well inside the uncertainty of any real estimate of costs and benefits.**

> **So the honest statement is that the project is MARGINAL at a 10 per cent discount rate — it would fail at 11 per cent, and a 10 per cent cost overrun would eliminate the surplus entirely.**

> **Reporting 'NPV positive, project justified' from these figures overstates what they show, and a sensitivity analysis is not optional here but essential.**

**THAT SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS IS WORTH SETTING OUT SINCE IT IS THE PROPER RESPONSE:**

| Variation | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Discount rate to 12 per cent** | **Factor falls to 4.968; PV = 1,987,000; NPV = −13,000 — the project FAILS** ← |
| **Cost overrun of 10 per cent** | **Cost 2,200,000; NPV = −66,000 — FAILS** ← |
| **Benefits 10 per cent lower** | **PV = 1,921,000; NPV = −79,000 — FAILS** ← |
| **Life extended to 10 years** | **Factor 6.145; PV = 2,458,000; NPV = +458,000 — passes comfortably** ← |

> **THE FIRST THREE ROWS ALL PRODUCE FAILURE FROM MODEST AND ENTIRELY PLAUSIBLE VARIATIONS, AND THAT IS THE FINDING THAT MATTERS: this project's justification depends on every assumption holding.**

> **A project whose NPV survives a 20 per cent adverse movement in each key variable is robust; this one is not.**

> **So the appraisal's conclusion should be that the project is justified only if the estimates are reliable and the discount rate is correct, and that its case should be strengthened before commitment — by firming up the cost estimate, by examining whether the benefits are understated, or by looking at whether the asset's life is longer than assumed.**

> **The fourth row shows where the most promising avenue lies: two extra years of life transform the case, so establishing the asset's realistic life is worth more effort than refining any of the other figures.**
tags: present value of a uniform series

examTip.trick: **400,000 × 5.335 = Rs 2,134,000.** The factor converts an annual series to a present sum.
examTip.trap: **Rs 3,200,000 is the undiscounted total** — 8 payments worth 5.335, not 8, is the time value made visible.
examTip.mnemonic: **NPV of +134,000 on 2,000,000 is MARGINAL** — it fails at 12%, or on a 10% overrun. Report it as marginal, not as justified.

questions.stem: SENSITIVITY ANALYSIS in project appraisal involves:
options: Testing how sensitive the local community is to the project's impacts
Varying each key input in turn to see how much the project's outcome CHANGES
Adjusting the results until the project appears viable
Measuring the accuracy of the survey instruments used
questions.solution:
**Varying each key input in turn to see how much the project's outcome CHANGES** — identifying which variables the result depends on most, and how much adverse movement the project can tolerate before it becomes unviable.

**What the analysis produces:**

| Output | Note |
|---|---|
| **Which variables the result is most SENSITIVE to** ← | **So effort can be concentrated on estimating those accurately** ← |
| **The SWITCHING VALUE of each variable** ← | **The value at which the decision changes — NPV becomes zero** ← |
| **The project's ROBUSTNESS** ← | **How much adverse movement it can absorb** ← |
| **Guidance on which RISKS need managing** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL SINGLE OUTPUT AND IT IS OFTEN NOT PRODUCED: the switching value states how far a variable must move before the conclusion reverses.**

> **'The project remains viable unless construction costs exceed the estimate by 18 per cent' is a far more useful statement than 'a 10 per cent cost increase reduces the NPV by Rs 40 million'.**

> **The first tells a decision-maker directly whether the risk is one to worry about, because they can judge whether an 18 per cent overrun is likely.**

> **The second requires them to do that conversion themselves, and usually nobody does — so presenting switching values rather than sensitivity percentages makes the analysis actionable.**

**THE LIMITATION OF ONE-AT-A-TIME SENSITIVITY IS FUNDAMENTAL AND MUST BE UNDERSTOOD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Varying one variable at a time assumes the others stay at their base values** ← | ← |
| **In reality, adverse movements tend to occur TOGETHER** ← | **A delayed project has higher costs AND later benefits AND more interest** ← |
| **So one-at-a-time analysis understates the combined risk** ← | ← |
| **SCENARIO analysis addresses this by varying several variables coherently** ← | **A 'pessimistic' case, a 'most likely' case, an 'optimistic' case** ← |
| **And MONTE CARLO simulation goes further** ← | **Assigning probability distributions to each variable and sampling thousands of combinations** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CORRELATION PROBLEM AND IT IS THE SAME ONE THAT UNDERMINED THE COMPLEMENTARY-FLOWS ARGUMENT IN HYDROPOWER: adverse events are correlated, so treating them independently understates the joint risk.**

> **A project that survives each individual sensitivity test may fail comfortably when two or three plausible adverse movements occur together, which is the situation that actually arises.**

> **So scenario analysis — constructing a coherent pessimistic case in which several things go moderately wrong at once — is more informative than a set of independent sensitivity tests, even though it is less systematic.**

> **The fifth row's Monte Carlo approach is the rigorous version, and its output is a probability distribution of NPV rather than a single figure, from which statements like 'there is an 85 per cent probability of a positive NPV' can be made.**

**A CAUTION ABOUT MONTE CARLO DESERVES THE CLOSING WORD BECAUSE ITS SOPHISTICATION IS SEDUCTIVE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The output's precision depends entirely on the input distributions** ← | ← |
| **Those distributions are usually GUESSED** ← | **There is rarely data on the distribution of a cost overrun** ← |
| **And the correlations between variables are usually ignored or guessed too** ← | ← |
| **So a beautifully precise output can rest on arbitrary inputs** ← | ← |
| **Producing false confidence rather than genuine insight** ← | ← |

> **The fifth row is the real hazard and it is worth naming explicitly: a probability distribution of NPV looks far more authoritative than a switching value, and it may be founded on less.**

> **A switching value is a fact about the model — at this cost, the NPV is zero — and it requires no assumption about probability at all.**

> **A Monte Carlo result is a fact about the model plus a set of assumed distributions, and the assumptions do most of the work.**

> **So the honest order of preference is switching values first, scenarios second, and simulation only where there is genuine data to support the distributions — which is the reverse of the order in which these methods tend to impress.**
tags: switching values are the key output

examTip.trick: **Vary each input to see how much the outcome moves** — identifying the variables that matter and the tolerance to adverse movement.
examTip.trap: **Report SWITCHING VALUES** — 'viable unless costs exceed the estimate by 18%' is actionable; 'a 10% increase cuts NPV by Rs 40m' is not.
examTip.mnemonic: **Adverse movements are correlated** — so one-at-a-time testing understates risk. Use a coherent pessimistic scenario.

questions.stem: VALUE ENGINEERING applied to a construction project seeks to:
options: Reduce the project's cost by lowering the specified quality
Value the contractor's work for interim payment
Determine the market value of the completed asset
Increase the project's value by improving the ratio of FUNCTION to COST
questions.solution:
**Increase the project's value by improving the ratio of FUNCTION to COST** — achieving the required functions at lower cost, or better functions for the same cost — through a structured examination of what each element is actually FOR.

**The central idea, which distinguishes it from cost cutting:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Value = FUNCTION ÷ COST** ← | ← |
| **Value rises if function rises OR cost falls** ← | ← |
| **COST CUTTING reduces cost and function together** ← | **Value may not improve at all** ← |
| **VALUE ENGINEERING reduces cost while PRESERVING function** ← | ← |
| **Which requires knowing precisely what function is required** ← | **The analytical heart of the method** ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS ARE THE DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS AND IT IS WORTH INSISTING ON, BECAUSE 'VALUE ENGINEERING' IS FREQUENTLY USED AS A EUPHEMISM FOR EXACTLY WHAT IT IS NOT: substituting a cheaper cladding that leaks is cost cutting.**

> **Substituting a different cladding that performs identically and costs less is value engineering.**

> **The test is whether the required FUNCTION is still delivered, and answering that requires the function to have been stated.**

> **So a project whose functional requirements are vague cannot be value engineered properly — the exercise degenerates into cost cutting, because there is no agreed standard against which to test whether function has been preserved.**

**THE FUNCTION ANALYSIS STEP IS THE METHOD'S DISTINCTIVE TECHNIQUE AND IT IS WORTH DESCRIBING:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Express each element's function as a VERB plus a NOUN** ← | **'Support load', 'exclude water', 'provide access', 'resist fire'** ← |
| **Classify functions as BASIC or SECONDARY** ← | **Basic functions must be delivered; secondary ones may be negotiable** ← |
| **Determine the COST of each function** ← | **Not of each component — the costs are reallocated to functions** ← |
| **Look for functions costing more than they are worth** ← | ← |
| **Generate alternative ways of delivering the same function** ← | **By structured creative techniques** ← |
| **Evaluate, develop and recommend** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW'S VERB-NOUN DISCIPLINE SOUNDS TRIVIAL AND IS SURPRISINGLY POWERFUL: forcing a description into two words strips away the assumed solution and leaves the actual requirement.**

> **A 'retaining wall' becomes 'retain soil', which immediately admits reinforced soil, a gabion structure, a regraded slope or a rearranged layout as candidates.**

> **Describing it as a retaining wall presupposes a wall, and the alternatives are never considered.**

> **So the verb-noun formulation is a device for escaping the solution that was assumed at the outset, which is where most of the value in value engineering is found.**

**THE TIMING OF THE EXERCISE DETERMINES HOW MUCH IT CAN ACHIEVE AND THIS IS THE PRACTICAL POINT:**

| Stage | Potential saving | Cost of change |
|---|---|---|
| **Concept and feasibility** ← | **GREATEST — the whole solution is still open** ← | **Negligible** ← |
| **Preliminary design** ← | **Large** ← | **Low** ← |
| **Detailed design** ← | **Moderate — confined to component choices** ← | **Moderate** ← |
| **During construction** ← | **Small** ← | **HIGH — redesign, delay, variation** ← |

> **THE TABLE IS THE SAME SHAPE AS THE ROAD SAFETY AUDIT TABLE AND FOR THE SAME REASON: influence is greatest when commitment is least, and both decline as the project proceeds.**

> **Yet value engineering, like safety auditing, is most commonly applied late — often when a tender has come in over budget and something must be cut.**

> **At that point the scope for genuine value engineering is small and the pressure to cost-cut is large, so the exercise usually delivers the latter under the former's name.**

> **The value engineering that actually works is a workshop held at the concept stage, before the solution has been fixed, and its output is a better project rather than a cheaper version of a project already designed.**

examTip.trick: **Improve the ratio of function to cost** — same function for less, or more function for the same.
examTip.trap: **Cost cutting reduces function too** — the test is whether the required function still survives, which needs the function to have been stated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Express the function as VERB + NOUN** — 'retaining wall' becomes 'retain soil', which admits gabions, reinforced soil or a regraded slope.

questions.stem: In life-cycle costing of a building or an infrastructure asset, the largest component of the total cost over the asset's life is usually:
options: The initial construction cost
The design and professional fees
The cost of land acquisition
The OPERATION and MAINTENANCE cost accumulated over the asset's service life
questions.solution:
**The OPERATION and MAINTENANCE cost accumulated over the asset's service life** — which for a long-lived building can exceed the construction cost several times over.

**The typical proportions over a building's life:**

| Component | Rough share of whole-life cost |
|---|---|
| **Design and professional fees** ← | **Around 1 per cent** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION** ← | **Around 10 to 20 per cent** ← |
| **OPERATION and MAINTENANCE** ← | **The remainder — often 80 per cent or more** ← |

> **THE FIGURES ARE OFTEN QUOTED AS A 1 : 5 : 200 RATIO — DESIGN : CONSTRUCTION : OPERATION OVER A BUILDING'S LIFE — AND WHILE THE EXACT RATIO IS CONTESTED, THE ORDER OF MAGNITUDE MAKES THE POINT: the decisions that determine operating cost are taken during design, which is the cheapest part of the whole.**

> **So a design decision that adds one per cent to the construction cost and reduces the operating cost by five per cent is enormously worthwhile, and a decision that saves construction cost at the expense of operating cost is almost always wrong.**

> **Yet construction cost is what is tendered, budgeted, reported and scrutinised, and operating cost falls to a different budget in a different year under a different manager.**

> **That misalignment is the reason so many assets are built cheap and expensive to run, and it is an institutional rather than a technical failure.**

**WHAT LIFE-CYCLE COSTING INCLUDES:**

| Component | Note |
|---|---|
| **Acquisition — land, design, construction, commissioning** ← | ← |
| **OPERATION — energy, water, cleaning, security, staff** ← | **Energy is often the largest single item for a building** ← |
| **MAINTENANCE — routine, periodic and major** ← | ← |
| **REPLACEMENT of components with lives shorter than the asset's** ← | **Services, finishes, roof coverings** ← |
| **ALTERATION and adaptation during the life** ← | ← |
| **DISPOSAL or decommissioning, less any residual value** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHERE DESIGN DECISIONS HAVE THEIR GREATEST LEVERAGE AND IT IS WORTH BEING SPECIFIC: a building's orientation, its glazing, its insulation, its thermal mass and its ventilation strategy are fixed at the concept stage and determine its energy consumption for fifty years.**

> **None of them can be economically changed afterwards.**

> **So an hour's thought about orientation at the sketch stage may be worth more than any subsequent efficiency measure, and it costs nothing.**

> **The same holds for infrastructure — a pumping station's static lift, a road's alignment, a water supply's gravity head are all set early and determine the energy bill for ever.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESERVES ITS OWN NOTE BECAUSE IT IS SYSTEMATICALLY UNDERESTIMATED: a building's structure may last a hundred years, its roof covering twenty-five, its services twenty and its finishes ten.**

> **So over a hundred-year life the services are replaced five times and the finishes ten times, each replacement costing a substantial fraction of the original construction.**

> **Designing for that — making services accessible and replaceable without disturbing the structure, separating long-life and short-life elements — is a major determinant of whole-life cost and of whether the building can be adapted at all.**

> **A building whose services are cast into its structure is one whose services cannot economically be replaced, which effectively fixes its life at the life of its shortest-lived buried component — and that is a design decision with hundred-year consequences taken, usually, without anyone noticing it was a decision.**

examTip.trick: **Operation and maintenance** — often 80% or more of whole-life cost, dwarfing construction.
examTip.trap: **Design costs about 1% and determines most of the rest** — yet construction cost is what gets tendered, budgeted and scrutinised.
examTip.mnemonic: **Separate long-life structure from short-life services** — services cast into structure fix the building's life at its shortest buried component.

questions.stem: A contractor's PRELIMINARIES (or general items) in a bill of quantities cover:
options: The preliminary design work carried out before construction
The first month's work on site
Site-wide costs that cannot be attributed to any particular measured item
Materials ordered in advance of the works
questions.solution:
**Site-wide costs that cannot be attributed to any particular measured item** — site establishment, supervision, plant standing on site, temporary works, insurances, scaffolding, welfare and site services.

**Typical preliminaries items:**

| Item | Note |
|---|---|
| **Site establishment and clearance at completion** ← | **Offices, stores, compounds, fencing, access** ← |
| **SUPERVISION and site staff** ← | **Agent, engineers, surveyors, foremen, safety officer** ← |
| **Temporary WORKS** ← | **Haul roads, temporary drainage, dewatering, falsework not otherwise measured** ← |
| **PLANT standing on site** ← | **Cranes, hoists, pumps — available whether or not used on a given day** ← |
| **Site SERVICES** ← | **Power, water, telecommunications, sanitation** ← |
| **INSURANCES, bonds and guarantees** ← | ← |
| **Safety, welfare and environmental provisions** ← | ← |
| **Setting out and survey** ← | ← |
| **Testing and quality control** ← | ← |

> **THE DEFINING CHARACTERISTIC IS THE ONE IN THE STEM AND IT IS WORTH GRASPING: these costs serve the WHOLE site rather than any particular item of work.**

> **A crane does not belong to the beams it lifts; the site office does not belong to any wall.**

> **So they cannot sensibly be distributed across the measured rates, and they are priced separately.**

> **A contractor who does not price them separately must load them onto the measured rates instead, which distorts every rate and causes problems as soon as quantities vary.**

**THE TIME-RELATED VERSUS FIXED DISTINCTION IS THE MOST IMPORTANT FEATURE OF PRELIMINARIES AND IT MATTERS COMMERCIALLY:**

| Type | Examples | Behaviour |
|---|---|---|
| **FIXED (one-off)** ← | **Bringing plant to site, erecting the offices, removing them at the end** ← | **Incurred once, regardless of duration** ← |
| **TIME-RELATED** ← | **Supervision, plant hire, site services, insurances** ← | **Incurred per week or month the site is open** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHY DELAY IS SO EXPENSIVE TO A CONTRACTOR AND IT IS THE BASIS OF MOST PROLONGATION CLAIMS: if the project takes twelve months instead of ten, the time-related preliminaries are incurred for two extra months.**

> **The site staff are paid, the plant is on hire, the offices are rented, the insurances run.**

> **None of that produces any additional measured work, so there is no revenue against it.**

> **That is why a bill of quantities should separate fixed from time-related preliminaries — so that if the contract period is extended through no fault of the contractor, the entitlement can be calculated from the stated time-related rate rather than argued about after the event.**

> **THE PRACTICAL SIGNIFICANCE FOR THE EMPLOYER DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE, BECAUSE IT CUTS AGAINST AN INTUITION: preliminaries typically run to 10 to 20 per cent of a contract's value, and they are largely INDEPENDENT of the quantity of work done.**

> **So a variation that halves the quantity of some measured item saves that item's cost and saves almost none of the preliminaries.**

> **And a variation that extends the programme adds time-related preliminaries without adding any measured work at all.**

> **Which means an employer seeking savings by reducing scope saves less than the measured rates suggest, and an employer causing delay pays more than the absence of work implies — both consequences flowing from the same fact that a large part of the cost is time-related rather than quantity-related, and both routinely surprising those who have not looked at how the preliminaries were priced.**
tags: preliminaries in a bill of quantities
typically 10-20 per cent of contract value
scope reduction saves less than expected

examTip.trick: **Site-wide costs not attributable to any measured item** — establishment, supervision, temporary works, plant, insurances, welfare.
examTip.trap: **Separate FIXED from TIME-RELATED** — the time-related portion is the basis of every prolongation claim when the programme extends.
examTip.mnemonic: **Cutting scope saves less than the rates suggest** — preliminaries are 10-20% and largely independent of quantity.

questions.stem: A contractor's estimate builds up a unit rate from first principles. The MARK-UP added to the net cost of an item typically covers:
options: Only the contractor's profit
Only the cost of materials wasted
The contractor's head office OVERHEADS
The client's professional fees
questions.solution:
**The contractor's head office OVERHEADS, an allowance for RISK and contingency, financing costs, and PROFIT** — all of which must be recovered from the measured work.

**The build-up of a unit rate:**

| Layer | Contents |
|---|---|
| **1. NET COST of the item** ← | **Labour, materials including waste, plant, subcontract** ← |
| **2. Site on-costs** ← | **Where not recovered separately in the preliminaries** ← |
| **3. HEAD OFFICE overheads** ← | **Directors, estimating, accounts, offices, vehicles — the cost of being in business** ← |
| **4. RISK and contingency** ← | **The contractor's judgement of what may go wrong** ← |
| **5. FINANCING** ← | **The cost of funding the work before payment is received** ← |
| **6. PROFIT** ← | **The return for the capital and the risk borne** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN OVERLOOKED BY THOSE UNFAMILIAR WITH CONTRACTING AND IT IS UNAVOIDABLE: a contracting business has substantial costs that no project creates and every project must contribute to.**

> **The estimating department that prepared the losing tenders, the accounts function, the directors, the yard, the insurances — all must be paid from the margin on the work that is won.**

> **So a contractor who prices at net cost plus a small profit and no overhead recovery will win work and go out of business, which happens regularly.**

> **Head office overhead recovery is typically 5 to 10 per cent of turnover, and it is the largest single component of most mark-ups — larger, often, than the profit.**

**THE FIFTH ROW DESERVES SPECIFIC ATTENTION BECAUSE CASH FLOW IS WHAT ACTUALLY KILLS CONTRACTORS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A contractor pays for labour weekly and materials monthly** ← | ← |
| **And is paid by the employer monthly IN ARREARS, after measurement and certification** ← | ← |
| **With a further delay before the money actually arrives** ← | ← |
| **And with RETENTION deducted** ← | ← |
| **So the contractor FUNDS the work for a period before being paid for it** ← | ← |
| **Which costs interest and consumes working capital** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS DESCRIBE WHY PROFITABLE CONTRACTORS FAIL AND IT IS A DISTINCTION WORTH HOLDING FIRMLY: profit and cash are not the same thing.**

> **A contractor can be profitable on paper and unable to pay wages, because the profit is tied up in work done and not yet paid for.**

> **Growth makes this worse rather than better — a rapidly growing contractor funds an ever-larger volume of unpaid work, and overtrading is a classic cause of failure among successful firms.**

> **So the financing allowance in the rate is not a refinement but a recognition of a real and substantial cost, and a contract with slow certification and payment is genuinely more expensive to perform, which a contractor who understands their business will price accordingly.**

> **THE FOURTH ROW'S RISK ALLOWANCE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS WHERE TENDERS ARE WON AND LOST: a contractor prices the risks the contract allocates to them.**

> **A contract transferring ground risk, weather risk and design risk to the contractor will be priced with allowances for all three.**

> **If those risks do not materialise, the employer has paid for nothing; if the allowances were too small, the contractor absorbs the loss or pursues a claim.**

> **So transferring risk to the contractor does not eliminate it — it converts an uncertain employer cost into a certain premium, and the premium may exceed the expected cost of the risk because the contractor is less able than the employer to bear or manage it.**

> **The principle that follows is a general one in procurement: risk should be allocated to the party best able to MANAGE it, not simply to the other party, and a contract that transfers everything is usually a contract that has paid too much.**
tags: overhead recovery is often the largest element
risk should go to whoever can manage it

examTip.trick: **Overheads, risk, financing and profit** — all recovered from the measured work, not profit alone.
examTip.trap: **Head office overhead recovery is often LARGER than the profit** — 5-10% of turnover, and a contractor who omits it wins work and fails.
examTip.mnemonic: **Profit is not cash** — a profitable contractor can fail by funding unpaid work, and growth makes it worse. Hence overtrading.

questions.stem: The CRITICAL PATH through a project network is:
options: The LONGEST path through the network in terms of duration
The path containing the most expensive activities
The path with the greatest number of activities
The sequence of activities that must be completed first
questions.solution:
**The LONGEST path through the network in terms of duration** — determining the project's minimum possible duration, and along which every activity has zero float.

**The defining properties:**

| Property | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is the LONGEST path from start to finish** ← | ← |
| **Its length IS the project's minimum duration** ← | **The project cannot finish sooner** ← |
| **Every activity on it has ZERO total float** ← | **No spare time at all** ← |
| **Delaying any critical activity delays the WHOLE PROJECT** ← | ← |
| **Shortening the project requires shortening the critical path** ← | **Accelerating a non-critical activity achieves nothing** ← |
| **There is always at least one, and there may be several** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS CONSTANTLY VIOLATED IN PRACTICE: putting extra resources onto an activity that is not on the critical path does not shorten the project by a single day.**

> **It merely completes that activity sooner and increases its float.**

> **So a manager under pressure who accelerates whatever looks behind, rather than whatever is critical, spends money and gains nothing.**

> **Identifying the critical path is therefore the first step in any acceleration decision, and it must be re-identified after each change — because shortening the critical path eventually makes some other path critical, and effort must then move there.**

**THE FLOAT DEFINITIONS ARE WHERE THE ANALYSIS BECOMES USEFUL AND THEY ARE WORTH DISTINGUISHING CAREFULLY:**

| Float | Definition |
|---|---|
| **TOTAL float** ← | **How long an activity can be delayed without delaying the PROJECT** ← |
| ** ** | **= Latest Finish − Earliest Finish, or Latest Start − Earliest Start** ← |
| **FREE float** ← | **How long it can be delayed without delaying the EARLIEST START of any following activity** ← |
| ** ** | **= Earliest Start of the successor − Earliest Finish of this activity** ← |
| **INDEPENDENT float** ← | **Float available even if predecessors finish as late as possible and successors start as early as possible** ← |

> **THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN TOTAL AND FREE FLOAT MATTERS OPERATIONALLY AND IS OFTEN BLURRED: total float is SHARED along a chain of non-critical activities.**

> **If three activities in sequence share ten days of total float and the first consumes all of it, the other two have none left.**

> **Free float belongs to the activity alone and consuming it affects nobody.**

> **So free float can be used freely and total float must be used with an awareness that it belongs to the chain — which is why a subcontractor who absorbs the whole of a chain's total float has taken something from those who follow, and why float ownership is a genuine contractual question rather than a technicality.**

**THE FLOAT OWNERSHIP QUESTION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS PRACTICALLY CONTENTIOUS:**

| Position | Note |
|---|---|
| **Float belongs to the CONTRACTOR** ← | **They created the programme and the float is their planning margin** ← |
| **Float belongs to the PROJECT** ← | **Whoever needs it first may use it — the common contractual position** ← |
| **Float belongs to the EMPLOYER** ← | **Rarely argued, and rarely accepted** ← |

> **The second row is the position most standard contracts take, and its practical effect is that an employer delay which consumes float does not entitle the contractor to an extension of time, because the completion date has not moved.**

> **The contractor's objection is that their planning margin has been consumed by someone else's delay, leaving them exposed to their own subsequent difficulties with no cushion.**

> **Both positions are reasonable and the contract should state which applies, because arguing it after a delay has occurred is expensive and the outcome then depends on the jurisdiction rather than on the parties' intentions.**

> **So a programme submitted and accepted under the contract should make its float visible and the contract should address its ownership — and a contractor who conceals float by padding durations has made the question unanswerable, which is itself a reason such padding is objected to.**

examTip.trick: **The LONGEST path** — it sets the minimum project duration and every activity on it has zero float.
examTip.trap: **Accelerating a non-critical activity shortens nothing** — and after shortening the critical path, another path becomes critical. Re-identify each time.
examTip.mnemonic: **Total float is SHARED along a chain; free float belongs to the activity alone** — which is why float ownership is a contractual question.

questions.stem: In PERT (Programme Evaluation and Review Technique), the expected duration of an activity is calculated from three time estimates as:
options: te = (to + tm + tp) / 3
te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6
te = (to + tp) / 2
te = tm, the most likely estimate alone
questions.solution:
**te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6** — the weighted average of the optimistic, most likely and pessimistic estimates, weighting the most likely estimate four times.

**The three estimates and the derived quantities:**

| Quantity | Expression |
|---|---|
| **to — OPTIMISTIC time** | **If everything goes well; roughly a 1 per cent chance of being bettered** ← |
| **tm — MOST LIKELY time** | **The modal value; the duration that would occur most often** ← |
| **tp — PESSIMISTIC time** | **If things go badly; roughly a 1 per cent chance of being exceeded** ← |
| **EXPECTED time** | **te = (to + 4tm + tp) / 6** ← |
| **STANDARD DEVIATION** | **σ = (tp − to) / 6** ← |
| **VARIANCE** | **σ² = [(tp − to) / 6]²** ← |

> **THE SIXES IN THE LAST THREE ROWS COME FROM THE SAME ASSUMPTION AND KNOWING IT MAKES BOTH FORMULAE MEMORABLE: the activity duration is assumed to follow a BETA distribution, and the range from optimistic to pessimistic is taken to span about six standard deviations.**

> **That is why the standard deviation is the range divided by six.**

> **And the expected value formula is the beta distribution's mean, which weights the mode at four-sixths and each extreme at one-sixth.**

> **So both formulae follow from one distributional assumption, and the choice of the beta distribution is itself a convenience — it is bounded at both ends, which durations are, and it can be skewed, which they usually are.**

**THE SKEW IS THE FEATURE THAT MAKES THE THREE-ESTIMATE APPROACH WORTHWHILE AND IT IS WORTH SEEING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Activity durations are typically skewed to the RIGHT** ← | ← |
| **Because things can go badly wrong by a lot, and can only go well by a little** ← | ← |
| **So tp − tm is usually greater than tm − to** ← | ← |
| **Which makes te GREATER than tm** ← | ← |
| **So the expected duration exceeds the most likely one** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE INSIGHT THAT SINGLE-ESTIMATE PLANNING MISSES AND IT EXPLAINS A GREAT DEAL ABOUT WHY PROJECTS OVERRUN: a planner asked for one duration gives the most likely one.**

> **The most likely duration is shorter than the expected duration, because the distribution has a long right tail.**

> **So a programme built from most-likely estimates is systematically optimistic, activity by activity, before any other effect is considered.**

> **An illustration: to = 4, tm = 6, tp = 14 gives te = (4 + 24 + 14)/6 = 7 days, against a most likely 6 — a 17 per cent understatement from the skew alone, repeated across every activity in the programme.**

**THE PROJECT-LEVEL ANALYSIS IS WHERE PERT DELIVERS ITS DISTINCTIVE OUTPUT:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Compute te for every activity and find the critical path using those values** ← | ← |
| **The project's expected duration is the sum of te along the critical path** ← | ← |
| **The project's VARIANCE is the SUM of the variances of the critical activities** ← | **Variances add; standard deviations do not** ← |
| **The project's standard deviation is the square root of that sum** ← | ← |
| **And the probability of finishing by any given date follows from the normal distribution** ← | **By the central limit theorem, the sum of many activity durations tends to normal** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE RULE MOST OFTEN GOT WRONG AND IT IS WORTH STATING EMPHATICALLY: VARIANCES add along a path; standard deviations do NOT.**

> **So to combine three critical activities with standard deviations of 2, 3 and 6 days, square them to get variances of 4, 9 and 36, add to get 49, and take the square root to get 7 days.**

> **Adding the standard deviations directly would give 11 days, which substantially overstates the project's uncertainty.**

> **The underlying reason is that independent variations partly cancel — some activities run long while others run short — and the root-sum-square captures that cancellation, which is why the combined uncertainty is less than the sum of the parts.**
tags: beta distribution and the six sigma range
right skew makes te exceed tm

examTip.trick: **te = (to + 4tm + tp)/6**, and σ = (tp − to)/6 — both from the beta assumption that the range spans six standard deviations.
examTip.trap: **te exceeds tm because durations are right-skewed** — so a programme built from most-likely estimates is systematically optimistic.
examTip.mnemonic: **VARIANCES add along a path, standard deviations do not** — root-sum-square, because independent variations partly cancel.

questions.stem: CRASHING a project activity means:
options: Deliberately SHORTENING its duration by applying additional resources
Abandoning the activity because it cannot be completed
Combining two activities into one
Delaying the activity to smooth the resource demand
questions.solution:
**Deliberately SHORTENING its duration by applying additional resources — overtime, extra crews, more plant, or a faster method** — at an increased cost, in order to reduce the project's overall duration.

**The cost-time relationship for an activity:**

| Term | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **NORMAL time and NORMAL cost** ← | **The duration and cost at the most economical method** ← |
| **CRASH time and CRASH cost** ← | **The shortest achievable duration and its cost** ← |
| **COST SLOPE** | **= (crash cost − normal cost) ÷ (normal time − crash time)** ← |
| ** ** | **The extra cost per day saved** ← |

> **THE COST SLOPE IS THE QUANTITY THAT DRIVES EVERY CRASHING DECISION AND THE RULE THAT FOLLOWS IS SIMPLE: crash the CRITICAL activity with the LOWEST cost slope first.**

> **It buys a day of project time more cheaply than any other.**

> **Then recompute, because the critical path may have changed, and crash the next cheapest critical activity.**

> **Continue until the target duration is reached, or until the cost of saving another day exceeds the benefit of saving it — which is the economic stopping point rather than the technical one.**

**THE PROCEDURE MUST ACCOUNT FOR THE CRITICAL PATH SHIFTING AND THAT IS WHERE IT BECOMES SUBTLE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
