| **Crashing a critical activity shortens the critical path** ← | ← |
| **Eventually another path becomes critical too** ← | ← |
| **From then on, BOTH paths must be shortened to gain a day** ← | ← |
| **So the cost per day saved RISES as crashing proceeds** ← | ← |
| **And where the paths share an activity, crashing that one shortens both at once** ← | **Usually the cheapest option once multiple paths are critical** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE TACTICAL INSIGHT WORTH CARRYING AND IT IS EASILY MISSED: once two paths are critical, an activity common to both is worth twice as much as one on a single path.**

> **Crashing it by a day shortens both paths by a day, and the project by a day, for one activity's crash cost.**

> **Crashing two separate activities, one on each path, costs two crash payments for the same one day.**

> **So the shared activity's effective cost slope is halved, and looking for such activities is what distinguishes a competent crashing analysis from a mechanical one.**

**THE TOTAL COST CURVE IS THE POINT OF THE WHOLE EXERCISE AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING TREATMENT:**

| Component | Behaviour as duration shortens |
|---|---|
| **DIRECT costs — labour, materials, plant** ← | **RISE, because of the crashing** ← |
| **INDIRECT costs — preliminaries, supervision, overheads, financing** ← | **FALL, because the site is open for less time** ← |
| **Any bonus for early completion or penalty for lateness** ← | **Favours shortening** ← |
| **TOTAL cost** ← | **Falls, reaches a MINIMUM, then rises** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OPTIMUM AND IT IS WHY CRASHING IS NOT SIMPLY A COST TO BE AVOIDED: shortening a project saves the time-related preliminaries identified earlier, and those savings can exceed the crashing cost over a useful range.**

> **So there is an economically optimal duration that is SHORTER than the normal duration, and a project run at its normal duration is not at its cheapest.**

> **The minimum is found by crashing in order of cost slope and tracking the total, and it lies where the marginal crash cost equals the daily indirect cost saving.**

> **That is a genuinely useful result for a contractor: the question is not whether to accelerate but how far, and the answer is the point at which another day saved costs more than a day of preliminaries — which is a number the contractor knows and can apply directly.**
tags: crash the lowest slope critical activity first
optimum duration is shorter than normal

examTip.trick: **Shorten an activity with extra resources at extra cost** — measured by the cost slope, (crash − normal cost)/(normal − crash time).
examTip.trap: **Recompute the critical path after each crash** — once two paths are critical, both must be shortened to gain a day.
examTip.mnemonic: **An activity on TWO critical paths is worth double** — one crash payment shortens both. Look for shared activities.

questions.stem: RESOURCE LEVELLING (smoothing) of a project programme aims to:
options: Reduce the total quantity of resources required by the project
Allocate resources equally to every activity
Shorten the project by adding resources
Reduce the PEAKS and TROUGHS in resource demand by rescheduling activities within their available FLOAT
questions.solution:
**Reduce the PEAKS and TROUGHS in resource demand by rescheduling activities within their available FLOAT** — giving a more uniform requirement, without extending the project duration.

**Why a level resource profile is worth achieving:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **Hiring and releasing labour repeatedly is expensive and disruptive** ← | **Recruitment, training, redundancy, loss of experienced people** ← |
| **A peak demand determines the plant that must be available** ← | **Plant sized for a brief peak stands idle the rest of the time** ← |
| **Site accommodation, welfare and supervision are sized for the peak** ← | ← |
| **A uniform demand improves productivity through continuity** ← | **Crews that stay together and learn the work** ← |
| **And cash flow is smoother and more predictable** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS AN EFFECT THAT IS EASILY UNDERVALUED AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL: a crew that works continuously on similar operations becomes markedly faster at them.**

> **Breaking that continuity — standing them down and re-forming a crew later — loses the learning and incurs the start-up inefficiency again.**

> **So a levelled programme is not merely cheaper in resource terms but faster in productivity terms, and the two effects compound.**

> **That is why continuity of work is a planning objective in its own right, and why line-of-balance and location-based methods, which plan for continuous crew movement, often outperform a network programme that happens to satisfy its logic.**

**THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN LEVELLING AND SMOOTHING IS WORTH MAKING SINCE THE TERMS ARE USED LOOSELY:**

| Technique | Constraint | Consequence |
|---|---|---|
| **Resource SMOOTHING** ← | **The project DURATION is fixed** ← | **Activities move within their float only; the peak may not be fully eliminated** ← |
| **Resource LEVELLING** ← | **The resource LIMIT is fixed** ← | **The project duration may have to EXTEND to respect the limit** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE IS WHICH CONSTRAINT IS TREATED AS BINDING AND IT DETERMINES WHAT THE TECHNIQUE CAN DELIVER: smoothing takes the completion date as fixed and does the best it can with the resource profile.**

> **Levelling takes the available resource as fixed and accepts whatever completion date results.**

> **So if only six carpenters exist and the smoothed programme still needs nine at its peak, smoothing has failed and levelling is required — with a later completion as its output.**

> **Recognising which situation applies is the first step, and a planner who smooths when the resource is genuinely capped produces a programme that cannot be executed.**

**THE PRACTICAL PROCEDURE IS SIMPLE IN PRINCIPLE AND THE COMPLICATION IS WORTH NOTING:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Produce the early-start programme and plot the resource histogram** ← | ← |
| **2. Identify the peaks** ← | ← |
| **3. Shift non-critical activities later within their float** ← | **Critical activities cannot move** ← |
| **4. Re-plot and repeat** ← | ← |
| **5. Accept the best profile achievable** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD STEP IS WHERE THE PROBLEM BECOMES COMPUTATIONALLY HARD AND THAT IS WORTH KNOWING: with many activities and several resources, the number of possible schedules is enormous and there is no efficient algorithm guaranteeing the optimum.**

> **Software uses heuristics — rules such as 'delay the activity with the most float first' or 'prioritise the activity with the least float' — which give good results and not provably optimal ones.**

> **So two planning packages can produce different levelled programmes from the same inputs, and neither is wrong.**

> **The practical implication is that the levelled output should be reviewed by someone who understands the work rather than accepted as an optimisation — because the heuristic knows nothing about which sequences are sensible on site, and a mathematically level programme that requires a crew to move across the site four times is worse than a slightly peakier one that does not.**
tags: smoothing fixes duration levelling fixes resource

examTip.trick: **Reduce peaks and troughs by moving activities within their float** — a uniform demand, same completion date.
examTip.trap: **SMOOTHING fixes the duration; LEVELLING fixes the resource and may extend the duration** — know which constraint actually binds.
examTip.mnemonic: **Levelling algorithms are heuristics, not optima** — review the output, because a mathematically level plan may move crews absurdly.

questions.stem: An activity has an earliest start of day 12, a duration of 6 days, and a latest finish of day 25. Its total float is:
options: 13 days
7 days
6 days
19 days
questions.solution:
**7 days.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Earliest Finish = Earliest Start + Duration** | **12 + 6 = 18** ← |
| **Total float = Latest Finish − Earliest Finish** | **25 − 18 = 7 days** ← |

> **THE EQUIVALENT ROUTE THROUGH THE STARTS GIVES THE SAME ANSWER AND IS WORTH KNOWING AS A CHECK: Latest Start = Latest Finish − Duration = 25 − 6 = 19.**

> **Total float = Latest Start − Earliest Start = 19 − 12 = 7 days.**

> **The two routes must always agree, because both are measuring the same slack, and computing it both ways catches an arithmetic slip immediately.**

> **The distractor at 13 is 25 − 12, the difference between the latest finish and the earliest start — which is the total WINDOW available, not the float, because it includes the 6 days the activity actually needs.**

**WHAT THE ANSWER MEANS OPERATIONALLY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The activity needs 6 days and has a 13-day window** ← | **Days 12 to 25** ← |
| **So 7 days of that window are spare** ← | ← |
| **It can start any time between day 12 and day 19** ← | ← |
| **And the project completion is unaffected** ← | **Provided the float is not needed by others in its chain** ← |
| **It is NOT on the critical path, since its float is non-zero** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE CLEANEST WAY TO SEE THE DISTINCTION THE DISTRACTOR EXPLOITS: the WINDOW is 13 days and the WORK is 6 days, so the SLACK is 7 days.**

> **Window minus work equals float.**

> **Holding it in those words makes the formula unnecessary, and it makes the 13-day answer obviously wrong — 13 days of float for an activity whose window is only 13 days would mean the work took no time at all.**

> **That sense-check takes a moment and is more reliable than remembering which quantity is subtracted from which.**

**THE FULL SET OF NETWORK CALCULATIONS IS WORTH HAVING IN ORDER SINCE THIS IS ONE STEP OF IT:**

| Pass | Computes | Rule |
|---|---|---|
| **FORWARD pass, start to finish** ← | **Earliest Start and Earliest Finish** ← | **ES = the LATEST of the predecessors' EFs; EF = ES + duration** ← |
| **BACKWARD pass, finish to start** ← | **Latest Finish and Latest Start** ← | **LF = the EARLIEST of the successors' LSs; LS = LF − duration** ← |
| **Float calculation** ← | **Total and free float** ← | **As above** ← |

> **THE TWO 'LATEST' AND 'EARLIEST' RULES IN THE RIGHT-HAND COLUMN ARE THE ONES MOST OFTEN CONFUSED AND THE LOGIC IS WORTH STATING: on the forward pass, an activity cannot start until ALL its predecessors are done, so its ES is the latest of their EFs.**

> **On the backward pass, an activity must finish before the earliest of its successors must start, so its LF is the earliest of their LSs.**

> **Both rules take the binding constraint — the last predecessor and the first successor — and both follow from asking what actually limits the activity.**

> **Reasoning it out that way each time is more reliable than memorising 'latest on the forward, earliest on the backward', which is easy to invert under pressure.**
tags: latest of predecessors earliest of successors

examTip.trap: **13 is the WINDOW, not the float** — window minus work equals float, and 13 days of float in a 13-day window would mean zero duration.
examTip.mnemonic: **Forward pass takes the LATEST predecessor; backward pass the EARLIEST successor** — both take the binding constraint.

questions.stem: A BAR (GANTT) CHART is widely used for construction programming. Its principal limitation compared with a network diagram is that it:
options: Cannot show the duration of activities
Shows only the activities of the main contractor
Cannot be produced without specialist software
Does not explicitly show the LOGICAL DEPENDENCIES between activities
questions.solution:
**It does not explicitly show the LOGICAL DEPENDENCIES between activities** — so it cannot reveal which activities are critical, what the consequence of a delay is, or how the sequence must change if one activity slips.

**The two tools compared:**

| Aspect | BAR CHART | NETWORK |
|---|---|---|
| **Shows durations and dates** | **YES, directly and clearly** ← | **Yes, but less readably** ← |
| **Shows LOGIC and dependencies** | **NO, not inherently** ← | **YES — that is its purpose** ← |
| **Identifies the critical path** | **No** ← | **Yes** ← |
| **Shows the effect of a delay** | **No** ← | **Yes, by recalculation** ← |
| **Readability for non-specialists** | **EXCELLENT** ← | **Poor** ← |
| **Shows progress against plan** | **Excellent — a second bar or shading** ← | **Awkward** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS ARE WHY BAR CHARTS SURVIVE DESPITE THEIR ANALYTICAL LIMITATION AND IT IS A GENUINE ADVANTAGE RATHER THAN MERE INERTIA: anyone can read a bar chart.**

> **A foreman, a client, a subcontractor and a minister can all see what should be happening this month and whether it is.**

> **A network diagram communicates to planners and to almost nobody else.**

> **So the standard modern practice resolves the tension rather than choosing between them: build the programme as a NETWORK, analyse it for the critical path and float, and PRESENT it as a linked bar chart with the logic links drawn on and the critical path highlighted.**

**THAT LINKED BAR CHART IS THE PRACTICAL ANSWER AND IT IS WORTH DESCRIBING:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Bars showing each activity's duration and dates** ← | **The bar chart's readability** ← |
| **Arrows between bars showing the dependencies** ← | **The network's logic, made visible** ← |
| **The critical path highlighted, conventionally in red** ← | ← |
| **Float shown as a tail on each non-critical bar** ← | ← |
| **Progress shown by shading or a second bar** ← | ← |
| **A time-now line** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A PARTICULARLY USEFUL CONVENTION AND IT IS OFTEN OMITTED: drawing each activity's float as a thin tail after its bar shows at a glance how much slack each has.**

> **An activity with a long tail can slip without consequence; one with no tail cannot.**

> **So a manager scanning the chart sees immediately where attention is needed, without consulting a float table.**

> **That is a small presentational choice that converts the chart from a schedule into a management tool, and it costs nothing once the network calculation exists.**

**A CAUTION ABOUT BAR CHARTS PRODUCED WITHOUT UNDERLYING LOGIC DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS COMMON:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A bar chart drawn directly, without a network behind it, encodes no logic at all** ← | ← |
| **Its bars sit where the planner put them** ← | ← |
| **So when an activity slips, nothing recalculates** ← | ← |
| **The planner must work out the consequences by hand, and usually does not** ← | ← |
| **The programme then becomes a picture of intentions rather than a model of the project** ← | ← |

> **The fifth row describes the state of a great many construction programmes, and its symptom is recognisable: the programme is updated by moving bars to match what happened, without the completion date changing.**

> **A programme that absorbs every delay without its end date moving is not modelling anything.**

> **So the test of whether a programme is real is whether a delay to a critical activity produces a later completion date automatically — and if it does not, the programme is a drawing rather than a plan.**

> **That test is worth applying to any programme submitted for approval, because it takes one question to ask and it distinguishes a managed project from a documented one.**
tags: linked bar chart resolves the tension
a programme without logic is a picture

examTip.trick: **It does not show logical dependencies** — so no critical path, and no way to see a delay's consequences.
examTip.trap: **Its readability is a real advantage** — hence the standard answer: build as a network, present as a linked bar chart with the critical path highlighted.
examTip.mnemonic: **If a critical delay does not move the end date automatically, the programme is a drawing, not a plan.**

questions.stem: In a WORK BREAKDOWN STRUCTURE (WBS), the project is decomposed into:
options: A list of the trades and subcontractors involved
A chronological list of activities in the order they will be performed
A HIERARCHY of progressively smaller DELIVERABLES and work packages
A breakdown of the project's budget by cost centre
questions.solution:
**A HIERARCHY of progressively smaller DELIVERABLES and work packages** — each level a complete decomposition of the level above, with the lowest level small enough to be estimated, scheduled, assigned and controlled.

**The defining rules of a WBS:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is DELIVERABLE-oriented, not activity-oriented** ← | **It describes what will be produced, not what will be done** ← |
| **The 100 PER CENT RULE: each level contains ALL of the work of the level above** ← | **No more and no less** ← |
| **Elements are MUTUALLY EXCLUSIVE** ← | **No work appears in two places** ← |
| **Decomposition continues until packages are manageable** ← | **Estimable, schedulable, assignable to one responsible party** ← |
| **Each element has a unique CODE** ← | **1, 1.1, 1.1.1 and so on — the WBS code** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE WBS'S CENTRAL DISCIPLINE AND ITS VIOLATION IS THE COMMONEST FAULT: if the sum of the children does not equal the parent, work has been lost or double-counted.**

> **Lost work appears later as a surprise — something that must be done and was never estimated, scheduled or budgeted.**

> **Double-counted work inflates the estimate and confuses responsibility.**

> **So the 100 per cent rule is checked at every level, and the check is simply to ask whether these children, together, constitute the whole of their parent — which is a question anyone can answer and which catches omissions before they become claims.**

**THE WBS'S ROLE AS THE PROJECT'S ORGANISING SPINE IS ITS REAL VALUE AND IT DESERVES SETTING OUT:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **The basis of the COST estimate** ← | **Each package is estimated, and they sum to the project cost** ← |
| **The basis of the SCHEDULE** ← | **Activities are derived from packages** ← |
| **The basis of RESPONSIBILITY assignment** ← | **Each package has one owner — the responsibility assignment matrix** ← |
| **The basis of PROGRESS measurement and earned value** ← | ← |
| **The basis of RISK identification** ← | **Risks are identified package by package** ← |
| **And the common CODE linking all of them** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHAT MAKES THE WBS MORE THAN A LIST AND IT IS THE PRACTICAL POINT: because cost, schedule, responsibility and progress all reference the same code, they can be related to one another.**

> **A question like 'is package 3.2.4 over budget, behind schedule, and whose is it' has a single answer assembled from three systems that share an identifier.**

> **Without that common structure, the cost system, the programme and the organisation chart describe the project in three incompatible ways, and reconciling them is manual, slow and usually not done.**

> **So establishing the WBS early and using it consistently across every system is one of the highest-leverage organisational decisions on a project — and changing it midway is disruptive enough that it is effectively permanent, which makes getting it right at the outset worth real effort.**

**THE DISTINCTION IN THE FIRST ROW DESERVES A CLOSING ILLUSTRATION BECAUSE IT IS SUBTLE AND IMPORTANT:**

> **A deliverable-oriented element is 'Bridge deck' or 'Pier 2 foundation' — a thing that will exist.**

> **An activity-oriented element is 'Concreting' or 'Excavation' — something that will be done.**

> **The difference matters because a deliverable can be inspected and declared complete, while an activity spread across the whole project cannot.**

> **So 'Pier 2 foundation' is 100 per cent complete or it is not, and progress against it is meaningful — whereas 'Excavation', covering every excavation on the project, gives no basis for saying what has been achieved, and it is precisely the kind of element that allows a project to report 80 per cent complete for months.**
tags: the common code links cost schedule and responsibility

examTip.trick: **A hierarchy of deliverables and work packages** — each level a complete decomposition of the one above.
examTip.trap: **The 100 per cent rule** — the children must sum to the parent exactly, or work is lost or double-counted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Deliverables, not activities** — 'Pier 2 foundation' can be complete; 'Excavation' lets a project report 80% for months.

questions.stem: In EARNED VALUE analysis, a project has a Budgeted Cost of Work Scheduled (BCWS/PV) of Rs 10 million, a Budgeted Cost of Work Performed (BCWP/EV) of Rs 8 million and an Actual Cost of Work Performed (ACWP/AC) of Rs 9 million. The project is:
options: Ahead of schedule and under budget
On schedule and on budget
BEHIND schedule and OVER budget
Behind schedule but under budget
questions.solution:
**BEHIND schedule and OVER budget.**

**The computation:**

| Measure | Formula | Value | Interpretation |
|---|---|---|---|
| **Schedule Variance** | **SV = EV − PV** | **8 − 10 = −2 million** ← | **NEGATIVE — behind schedule** ← |
| **Cost Variance** | **CV = EV − AC** | **8 − 9 = −1 million** ← | **NEGATIVE — over budget** ← |
| **Schedule Performance Index** | **SPI = EV ÷ PV** | **8 ÷ 10 = 0.80** ← | **Below 1 — behind** ← |
| **Cost Performance Index** | **CPI = EV ÷ AC** | **8 ÷ 9 = 0.89** ← | **Below 1 — over budget** ← |

> **THE KEY TO EVERY EARNED VALUE CALCULATION IS THAT EV APPEARS IN BOTH FORMULAE AND IS ALWAYS THE FIRST TERM, which makes the two variances easy to reconstruct: EV minus PV for schedule, EV minus AC for cost.**

> **And in both cases NEGATIVE is bad and an index BELOW 1 is bad.**

> **So the whole system reduces to one rule — compare what you EARNED against what you PLANNED to earn, and against what you PAID — and the consistency of sign and direction means no separate conventions need remembering.**

> **The three quantities themselves are the thing to keep straight: PV is the budgeted cost of the work that SHOULD have been done, EV is the budgeted cost of the work ACTUALLY done, and AC is what that work actually COST.**

**THE INTERPRETATION IS WHERE THE METHOD EARNS ITS KEEP AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING OUT:**

| Observation | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **Rs 10 million of work was planned by now** ← | ← |
| **Only Rs 8 million of it has been achieved** ← | **Measured at BUDGET rates, so this is a genuine work shortfall** ← |
| **And that Rs 8 million of work cost Rs 9 million to do** ← | ← |
| **So the project is achieving 80 per cent of the planned rate** ← | ← |
| **And paying Rs 1.125 for every Rs 1 of work** ← | **1 ÷ 0.89** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE INSIGHT THAT MAKES EARNED VALUE SUPERIOR TO COMPARING SPENDING AGAINST BUDGET: measuring the work done at BUDGET rates separates the question of how much was achieved from how much it cost.**

> **A simple comparison of Rs 9 million spent against Rs 10 million planned suggests the project is underspent and therefore fine.**

> **Earned value reveals that only Rs 8 million of work was done, so the project is both behind and overspent — a completely different picture from the same two numbers plus one more.**

> **That is why EV is the crucial third quantity, and why a project tracking only budget against actual cost cannot tell the difference between being underspent because it is efficient and being underspent because it has done nothing.**

**THE FORECAST THAT FOLLOWS IS THE MOST USEFUL OUTPUT AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Forecast | Formula | Here |
|---|---|---|
| **Estimate At Completion** | **EAC = BAC ÷ CPI** | **If the total budget were Rs 40 million, EAC = 40 ÷ 0.89 = Rs 45 million** ← |
| **Variance At Completion** | **VAC = BAC − EAC** | **−Rs 5 million** ← |
| **To-Complete Performance Index** | **TCPI = (BAC − EV) ÷ (BAC − AC)** | **The efficiency now needed to finish on budget** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW EMBODIES AN ASSUMPTION WORTH EXAMINING RATHER THAN ACCEPTING: dividing the budget by the CPI assumes the efficiency achieved so far will continue for the rest of the project.**

> **Empirically that assumption holds remarkably well — a project's CPI tends to stabilise early and rarely improves substantially thereafter.**

> **So the forecast is more reliable than optimism suggests, and a project reporting that it will recover its overrun through future efficiency is making a claim that the evidence generally does not support.**

> **The third row makes that explicit: the TCPI states what efficiency the remaining work must achieve, and where that figure is far above the CPI achieved so far, the recovery plan is not credible — which is a quantitative test of a claim that would otherwise be a matter of assertion.**
tags: SV = EV - PV and CV = EV - AC

examTip.trick: **SV = 8 − 10 = −2 (behind); CV = 8 − 9 = −1 (over).** EV is the first term in both, and negative is always bad.
examTip.trap: **Spending Rs 9m against Rs 10m planned looks underspent** — until EV shows only Rs 8m of work was done. That third figure changes everything.
examTip.mnemonic: **EAC = BAC ÷ CPI, and CPI rarely improves** — so a claimed recovery through future efficiency is usually not credible. Test it with TCPI.

questions.stem: In precedence network notation, a FINISH-TO-START relationship with a LAG of 7 days between activity A and activity B means:
options: B must finish 7 days after A finishes
B cannot start until 7 days AFTER A has finished
A and B must both start within 7 days of each other
B must start 7 days before A finishes
questions.solution:
**B cannot start until 7 days AFTER A has finished** — the lag representing a necessary waiting period such as concrete curing, delivery time or ground settlement.

**The four precedence relationships:**

| Relationship | Meaning | Typical use |
|---|---|---|
| **FINISH to START (FS)** ← | **B starts after A finishes** ← | **The commonest; sequential work** ← |
| **START to START (SS)** ← | **B starts after A starts** ← | **Overlapping work — B can begin once A is under way** ← |
| **FINISH to FINISH (FF)** ← | **B finishes after A finishes** ← | **B cannot complete until A has** ← |
| **START to FINISH (SF)** ← | **B finishes after A starts** ← | **Rare — shift handovers and similar** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS TOGETHER ARE WHAT MAKE PRECEDENCE NOTATION MORE EXPRESSIVE THAN SIMPLE SEQUENCING AND THEY MODEL REAL CONSTRUCTION FAR BETTER: excavating and laying a pipe do not happen one after the other along a whole trench.**

> **Pipe-laying starts once excavation has progressed some distance — a start-to-start relationship with a lag — and finishes some time after excavation finishes, which is a finish-to-finish relationship with a lag.**

> **Using the two together models continuous overlapping operations properly, with both crews working simultaneously along the trench.**

> **Forcing that into finish-to-start relationships would require the trench to be divided into artificial sections, which clutters the network and misrepresents how the work is actually done.**

**THE LAG DESERVES CAREFUL TREATMENT BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN MISUSED:**

| Legitimate use | Questionable use |
|---|---|
| **A physical waiting period — curing, drying, settlement, testing** ← | **Padding to make the programme fit a desired date** ← |
| **A procurement or delivery lead time** ← | **Concealing an activity that should be shown explicitly** ← |
| **An overlap allowance in an SS or FF relationship** ← | **Representing a resource constraint as though it were logic** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW OF THE RIGHT-HAND COLUMN IS THE MOST COMMON ABUSE AND IT DAMAGES THE PROGRAMME'S USEFULNESS: a 14-day lag representing a procurement period hides a real activity.**

> **Procurement has a start, a duration, a responsible party and a risk of delay, and none of those are visible in a lag.**

> **Shown as an activity, it can be tracked, expedited and reported on.**

> **Shown as a lag, it is invisible until it fails — so the rule is that anything that could go wrong, that someone is responsible for, or that could be accelerated should be an ACTIVITY, and a lag should represent only an unavoidable passage of time that nobody controls.**

> **THE THIRD ROW'S POINT ABOUT RESOURCE CONSTRAINTS IS SUBTLER AND EQUALLY IMPORTANT: if B follows A only because the same crew does both, that is a RESOURCE constraint, not a logical one.**

> **Encoding it as a logical dependency makes the network say that B cannot physically start until A ends, which is untrue.**

> **So if the crew is later doubled, the network will not permit the acceleration that is in fact available, and the planner must go back and edit logic that should never have been there.**

> **The correct treatment is to model the logic as it truly is and to handle the crew limitation through resource levelling — which keeps the two kinds of constraint separate and means the programme remains valid when the resources change.**
tags: SS and FF model overlapping work

examTip.trick: **B starts 7 days after A finishes** — the lag is a required waiting period such as curing or delivery.
examTip.trap: **SS and FF with lags model overlapping work properly** — pipe-laying following excavation along a trench, both crews working at once.
examTip.mnemonic: **If it can go wrong or be accelerated, make it an ACTIVITY, not a lag** — and never encode a resource constraint as logic.

questions.stem: A DUMMY ACTIVITY in an activity-on-arrow network is used to:
options: Represent an activity whose duration is not yet known
Show a waiting period between two activities
Maintain the correct LOGICAL RELATIONSHIPS
Indicate an activity that has been cancelled
questions.solution:
**Maintain the correct LOGICAL RELATIONSHIPS, or to give two concurrent activities unique start and end event numbers** — consuming no time and no resources.

**The two distinct purposes:**

| Purpose | Note |
|---|---|
| **LOGIC dummy** ← | **Where activity C depends on both A and B, but D depends on A only — a dependency that cannot be drawn without it** ← |
| **IDENTITY (grammatical) dummy** ← | **Where two activities share the same start and end events, which would give them identical i-j identifiers** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A LIMITATION OF THE NOTATION RATHER THAN OF THE PROJECT AND IT IS WORTH RECOGNISING AS SUCH: in activity-on-arrow notation, an activity is identified by its start and end event numbers.**

> **So two activities running between the same pair of events would both be '4-7', which is ambiguous.**

> **A dummy is inserted to give one of them a different end event, restoring unique identification.**

> **That has nothing to do with the project's logic and everything to do with the drawing convention, which is why the whole class of dummy disappears in activity-on-node notation — where each activity is a box with its own identity and no such ambiguity can arise.**

**THE ACTIVITY-ON-NODE NOTATION HAS LARGELY SUPERSEDED ARROW DIAGRAMS AND THE REASONS ARE WORTH KNOWING:**

| Aspect | Activity on ARROW | Activity on NODE (precedence) |
|---|---|---|
| **Activities are** | **Arrows between numbered events** ← | **Boxes, with arrows showing dependencies** ← |
| **Dummies** | **REQUIRED, for both purposes above** ← | **Not needed at all** ← |
| **Relationship types** | **Finish-to-start only** ← | **FS, SS, FF, SF, with lags** ← |
| **Events** | **Explicit and numbered** ← | **Implicit** ← |
| **Ease of drawing and editing** | **Harder — adding an activity may renumber events** ← | **Easy** ← |
| **Current usage** | **Largely historical; still examined** ← | **Universal in software** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE DECISIVE PRACTICAL ADVANTAGE AND IT CONNECTS TO THE PREVIOUS MATERIAL: arrow diagrams can express only finish-to-start logic, so overlapping operations must be modelled by artificially subdividing activities.**

> **Precedence notation expresses the overlap directly with a start-to-start relationship and a lag.**

> **Since real construction is full of overlapping continuous operations, that expressiveness matters a great deal.**

> **So the shift from arrow to node notation was driven by the need to model real work rather than by any preference of drawing style, and the dummy activity is a historical artefact of a notation that could not do so.**

**THE CLASSIC DUMMY SITUATION IS WORTH SETTING OUT SINCE IT IS THE STANDARD EXAMINATION QUESTION:**

| Requirement | Note |
|---|---|
| **Activity C depends on BOTH A and B** ← | ← |
| **Activity D depends on A ONLY** ← | ← |
| **Drawing A and B into a common event, with C and D out of it, wrongly makes D depend on B** ← | ← |
| **The solution: A ends at event 3, B ends at event 4, a DUMMY runs from 3 to 4** ← | ← |
| **C starts from event 4 — so it waits for both** ← | ← |
| **D starts from event 3 — so it waits for A only** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH TO SIXTH ROWS ARE THE CONSTRUCTION AND THE DUMMY'S DIRECTION IS THE PART THAT MUST BE RIGHT: the dummy runs from the event that must be reached first toward the activity that needs both.**

> **Reversing it makes B depend on A rather than C depend on both, which is a different network entirely.**

> **So the test is to read each activity's dependencies back off the finished diagram and check them against the requirement, one by one.**

> **That check takes moments and it catches the reversed dummy, which is by far the commonest error in drawing such networks — and it is worth doing because a reversed dummy produces a network that computes cleanly and answers the wrong question.**
tags: check dependencies back off the diagram

examTip.trick: **To preserve correct logic, or to give concurrent activities unique i-j numbers** — zero duration, zero resources.
examTip.trap: **The identity dummy is a limitation of the NOTATION, not of the project** — it vanishes entirely in activity-on-node.
examTip.mnemonic: **Read the dependencies back off the finished diagram** — a reversed dummy computes cleanly and answers the wrong question.

questions.stem: The LINE OF BALANCE technique is particularly suited to projects that involve:
options: REPETITIVE work
A single complex one-off structure
Projects with highly uncertain activity durations
Projects with only a few activities
questions.solution:
**REPETITIVE work — a series of identical or similar units such as housing units, bridge spans, or successive kilometres of road** — where the objective is to keep each crew working CONTINUOUSLY as it moves from unit to unit.

**Why network methods serve repetitive work poorly:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A network of 50 identical houses has 50 copies of every activity** ← | **Enormous and unreadable** ← |
| **The network's objective is to satisfy the LOGIC, not to keep crews busy** ← | ← |
| **So a network-optimal schedule may leave a crew idle between units** ← | ← |
| **Which is precisely what a repetitive project must avoid** ← | ← |
| **Line of balance instead plans for CONTINUOUS crew working** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE A MISMATCH OF OBJECTIVES RATHER THAN A DEFECT IN THE METHOD, AND THAT IS THE POINT: critical path analysis minimises the project's duration subject to the logic.**

> **Repetitive construction's dominant cost driver is crew continuity, because a crew stood down and re-mobilised loses its learning and its productivity.**

> **So the right objective is a schedule in which every crew moves steadily from unit to unit without waiting, even if that means the project takes slightly longer.**

> **Line of balance optimises for that directly, which is why it outperforms network methods on this class of work despite being the older and simpler technique.**

**THE DIAGRAM AND WHAT IT SHOWS:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **The horizontal axis is TIME** ← | ← |
| **The vertical axis is the UNIT number, or location, or chainage** ← | ← |
| **Each activity is a SLOPING LINE** ← | **Its slope is the rate of progress — units per week** ← |
| **PARALLEL lines mean crews progressing at the same rate** ← | **The ideal — the gap between them stays constant** ← |
| **CONVERGING lines mean a following crew is catching up** ← | **They will collide, so a buffer or a rate change is needed** ← |
| **DIVERGING lines mean the gap is opening** ← | **Wasteful, but not a clash** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS CONTAIN THE DIAGRAM'S CENTRAL INSIGHT AND IT IS VISUAL RATHER THAN COMPUTATIONAL: whether two trades will interfere is visible at a glance from whether their lines converge.**

> **Two lines that converge will meet, and at that point the second crew arrives at a unit the first has not finished.**

> **A network of the same project contains that information and buries it in hundreds of activities, where nobody sees it until it happens on site.**

> **So the line of balance diagram's value is diagnostic — it makes the rate relationships between trades immediately apparent, and rate relationships are exactly what govern a repetitive project.**

**THE DESIGN VARIABLE IS THE RATE OF WORKING AND THAT IS WHAT THE TECHNIQUE ADJUSTS:**

| Adjustment | Effect |
|---|---|
| **Change a crew's SIZE, or add a second crew** ← | **Changes the slope of that activity's line** ← |
| **The aim is to make all the lines PARALLEL** ← | **All trades progressing at the same rate** ← |
| **The common rate is set by the project's required delivery rate** ← | **Or by the slowest trade that cannot be accelerated** ← |
| **And buffers are inserted between trades** ← | **So a minor delay in one does not immediately stop the next** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE OBJECTIVE AND IT IS A DIFFERENT KIND OF PLANNING FROM NETWORK SCHEDULING: the planner is choosing crew sizes so that every trade advances at the same pace, like a production line.**

> **A trade that is faster than the others is not an advantage — it simply runs ahead and then waits, which is the discontinuity the technique exists to prevent.**

> **So resources are adjusted DOWN as well as up, which is counter-intuitive to anyone trained to think of more resources as better.**

> **That production-line thinking is the conceptual contribution of the method, and it is why line of balance and its modern descendants — location-based management and takt planning — have been rediscovered as construction has borrowed more from manufacturing.**
tags: sloping lines show rate of progress
balance the rates like a production line

examTip.trick: **Repetitive units, with crews moving continuously from one to the next** — housing, spans, kilometres of road.
examTip.trap: **A network optimises the LOGIC; line of balance optimises CREW CONTINUITY** — different objectives, and continuity dominates repetitive work.
examTip.mnemonic: **Converging lines mean a collision is coming** — visible at a glance, and buried in hundreds of activities in a network.

questions.stem: A project has activities on its critical path with durations of 5, 8, 12 and 6 days, and a parallel non-critical path of 4, 9 and 7 days. The project duration and the total float on the parallel path are:
options: 31 days and 20 days
31 days and 11 days
20 days and 11 days
51 days and 0 days
questions.solution:
**31 days and 11 days.**

**The computation:**

| Step | Working |
|---|---|
| **Critical path length** | **5 + 8 + 12 + 6 = 31 days** ← |
| **Parallel path length** | **4 + 9 + 7 = 20 days** ← |
| **Project duration** | **The LONGEST path = 31 days** ← |
| **Total float on the parallel path** | **31 − 20 = 11 days** ← |

> **THE FLOAT ON A PARALLEL PATH IS SIMPLY THE DIFFERENCE BETWEEN THE TWO PATH LENGTHS, WHICH IS WORTH SEEING DIRECTLY: the parallel path must be complete by the time the critical path is, and it needs only 20 of the 31 days available.**

> **So 11 days are spare, and that 11 days is the TOTAL float shared among all three activities on that path.**

> **It is not 11 days each — if the first activity consumes all 11, the other two have none.**

> **That is the shared-float property established earlier, and it is why the answer is a property of the path rather than of any individual activity on it.**

**THE DISTRACTORS ARE EACH A RECOGNISABLE CONFUSION:**

| Option | The error |
|---|---|
| **31 and 20** | **Quoting the parallel path's LENGTH as its float** ← |
| **20 and 11** | **Taking the SHORTER path as the project duration** ← |
| **51 and 0** | **Adding both paths together, as though they were sequential** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST FUNDAMENTAL MISUNDERSTANDING AND IT IS WORTH NAMING: parallel paths run SIMULTANEOUSLY, so their durations do not add.**

> **The project takes as long as its longest path, not as long as all its work would take end to end.**

> **The second row's error is the opposite — taking the shortest path — and it fails the basic test that a project cannot finish before all its work is done.**

> **So both wrong durations can be rejected by asking whether the answer is at least as long as the longest single path and no longer than the sum of everything, which bounds the answer between 31 and 51 and leaves only one candidate.**

**AN IMPORTANT QUALIFICATION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT LIMITS THIS TIDY RESULT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **This calculation assumes the two paths are genuinely INDEPENDENT** ← | **Diverging at the start and converging at the end, with no links between** ← |
| **Real networks usually have cross-links between paths** ← | ← |
| **A cross-link can reduce the float on part of the parallel path** ← | ← |
| **So path-length subtraction gives the right answer only for a simple parallel structure** ← | ← |
| **In general, float must be computed activity by activity from the forward and backward passes** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE HONEST LIMIT OF THE SHORTCUT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING WHEN IT APPLIES: two paths sharing only their start and end events can be compared by length.**

> **The moment an activity on one path feeds an activity on the other, the simple subtraction breaks down, because the cross-link imposes a constraint that the path lengths do not capture.**

> **So the shortcut is a legitimate examination technique for a simple structure and an unreliable habit on a real network.**

> **The general method — forward pass, backward pass, float as the difference — always works, and it is worth doing that way on anything with cross-links rather than trusting a comparison of totals.**
tags: critical path and float from path lengths
project duration is the longest path

examTip.trick: **Longest path 31 days; parallel path 20 days; float = 31 − 20 = 11 days** shared along that path.
examTip.trap: **51 adds the parallel paths as if sequential** — they run simultaneously. The answer must lie between the longest path and the total.
examTip.mnemonic: **Path subtraction works only without cross-links** — otherwise compute float activity by activity from the two passes.

questions.stem: A project's S-CURVE plots cumulative cost or progress against time. Its characteristic shape arises because:
options: Work proceeds SLOWLY at first during mobilisation and setting up
Costs are always highest at the beginning of a project
The curve is drawn that way by convention regardless of the actual data
Inflation causes costs to rise exponentially
questions.solution:
**Work proceeds SLOWLY at first during mobilisation and setting up, ACCELERATES as full production is reached, and slows again during completion and finishing** — giving a shallow-steep-shallow curve.

**The three phases and why each behaves as it does:**

| Phase | Rate | Reason |
|---|---|---|
| **EARLY** ← | **Slow** ← | **Mobilisation, site establishment, few trades on site, learning, early design queries** ← |
| **MIDDLE** ← | **FAST** ← | **Full production, all trades working, methods established, learning complete** ← |
| **LATE** ← | **Slow** ← | **Finishing trades, snagging, commissioning, many small items, trades demobilising** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PHASE MOST CONSISTENTLY UNDERESTIMATED AND IT IS WHERE PROJECTS MOST OFTEN OVERRUN: the last 10 per cent of the value routinely takes 20 or 30 per cent of the time.**

> **Finishing work is fragmented — a great many small items in many places, each needing a different trade, each dependent on others being complete.**

> **Coordination cost per unit of value rises sharply, and the productivity that characterised the middle phase is unavailable.**

> **So a programme that assumes the middle-phase rate continues to completion will finish late, and a manager watching a project that is ahead at 70 per cent complete should not conclude that it will finish early.**

**THE S-CURVE'S USES IN PROJECT CONTROL:**

| Use | Note |
|---|---|
| **Forecasting the CASH FLOW requirement over time** ← | **For both the employer and the contractor** ← |
| **Comparing ACTUAL cumulative progress against planned** ← | **The gap between the curves is the variance** ← |
| **Early WARNING of a developing shortfall** ← | **A divergence that grows is more informative than any single reading** ← |
| **Establishing the planned value curve for earned value analysis** ← | **The PV line is precisely this curve** ← |
| **Judging whether a claimed recovery is plausible** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A PARTICULARLY USEFUL APPLICATION AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT: a contractor behind at the 60 per cent point who forecasts recovery by completion is proposing to work at a rate faster than the planned peak.**

> **The S-curve shows whether that is credible — the remaining work must be done on a steeper slope than the middle phase achieved, in the finishing phase, when the rate naturally falls.**

> **Drawing the proposed recovery curve alongside the original makes the implausibility visible immediately.**

> **So the curve turns an argument about optimism into a comparison of slopes, which is a far more productive conversation and one that can be had without accusing anyone of anything.**

**A CAUTION ABOUT READING THE CURVE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A cost S-curve and a PROGRESS S-curve are not the same thing** ← | ← |
| **Money can be spent without progress being made** ← | **Materials on site, advance payments, mobilisation** ← |
| **And progress can be made without cost being incurred yet** ← | **Work done and not yet paid for** ← |
| **So the two curves diverge, and each tells a different story** ← | ← |
| **Plotting both, alongside the earned value, is what reveals the truth** ← | ← |

> **The fifth row returns to the earned value point made earlier and it is the same lesson from a different direction: the planned curve, the actual cost curve and the earned value curve are three different lines.**

> **Where the actual cost is above the planned and the earned value below both, the project is overspending and under-delivering, which is the worst case.**

> **Where the actual cost is below the planned and the earned value tracks the plan, the project is efficient.**

> **Only the three curves together distinguish those situations, and a report showing expenditure against budget alone — which is the commonest form of project reporting — cannot.**
tags: the last 10 per cent takes disproportionate time

examTip.trick: **Slow mobilisation, fast full production, slow finishing** — the shallow-steep-shallow shape.
examTip.trap: **The last 10% of value takes 20-30% of the time** — fragmented finishing work. Being ahead at 70% does not predict an early finish.
examTip.mnemonic: **Draw the proposed recovery curve against the original** — it turns an argument about optimism into a comparison of slopes.

questions.stem: A MILESTONE in a project programme is:
options: An activity of particularly long duration
The physical marker placed at each kilometre of a road
A SIGNIFICANT EVENT of zero duration marking the achievement of a defined state
The point at which half the project's work is complete
questions.solution:
**A SIGNIFICANT EVENT of zero duration marking the achievement of a defined state** — the completion of a phase, a handover, an approval, or the start of a key operation — used for reporting and often tied to payment or contractual obligations.

**The characteristics of a good milestone:**

| Characteristic | Note |
|---|---|
| **ZERO duration — it is an event, not a task** ← | ← |
| **UNAMBIGUOUS — it has either been achieved or it has not** ← | **No partial achievement** ← |
| **VERIFIABLE — someone can confirm it objectively** ← | ← |
| **SIGNIFICANT — it marks something a stakeholder cares about** ← | ← |
| **Few in number** ← | **A programme with fifty milestones has none** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE PROPERTY THAT GIVES MILESTONES THEIR VALUE AND IT DISTINGUISHES THEM FROM PERCENTAGE REPORTING: an activity can be reported as 80 per cent complete more or less indefinitely.**

> **A milestone cannot be 80 per cent achieved.**

> **So a programme reported by milestones is far harder to misrepresent than one reported by percentages, and that resistance to optimistic reporting is the main reason milestones are used for external reporting and for payment.**

> **Which in turn means a milestone must be defined precisely enough that its achievement is not arguable — 'foundations complete' is weak, and 'all foundations concreted, cured and accepted by the engineer' is not.**

**MILESTONE PAYMENTS ARE A DISTINCT CONTRACTUAL ARRANGEMENT AND THEY DESERVE COMPARISON:**

| Payment basis | Note |
|---|---|
| **MEASURED work, valued monthly** ← | **The traditional arrangement; the contractor is paid for what has been measured** ← |
| **MILESTONE payments** ← | **A defined sum on achieving a defined state** ← |
| **The difference in risk** ← | **Milestone payment transfers cash flow risk to the CONTRACTOR** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE COMMERCIAL CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS SUBSTANTIAL: under milestone payment, a contractor who is 90 per cent of the way to a milestone receives nothing.**

> **They have funded all of that work and will continue to fund it until the milestone is achieved.**

> **That is a heavy cash flow burden, and it is priced — a contract with widely spaced milestones will be tendered higher than one with monthly measurement, all else being equal.**

> **Its advantage to the employer is simplicity and a strong incentive to complete rather than to start many things, and the balance between those effects is what determines whether the arrangement is worth its price.**

**THE DANGER OF POORLY CHOSEN MILESTONES DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS A REAL BEHAVIOURAL EFFECT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **What is measured is what gets managed** ← | ← |
| **So work leading to a milestone is prioritised** ← | ← |
| **And work that leads to none is deferred** ← | ← |
| **Even where the deferred work is on the critical path** ← | ← |
| **So milestones must be chosen to reflect the project's real structure** ← | **Not merely its visible achievements** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW DESCRIBES A GENUINE PERVERSE OUTCOME AND IT IS WORTH GUARDING AGAINST: a contractor paid on milestones will rationally direct resources to whatever unlocks the next payment.**

> **If an unglamorous but critical activity — a diversion, a service relocation, a long-lead procurement — sits between milestones and attracts no payment, it may be starved of attention while a visible milestone is chased.**

> **The project then reaches its milestone on time and is delayed afterwards by the neglected work.**

> **So milestone selection is an exercise in incentive design as much as in reporting, and the test to apply is whether achieving every milestone on time would actually deliver the project on time — which is not automatic and is worth checking explicitly against the critical path.**
tags: milestone payments transfer cash flow risk

examTip.trick: **A zero-duration event marking a defined, verifiable state** — used for reporting and often tied to payment.
examTip.trap: **A milestone cannot be 80% achieved** — which is exactly why it resists the optimistic reporting that percentages invite.
examTip.mnemonic: **Check that hitting every milestone would actually deliver on time** — otherwise critical work between milestones gets starved.

questions.stem: CONCURRENT DELAY in a construction contract arises when:
options: Two contractors are working on the same site at the same time
An activity is delayed on two separate occasions
A delay occurs at the same time as an acceleration
Two or more delay events
questions.solution:
**Two or more delay events, one the employer's responsibility and one the contractor's, occur over the SAME period and each would independently have delayed completion** — raising the question of who bears the consequences.

**Why concurrency is legally and practically difficult:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An EMPLOYER delay normally entitles the contractor to an extension of time AND to loss and expense** ← | ← |
| **A CONTRACTOR delay normally entitles the employer to liquidated damages** ← | ← |
| **When both occur together, the entitlements conflict** ← | ← |
| **Neither party can say the other's delay alone caused the overrun** ← | ← |
| **Because either would have caused it independently** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE LOGICAL DIFFICULTY AT THE HEART OF THE PROBLEM AND IT IS GENUINELY HARD RATHER THAN MERELY CONTESTED: causation normally asks whether the outcome would have occurred but for the event.**

> **With true concurrency, the answer for each event separately is yes — the delay would have occurred anyway because of the other.**

> **So the 'but for' test fails for both events simultaneously, and some other rule is needed.**

> **That is why concurrency generates so much litigation: it is not that the law is unclear about a simple question, but that the standard test genuinely does not resolve the situation.**

**THE APPROACHES THAT HAVE DEVELOPED ARE WORTH KNOWING:**

| Approach | Outcome |
|---|---|
| **The MALMAISON approach** ← | **The contractor gets the EXTENSION OF TIME but NOT the loss and expense** ← |
| ** ** | **So neither party pays the other — time is granted, money is not** ← |
| **APPORTIONMENT** ← | **The delay is divided between the parties on some rational basis** ← |
| ** ** | **Used in Scotland; rarely elsewhere** ← |
| **The DOMINANT CAUSE approach** ← | **The more significant cause governs entirely** ← |
| ** ** | **Attractive in principle, hard to apply where causes are genuinely equal** ← |
| **Contractual allocation** ← | **Many modern contracts simply STATE the rule to be applied** ← |

> **THE FIRST APPROACH IS THE MOST WIDELY FOLLOWED AND ITS LOGIC IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the contractor is relieved of liquidated damages because the employer's delay would have caused the overrun anyway.**

> **But the contractor cannot recover its prolongation costs, because its own delay would have caused it to incur them regardless.**

> **So each party bears its own consequences, which is a defensible and roughly symmetrical outcome.**

> **The last row is the practical answer for anyone drafting a contract: state the rule in advance, because litigating it afterwards costs both parties far more than accepting whichever rule was written down.**

**THE PRACTICAL DEFENCE AGAINST CONCURRENCY DISPUTES DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE AND IT IS ABOUT RECORDS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Concurrency is established or refuted by CONTEMPORANEOUS RECORDS** ← | ← |
| **A properly maintained and regularly updated programme** ← | **Showing what was critical when** ← |
| **Daily site records, progress photographs, labour and plant returns** ← | ← |
| **Prompt written NOTICES of delay events as they occur** ← | **Usually a contractual precondition to any entitlement** ← |
| **Without these, the analysis becomes a reconstruction argued years later** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE REQUIREMENT MOST OFTEN FATAL TO AN OTHERWISE GOOD CLAIM AND IT IS PURELY PROCEDURAL: most contracts require notice of a delay event within a defined period, and make that notice a condition of entitlement.**

> **A contractor genuinely delayed by the employer, who did not give notice in time, may lose the entitlement entirely regardless of the merits.**

> **That seems harsh and it has a purpose — timely notice lets the employer take action to mitigate, which is impossible if they learn of the delay a year later.**

> **So the discipline of issuing notices promptly is worth far more than the quality of the claim assembled afterwards, and it is the single most valuable contractual habit a site engineer can acquire.**
tags: state the rule in the contract

examTip.trick: **Two delays over the same period, one each party's responsibility, each sufficient alone** — so the entitlements conflict.
examTip.trap: **The 'but for' test fails for BOTH events** — which is why this generates litigation rather than having an obvious answer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Malmaison: time granted, money not** — each party bears its own consequences. And give NOTICE in time or lose the entitlement regardless of merit.

questions.stem: In construction planning, the LOOK-AHEAD PROGRAMME (typically covering the next 3 to 6 weeks) serves to:
options: Replace the master programme for contractual purposes
Bridge between the master programme and the work actually about to be done
Record what was achieved in the preceding weeks
Provide the basis for the final account
questions.solution:
**Bridge between the master programme and the work actually about to be done** — breaking the coming weeks' work into detail, identifying and removing CONSTRAINTS in advance, and ensuring that what is promised can actually be executed.

**The planning hierarchy and what each level does:**

| Level | Horizon | Purpose |
|---|---|---|
| **MASTER programme** ← | **The whole project** ← | **Contractual dates, milestones, overall strategy** ← |
| **PHASE or stage programme** ← | **A few months** ← | **Coordinating a phase, worked out with the trades involved** ← |
| **LOOK-AHEAD programme** ← | **3 to 6 weeks** ← | **Making work READY — removing constraints before it is due** ← |
| **WEEKLY work plan** ← | **1 week** ← | **Commitments to what will actually be done** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S FUNCTION — MAKING WORK READY — IS THE DISTINCTIVE CONTRIBUTION AND IT IS WORTH SPELLING OUT: an activity on the master programme is due in five weeks.**

> **The look-ahead asks what must be true for it to proceed: is the design issued, the material ordered, the permit obtained, the preceding work complete, the crew available, the access clear?**

> **Each of those is a CONSTRAINT, and each has an owner and a date by which it must be removed.**

> **So the look-ahead's output is not a schedule but a list of constraints to be cleared, and the schedule follows from clearing them — which inverts the usual relationship between planning and doing.**

**THE CONSTRAINT CATEGORIES ARE WORTH LISTING SINCE THE CHECKLIST IS THE TECHNIQUE:**

| Constraint | Question |
|---|---|
| **DESIGN and information** ← | **Is the drawing issued, the query answered, the detail resolved?** ← |
| **MATERIALS** ← | **Ordered, delivered, on site, accepted?** ← |
| **LABOUR** ← | **Crew available, skilled, briefed?** ← |
| **EQUIPMENT** ← | **Plant available, serviced, operator present?** ← |
| **PRECEDING work** ← | **Complete and accepted?** ← |
| **SPACE and access** ← | **Area available, free of other trades, safe?** ← |
| **EXTERNAL** ← | **Permits, approvals, utility shutdowns, weather windows?** ← |

> **THE SEVEN CATEGORIES ARE A CHECKLIST THAT CAN BE RUN THROUGH IN MINUTES FOR EACH UPCOMING ACTIVITY, AND THAT SPEED IS WHY THE TECHNIQUE WORKS IN PRACTICE: the value lies not in any sophistication but in asking the questions before the crew arrives rather than after.**

> **An activity that cannot proceed because a drawing is missing wastes a crew's day and disrupts everything around it.**

> **The same missing drawing identified three weeks earlier is a routine request that is answered in time.**

> **So the look-ahead converts a series of on-the-day failures into a manageable list of advance actions, which is a large improvement for very little effort.**

**THE WEEKLY WORK PLAN'S DISCIPLINE COMPLETES THE SYSTEM AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Rule | Note |
|---|---|
| **Only work with ALL constraints removed may be committed to** ← | **A promise, not a hope** ← |
| **The commitments are made BY the people who will do the work** ← | **Not imposed on them** ← |
| **Performance is measured as PERCENT PLAN COMPLETE** ← | **Commitments met ÷ commitments made** ← |
| **And the REASONS for non-completion are recorded and analysed** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHERE THE SYSTEM IMPROVES OVER TIME AND IT IS THE PART MOST OFTEN OMITTED: recording why a commitment was missed builds a picture of the recurring causes.**

> **If a third of failures are due to late information, that is a design management problem and it can be addressed.**

> **If they are due to preceding trades running late, that is a coordination problem.**

> **Without the reasons, the percent plan complete is a score rather than a diagnosis — and the point of measuring it is to find and fix the causes, not to report a number, which is a distinction that determines whether the system produces improvement or merely paperwork.**
tags: making work ready by removing constraints

examTip.trick: **Bridge between the master programme and the work about to start** — identifying and clearing constraints in advance.
examTip.trap: **Its output is a CONSTRAINT list, not a schedule** — design, materials, labour, equipment, preceding work, space, external approvals.
examTip.mnemonic: **Record WHY commitments were missed** — percent plan complete is a diagnosis, not a score. Without reasons it is only paperwork.

questions.stem: A project's programme should be updated during construction principally in order to:
options: Demonstrate to the client that the project is on schedule
Satisfy an administrative requirement of the contract
Provide a record for the final account
Maintain an accurate FORECAST of the remaining work
questions.solution:
**Maintain an accurate FORECAST of the remaining work** — so that the current critical path, the effect of what has already happened, and the actions needed to recover or to re-plan are all known while there is still time to act.

**What a proper update involves:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Record ACTUAL start and finish dates for completed activities** ← | ← |
| **Record actual progress and REMAINING DURATION for activities in progress** ← | **Remaining duration, not percentage complete** ← |
| **Revise the durations of future activities in the light of experience** ← | **If the first ten piles took twice as long as planned, so will the rest** ← |
| **Revise the LOGIC where the method has changed** ← | ← |
| **Recalculate — producing a new critical path and a new completion date** ← | ← |
| **Compare against the baseline and report the variance** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS A DISTINCTION THAT MATTERS MORE THAN IT APPEARS TO: an activity should be updated by its REMAINING DURATION, not by a percentage complete.**

> **'Sixty per cent complete' on a ten-day activity implies four days remain, and that inference is often wrong — the remaining 40 per cent may be the difficult part, or the crew may have been withdrawn.**

> **Asking 'how many more days do you need' gets the information directly from the person who knows, and it is the figure the calculation actually requires.**

> **So the update question is 'when will it finish', not 'how much is done' — and the two produce different programmes from the same site.**

**THE THIRD ROW IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN SKIPPED AND IT IS WHERE UPDATES LOSE THEIR VALUE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Updating actual dates and leaving future durations untouched is a partial update** ← | ← |
| **It shows what has happened and forecasts the future using the original assumptions** ← | ← |
| **Those assumptions have just been shown to be wrong** ← | **By the activities that overran** ← |
| **So the forecast is known to be optimistic and is presented anyway** ← | ← |
| **Which is how a programme shows recovery that will not occur** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW DESCRIBES THE COMMONEST PATHOLOGY IN CONSTRUCTION PROGRAMMING AND IT IS RECOGNISABLE FROM THE OUTSIDE: each monthly update shows the project a little further behind and still finishing on the contract date.**

> **The delay is absorbed by an assumed future acceleration that never materialises, and the completion date holds until it suddenly cannot.**

> **The test is whether the programme's forecast productivity for future work is consistent with the productivity actually achieved.**

> **Where it is not, the difference must be justified by a specific and credible change — more crews arriving, a different method, better weather — and where no such justification exists, the future durations must be revised and the completion date allowed to move.**

**THE BASELINE'S ROLE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS WHAT MAKES COMPARISON POSSIBLE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The BASELINE is the accepted programme against which progress is measured** ← | ← |
| **It is frozen and not changed by updates** ← | ← |
| **Updates produce the CURRENT programme, compared against it** ← | ← |
| **The baseline is re-set only by a formal agreed REVISION** ← | **Following an extension of time, or a major change of scope** ← |
| **A baseline quietly re-set at each update makes variance invisible** ← | ← |

> **The fifth row is the abuse the discipline exists to prevent and it is easily done: if the baseline moves with each update, every update shows the project on programme against a baseline that was adjusted to match it.**

> **The comparison becomes circular and conveys nothing.**

> **So the baseline must be a fixed reference, formally changed only when the contract entitles it to change, and the current programme measured against it however uncomfortable the variance.**

> **That discipline is what makes the reporting honest, and it is one of the first things to check when reviewing a project's programme records — because a project with no stable baseline has no measured performance at all, whatever its reports say.**

examTip.trick: **To keep an accurate FORECAST of the remaining work** — the current critical path, while there is still time to act.
examTip.trap: **Update by REMAINING DURATION, not percentage complete** — ask when it will finish, not how much is done.
examTip.mnemonic: **Revise future durations from actual productivity** — otherwise each update shows more delay and the same completion date, until it suddenly cannot.

questions.stem: The PROJECT MANAGEMENT TRIANGLE (iron triangle) expresses the relationship between:
options: SCOPE, TIME and COST, with QUALITY at the centre
The client, the consultant and the contractor
Planning, execution and control
Design, construction and maintenance
questions.solution:
**SCOPE, TIME and COST, with QUALITY at the centre** — the three being interdependent, so that changing one necessarily affects at least one of the others.

**The interdependence, which is the whole point:**

| Change requested | Consequence |
|---|---|
| **Increase the SCOPE** ← | **Either the time or the cost must increase** ← |
| **Reduce the TIME** ← | **Either the cost must increase or the scope must reduce** ← |
| **Reduce the COST** ← | **Either the scope must reduce or the time must extend** ← |
| **Change none of them and demand more** ← | **QUALITY absorbs the difference — and it is the variable nobody names** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND IT IS THE REASON QUALITY IS DRAWN AT THE CENTRE RATHER THAN AS A FOURTH CORNER: when scope, time and cost are all fixed and pressure is applied, something must give, and what gives is quality.**

> **Nobody decides to reduce quality; it degrades because the resources available are insufficient for the work demanded in the time allowed.**

> **Corners are cut, checks are skipped, supervision is thinned, and the degradation appears years later as defects.**

> **So the triangle's practical use is as a device for making that trade EXPLICIT — when a change is demanded, the question 'which of the other two moves' forces the consequence into the open rather than leaving it to be absorbed silently.**

**THE TRIANGLE'S USE IN MANAGING CHANGE IS ITS REAL VALUE AND IT DESERVES SETTING OUT:**

| Situation | The right response |
|---|---|
| **The client adds scope** ← | **Quantify the time and cost effect and present it before agreeing** ← |
| **The client wants an earlier date** ← | **Present the crash cost, or the scope that must be removed** ← |
| **The budget is cut** ← | **Present the scope reduction or the programme extension that follows** ← |
| **The client wants all three improved** ← | **Say clearly that this is not available** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE HARDEST CONVERSATION AND IT IS THE ONE THE TRIANGLE EXISTS TO SUPPORT: a request to deliver more, sooner, for less is a request to accept lower quality, whether or not it is expressed that way.**

> **Saying so at the time is difficult and it is far easier than explaining the defects afterwards.**

> **And presenting the trade as a choice between defined options — this scope at this date for this cost, or that scope at that date — is more constructive than refusing, because it leaves the decision with the client where it belongs.**

> **So the triangle is a communication tool as much as a conceptual one, and its value lies in converting an impossible demand into a choice among possible ones.**

**MODERN FORMULATIONS EXTEND THE MODEL AND THEY ARE WORTH KNOWING:**

| Constraint | Note |
|---|---|
| **Scope, Time, Cost** ← | **The classic three** ← |
| **QUALITY** ← | **Sometimes a fourth corner rather than the centre** ← |
| **RISK** ← | **Accepting more risk can buy time or cost** ← |
| **RESOURCES** ← | **Distinguished from cost where availability, not money, is the limit** ← |
| **BENEFITS or value** ← | **The reason for the project, and the ultimate test** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A GENUINELY USEFUL ADDITION AND IT DESCRIBES A TRADE THAT IS MADE CONSTANTLY WITHOUT BEING ACKNOWLEDGED: accelerating a project by overlapping design and construction buys time at the cost of RISK, because construction begins on incomplete information.**

> **That is a legitimate choice, and it should be made knowingly.**

> **Presenting fast-track delivery as simply faster, without naming the risk it accepts, misrepresents the decision — and the risk materialises later as rework, variations and disputes, at which point the time saved is often more than lost.**

> **So adding risk to the model makes visible a trade that the classic triangle leaves out, and it is the trade most often made implicitly in the pursuit of an earlier date.**

examTip.trick: **Scope, time and cost, with quality at the centre** — change one and at least one other must move.
examTip.trap: **When all three are fixed and pressure is applied, QUALITY absorbs it** — nobody decides to reduce it; it degrades silently.
examTip.mnemonic: **Fast-track buys time with RISK** — construction on incomplete information. Name the trade rather than presenting it as simply faster.

questions.stem: A RISK REGISTER on a construction project should record, for each identified risk:
options: Only a description of the risk and its estimated cost
A description, its CAUSE and its EFFECT, an assessment of LIKELIHOOD and IMPACT, the planned RESPONSE, a named OWNER, and the residual risk after the response
Only those risks that have already materialised
A list of insurance policies held
questions.solution:
**A description, its CAUSE and its EFFECT, an assessment of LIKELIHOOD and IMPACT, the planned RESPONSE, a named OWNER, and the residual risk after the response** — reviewed and updated throughout the project.

**The essential columns and why each matters:**

| Column | Why |
|---|---|
| **Risk ID and description** ← | **Identification and tracking** ← |
| **CAUSE — what might trigger it** ← | **Because preventive action addresses the cause** ← |
| **EFFECT — what the consequence would be** ← | **Because mitigation addresses the effect** ← |
| **LIKELIHOOD and IMPACT, scored** ← | **For prioritisation** ← |
| **RESPONSE — the planned action** ← | ← |
| **OWNER — one named person** ← | **A risk owned by everyone is owned by nobody** ← |
| **RESIDUAL risk after the response** ← | **What remains, and whether it is acceptable** ← |
| **Status and review date** ← | ← |

> **THE SEPARATION OF CAUSE AND EFFECT IN THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS IS MORE USEFUL THAN IT APPEARS AND IT IS OFTEN COLLAPSED: 'the project may be delayed' is an effect with no cause, and nothing can be done about it.**

> **'Late issue of foundation drawings may delay the start of piling, delaying completion by up to six weeks' names a cause, a mechanism and an effect.**

> **From that formulation the responses are obvious — expedite the drawings, re-sequence to start elsewhere, or agree a later piling date.**

> **So the discipline of writing risks in cause-mechanism-effect form is what makes the register actionable, and a register full of vague effects is a document rather than a management tool.**

**THE FOUR STANDARD RESPONSES ARE WORTH KNOWING AND THE CHOICE BETWEEN THEM IS THE SUBSTANCE OF RISK MANAGEMENT:**

| Response | Meaning |
|---|---|
| **AVOID** ← | **Change the plan so the risk cannot arise — a different method, route or design** ← |
| **REDUCE (mitigate)** ← | **Lower the likelihood, the impact, or both** ← |
| **TRANSFER** ← | **Move it to a party better able to bear it — insurance, a contract term, a subcontract** ← |
| **ACCEPT (retain)** ← | **Bear it, with or without a contingency** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW DESERVES THE CAUTION MADE EARLIER ABOUT CONTRACTUAL RISK ALLOCATION: transferring a risk does not eliminate it, and it is not free.**

> **Insurance costs a premium; a contract term transferring ground risk to a contractor is priced into the tender.**

> **So transfer is worthwhile when the receiving party can MANAGE the risk better or bear it more cheaply, and wasteful when they can do neither and simply price it higher than the expected cost.**

> **The fourth row is equally legitimate and is often treated as a failure of management: accepting a small, unlikely, cheap-to-remedy risk, with a contingency allowance, is frequently the correct and most economical response.**

**THE REGISTER'S LIVING NATURE IS WHAT MOST OFTEN FAILS AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A register compiled at the start and filed is worthless** ← | ← |
| **Risks change: some pass, some materialise, new ones appear** ← | ← |
| **So it must be reviewed at a defined frequency** ← | **Monthly on most projects** ← |
| **With owners reporting on their risks** ← | ← |
| **And the top risks reported to the project board each period** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MECHANISM THAT KEEPS IT ALIVE AND IT IS AN ORGANISATIONAL RATHER THAN A TECHNICAL DEVICE: if each risk owner must say what they have done about their risk at a regular meeting, the register drives action.**

> **If nobody is asked, it does not.**

> **So the register's value depends almost entirely on whether the review meeting happens and whether owners are held to account at it.**

> **That is why risk management is better understood as a management routine than as a document, and a project with an excellent register and no review process has the appearance of risk management without any of its substance.**

examTip.trick: **Description, cause, effect, likelihood, impact, response, owner, residual risk** — reviewed throughout.
examTip.trap: **Write risks as cause-mechanism-effect** — 'the project may be delayed' is an effect with no cause and admits no action.
examTip.mnemonic: **Avoid, Reduce, Transfer, Accept** — and transferring is not free, it is priced into the tender.

questions.stem: In a MATRIX organisation structure for project delivery:
options: Staff report BOTH to a functional head (their discipline) and to a project manager (their current project)
Each project has a completely dedicated team reporting only to the project manager
All staff report only to their functional department head
The organisation has no formal reporting structure
questions.solution:
**Staff report BOTH to a functional head (their discipline) and to a project manager (their current project)** — combining the technical depth of the functional structure with the project focus of a dedicated team, at the cost of dual reporting.

**The three structures compared:**

| Structure | Authority | Strengths | Weaknesses |
|---|---|---|---|
| **FUNCTIONAL** ← | **Functional heads hold it; the project manager coordinates** ← | **Technical depth, career paths, efficient resource use** ← | **Weak project focus; slow decisions; nobody owns the project** ← |
| **PROJECTISED** ← | **The project manager holds it fully** ← | **Clear accountability, fast decisions, strong commitment** ← | **Resource duplication; specialists under-used; no home between projects** ← |
| **MATRIX** ← | **SHARED** ← | **Both technical depth and project focus** ← | **Dual reporting; conflicting priorities; potential for confusion** ← |

> **THE MATRIX'S WEAKNESS IN THE LAST CELL IS ITS DEFINING PROBLEM AND IT IS REAL RATHER THAN THEORETICAL: an engineer serving two masters receives conflicting instructions about what to work on.**

> **The functional head wants technical standards maintained and staff developed; the project manager wants the project delivered this week.**

> **Both are legitimate, and the engineer in the middle must reconcile them without the authority to do so.**

> **So a matrix works only where the two managers communicate and where the division of authority between them is stated explicitly — typically the functional head owning HOW the work is done and the project manager owning WHAT is done and WHEN.**

**THE DEGREES OF MATRIX ARE WORTH KNOWING SINCE THE TERM COVERS A WIDE RANGE:**

| Type | Balance of authority |
|---|---|
| **WEAK matrix** ← | **Close to functional; the project manager is a coordinator with little authority** ← |
| **BALANCED matrix** ← | **Authority genuinely shared; the hardest to operate** ← |
| **STRONG matrix** ← | **Close to projectised; the project manager has substantial authority and staff are largely dedicated** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE MOST DIFFICULT IN PRACTICE AND THE REASON IS WORTH STATING: a genuinely balanced matrix has no tiebreaker.**

> **Where the two managers disagree and neither can overrule the other, the conflict escalates or, more commonly, is settled by whoever is more persistent.**

> **So balanced matrices work where the managers cooperate well and fail badly where they do not, which makes the structure's success depend on personalities rather than on design.**

> **Weak and strong matrices are more robust precisely because they have a default answer, and choosing one deliberately is usually better than aiming for balance and discovering which way it actually tips.**

**THE CHOICE OF STRUCTURE SHOULD FOLLOW THE WORK AND THAT IS THE PRACTICAL CONCLUSION:**

| Situation | Suitable structure |
|---|---|
| **Many small projects sharing scarce specialists** ← | **Functional or weak matrix** ← |
| **One large, urgent, high-profile project** ← | **Projectised or strong matrix** ← |
| **A steady portfolio of medium projects** ← | **Balanced or strong matrix** ← |
| **Routine repetitive work** ← | **Functional** ← |
