> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHY MAJOR INFRASTRUCTURE PROJECTS ARE USUALLY RUN AS DEDICATED PROJECT ORGANISATIONS AND THE LOGIC IS SOUND: a large project needs undivided attention, rapid decisions and clear accountability, and it is big enough to justify its own full-time specialists.**

> **The resource inefficiency that makes a projectised structure wasteful for small work is immaterial at that scale.**

> **So the structure follows the size and urgency of the work rather than being an organisational preference.**

> **And an organisation running both large and small projects will rationally use different structures for each, which is more effective than imposing one model and is frequently resisted on grounds of consistency.**

examTip.trick: **Dual reporting — to a functional head and to a project manager** — combining technical depth with project focus.
examTip.trap: **The functional head owns HOW; the project manager owns WHAT and WHEN** — state that division or the dual reporting paralyses people.
examTip.mnemonic: **A balanced matrix has no tiebreaker** — it works on good personal relations and fails without them. Weak or strong is more robust.

questions.stem: In construction procurement, a DESIGN-BUILD contract differs from the traditional design-bid-build arrangement in that:
options: The contractor is appointed before any design work is done, and the employer's requirements are never defined
The design is carried out by the employer's own staff
A SINGLE party takes responsibility for both the design and the construction
The contract price is always fixed and can never change
questions.solution:
**A SINGLE party takes responsibility for both the design and the construction** — giving the employer one point of responsibility and removing the interface between designer and builder, at the cost of reduced employer control over the design detail.

**The two arrangements compared:**

| Aspect | DESIGN-BID-BUILD | DESIGN-BUILD |
|---|---|---|
| **Design responsibility** | **The employer's consultant** ← | **The contractor** ← |
| **Points of responsibility for the employer** | **TWO — designer and builder** ← | **ONE** ← |
| **Who bears a design error** | **The employer, who may recover from the designer** ← | **The CONTRACTOR** ← |
| **Employer's control over design detail** | **HIGH** ← | **Lower — defined by the Employer's Requirements** ← |
| **Price certainty** | **Later — after design and tender** ← | **EARLIER** ← |
| **Buildability input** | **Late or absent** ← | **Built in — the builder designs it** ← |
| **Overall duration** | **Longer — sequential** ← | **Shorter — design and construction overlap** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MOST CONSEQUENTIAL DIFFERENCE FOR THE EMPLOYER AND IT IS THE USUAL REASON FOR CHOOSING DESIGN-BUILD: under the traditional arrangement, a design error that causes delay and cost is the employer's problem in the first instance.**

> **The contractor claims against the employer, and the employer pursues the designer separately, with all the difficulty of proving negligence.**

> **Under design-build the contractor cannot claim against the employer for their own design's errors.**

> **So the interface between design and construction — historically the source of a great many claims — is removed, and that single change accounts for much of the arrangement's appeal.**

**THE EMPLOYER'S REQUIREMENTS DOCUMENT IS THE CRITICAL DELIVERABLE AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The employer defines WHAT is required, not HOW** ← | ← |
| **Performance and functional requirements rather than prescriptive detail** ← | ← |
| **Anything not specified will be provided to the contractor's standard** ← | **Which will be the minimum that satisfies the requirements** ← |
| **So a vague requirement produces a disappointing building at the agreed price** ← | ← |
| **And the employer has no remedy, because the contract was satisfied** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESCRIBE THE CHARACTERISTIC FAILURE OF DESIGN-BUILD AND IT IS ENTIRELY PREVENTABLE: the contractor's obligation is to satisfy the Employer's Requirements and nothing more.**

> **A requirement stating 'adequate natural light' will be satisfied by whatever the contractor judges adequate.**

> **A requirement stating a daylight factor, a glazing ratio and an orientation will be satisfied properly.**

> **So the effort saved on detailed design must be reinvested in writing the requirements precisely, and an employer who treats design-build as a way to avoid thinking about the design has misunderstood the arrangement and will get what they specified rather than what they wanted.**

**THE OTHER COMMON PROCUREMENT ROUTES ARE WORTH PLACING ALONGSIDE:**

| Route | Character |
|---|---|
| **DESIGN-BID-BUILD** ← | **Sequential; maximum employer control; longest** ← |
| **DESIGN-BUILD** ← | **Single responsibility; faster; less control** ← |
| **CONSTRUCTION MANAGEMENT** ← | **The employer contracts directly with trade packages; a manager coordinates; maximum flexibility, maximum employer risk** ← |
| **MANAGEMENT CONTRACTING** ← | **Similar, but the management contractor holds the trade contracts** ← |
| **EPC / TURNKEY** ← | **Design-build extended to commissioning and handover of a working facility** ← |
| **PPP / BOT** ← | **The private party also finances and operates, recovering through tolls or payments** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WORTH A NOTE BECAUSE ITS RISK PROFILE IS OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD: under construction management, the employer holds every trade contract directly.**

> **That gives great flexibility — packages can be let as the design develops, and the project can start before it is fully designed.**

> **It also means the employer bears the risk of every interface between packages, and there is no single contractor to hold responsible for the whole.**

> **So it suits a sophisticated, experienced employer with in-house capability and a project where speed and flexibility matter more than price certainty, and it is a poor choice for an inexperienced employer seeking a quiet life — which is the situation in which it is occasionally and unwisely recommended on grounds of the fee savings it appears to offer.**

examTip.trick: **One party for design and construction** — single responsibility, faster, with less employer control over detail.
examTip.trap: **Anything not in the Employer's Requirements is provided to the contractor's minimum standard** — and the employer has no remedy.
examTip.mnemonic: **Effort saved on detailed design must go into writing the requirements** — design-build is not a way to avoid thinking about the design.

questions.stem: LIQUIDATED DAMAGES in a construction contract are:
options: A penalty imposed to punish the contractor for late completion
The actual losses proved by the employer after the event
A sum stated in the contract
An amount the contractor pays to be released from the contract
questions.solution:
**A sum stated in the contract, representing a GENUINE PRE-ESTIMATE of the loss the employer would suffer from late completion** — payable at a defined rate without the employer having to prove actual loss.

**The essential characteristics:**

| Characteristic | Note |
|---|---|
| **Stated in the contract, agreed in ADVANCE** ← | ← |
| **A genuine PRE-ESTIMATE of the likely loss** ← | **Not a figure chosen to deter** ← |
| **Expressed as a rate — per day or per week of delay** ← | ← |
| **Usually subject to a CAP** ← | **A maximum total, commonly 5 to 10 per cent of the contract sum** ← |
| **Payable WITHOUT proof of actual loss** ← | **The employer need not demonstrate what they lost** ← |
| **And it is the employer's EXCLUSIVE remedy for delay** ← | **They cannot also claim their actual losses** ← |

> **THE FIFTH AND SIXTH ROWS TOGETHER EXPLAIN WHY THE ARRANGEMENT BENEFITS BOTH PARTIES, WHICH IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE IF IT IS SEEN AS A PENALTY: the employer gains certainty of recovery without the burden of proving loss, which for a public building or a road may be very difficult to quantify.**

> **The contractor gains certainty of exposure — they know the maximum liability for delay and can price it, insure it or manage it.**

> **Without liquidated damages, a delayed contractor faces an unliquidated claim for whatever the employer can prove, which could be far larger and is unknowable in advance.**

> **So liquidated damages are a risk-allocation device that caps and quantifies a liability, and a contractor who understands this prefers them to the alternative.**

**THE DISTINCTION FROM A PENALTY IS LEGALLY CRITICAL AND IT IS WHY OPTION (a) IS WRONG:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A PENALTY is a sum designed to DETER breach by being punitive** ← | ← |
| **Penalties are generally UNENFORCEABLE in common law jurisdictions** ← | ← |
| **Liquidated damages are enforceable because they are compensatory** ← | ← |
| **So the sum must be a genuine estimate, arrived at by reasoning** ← | ← |
| **And the calculation should be RECORDED at the time it is set** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS PRACTICAL ADVICE THAT IS ROUTINELY IGNORED AND IT MATTERS IF THE FIGURE IS EVER CHALLENGED: a liquidated damages rate should be derived from something — the employer's financing cost during the extended period, lost revenue, the cost of alternative accommodation, additional supervision.**

> **Writing that derivation down when the contract is drafted costs an hour.**

> **If the rate is later challenged as a penalty, that contemporaneous calculation is the evidence that it was a genuine pre-estimate.**

> **Without it, a figure that looks like a round percentage chosen for effect is hard to defend — and a rate struck down as a penalty leaves the employer with no liquidated remedy at all, having to prove actual loss after all.**

**THE 'TIME AT LARGE' DOCTRINE IS THE OTHER SIDE OF THIS AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Liquidated damages run from the CONTRACT completion date** ← | ← |
| **If the employer causes delay and the contract has no mechanism to extend that date** ← | ← |
| **Or the mechanism is not properly operated** ← | ← |
| **Then time becomes 'AT LARGE'** ← | ← |
| **The completion date falls away, the contractor must finish in a REASONABLE time** ← | ← |
| **And the employer LOSES the right to liquidated damages entirely** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A SEVERE CONSEQUENCE AND IT FOLLOWS FROM A PRINCIPLE THAT IS EASY TO STATE: a party cannot benefit from a deadline it prevented the other from meeting.**

> **So an employer who delays the works and does not grant the extension of time the contract provides for cannot then charge damages for the resulting lateness.**

> **This is why the extension of time machinery matters so much to the EMPLOYER as well as to the contractor — granting an extension preserves the employer's right to damages for any further delay, and refusing one may destroy it.**

> **That is counter-intuitive enough to be worth stating plainly: the engineer who refuses a justified extension of time in order to protect the employer's position has in fact endangered it.**

examTip.trick: **A pre-agreed genuine estimate of the employer's loss** — payable at a stated rate without proving actual loss.
examTip.trap: **A PENALTY is punitive and unenforceable** — so record the derivation of the rate when the contract is drafted.
examTip.mnemonic: **Refusing a justified extension of time can make time 'AT LARGE'** — destroying the employer's right to damages entirely.

questions.stem: A PERFORMANCE BOND provided by a contractor:
options: Guarantees that the contractor will make a profit on the contract
Is a payment made by the employer to secure the contractor's services
Insures the works against damage by fire and flood
Is a security, usually from a bank or insurer, under which a stated sum
questions.solution:
**It is a security, usually from a bank or insurer, under which a stated sum — commonly 10 per cent of the contract value — becomes payable to the employer if the contractor fails to perform**, providing the employer with a remedy that does not depend on the contractor's solvency.

**Why the bond exists:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A contractor who fails to perform is liable in damages** ← | ← |
| **But a contractor who has FAILED is often insolvent** ← | ← |
| **So the legal right is worthless in exactly the circumstances it is needed** ← | ← |
| **A bond provides a THIRD PARTY — a bank — who will pay** ← | ← |
| **And banks are chosen for their solvency** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE PROBLEM THE BOND SOLVES AND IT IS WORTH SEEING CLEARLY: contractual remedies against a failed counterparty are of limited value.**

> **The employer's loss on a contractor's insolvency is real and immediate — the works stop, a replacement must be found at a higher price, and the programme is destroyed.**

> **A judgement against an insolvent company recovers a fraction at best, years later.**

> **So the bond converts an unenforceable right into a payable sum, and that is its entire purpose — which also explains why the identity and standing of the bond's issuer matters as much as its amount.**

**THE TWO TYPES OF BOND DIFFER IMPORTANTLY AND THE DISTINCTION IS OFTEN MISSED:**

| Type | Note |
|---|---|
| **ON-DEMAND (unconditional) bond** ← | **Payable on the employer's demand, WITHOUT proof of default or loss** ← |
| ** ** | **The bank pays first and questions follow — strong for the employer, risky for the contractor** ← |
| **CONDITIONAL (default) bond** ← | **Payable only on PROOF of the contractor's default and of the employer's loss** ← |
| ** ** | **Fairer to the contractor, slower and less certain for the employer** ← |

> **THE FIRST TYPE IS SUBSTANTIALLY MORE ONEROUS AND ITS RISK TO THE CONTRACTOR IS WORTH STATING: an on-demand bond can be called even where the contractor is not in default, and the bank must pay regardless.**

> **The contractor's recourse is to sue the employer afterwards for a wrongful call, having already lost the money.**

> **So a contractor providing an on-demand bond has given the employer a substantial and largely unchecked power, and it is priced accordingly and sometimes refused.**

> **International contracts in some markets require on-demand bonds as standard, and the risk of an unjustified call is a real commercial consideration in deciding whether to tender.**

**THE FAMILY OF SECURITIES ON A CONSTRUCTION PROJECT IS WORTH LISTING FOR COMPLETENESS:**

| Security | Purpose |
|---|---|
| **TENDER (bid) bond** ← | **That the tenderer will enter the contract if awarded — typically 1 to 2 per cent** ← |
| **PERFORMANCE bond** ← | **Performance of the contract — typically 10 per cent** ← |
| **ADVANCE PAYMENT guarantee** ← | **Repayment of an advance if the contractor fails — for the full advance** ← |
| **RETENTION bond** ← | **Substitutes for cash retention, releasing the contractor's working capital** ← |
| **PARENT COMPANY guarantee** ← | **The parent stands behind a subsidiary's obligations — free, and only as good as the parent** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS A DEVICE WORTH KNOWING BECAUSE IT ADDRESSES THE CASH FLOW PROBLEM IDENTIFIED EARLIER: cash retention withholds 5 or 10 per cent of every payment, which the contractor funds.**

> **A retention bond substitutes a bank guarantee for that cash, so the contractor is paid in full and the employer retains equivalent security.**

> **The contractor pays a bond fee and recovers their working capital, which is usually a good trade for them.**

> **The employer gets a security that is arguably better than cash — a bank's obligation rather than a sum they must account for and eventually release — so the arrangement can suit both, and its main obstacle is unfamiliarity rather than any defect.**

examTip.trick: **A third-party security, typically 10%, payable if the contractor fails** — a remedy that survives the contractor's insolvency.
examTip.trap: **ON-DEMAND bonds pay without proof of default** — the contractor must sue afterwards to recover a wrongful call.
examTip.mnemonic: **A judgement against an insolvent contractor is worthless** — which is exactly when the remedy is needed, and why bonds exist.

questions.stem: A VARIATION (change order) in a construction contract is:
options: Any difference between the tender price and the final account
A change in the working hours agreed with the contractor
An instructed CHANGE to the scope
A dispute referred to arbitration
questions.solution:
**An instructed CHANGE to the scope, quality, sequence or conditions of the work, issued under the contract's variation clause** — which obliges the contractor to carry it out and entitles them to have it valued and paid.

**The essential features:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **It must be INSTRUCTED by the person authorised to do so** ← | **Usually the engineer or the contract administrator, in writing** ← |
| **It must fall within the variation clause's scope** ← | **A change so fundamental it alters the nature of the contract may not be a variation at all** ← |
| **The contractor is OBLIGED to carry it out** ← | **They cannot refuse a properly instructed variation** ← |
| **And ENTITLED to be paid for it** ← | ← |
| **Valued by the contract's valuation rules** ← | **Bill rates where applicable, pro-rata rates, or fair valuation** ← |
| **With any time effect dealt with under the extension of time provisions** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS WHERE MOST VARIATION DISPUTES ORIGINATE AND THE REMEDY IS PROCEDURAL: a change directed verbally on site by someone without authority is not a variation.**

> **The contractor who acts on it may have no entitlement to payment, and the person who gave it may have committed the employer to nothing.**

> **So the contract names who may instruct variations, and the discipline is that nothing changes without a written instruction from that person.**

> **Where an urgent verbal instruction is unavoidable, it must be confirmed in writing immediately — and a contractor who proceeds on an unconfirmed verbal instruction is taking a commercial risk that is entirely avoidable.**

**THE VALUATION RULES FOLLOW A HIERARCHY AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Order | Rule |
|---|---|
| **1** | **Where the work is of the SAME character and conditions as billed work — use the BILL RATES** ← |
| **2** | **Where it is similar but the conditions differ — use the bill rates as a BASIS, adjusted** ← |
| **3** | **Where it is of a different character — a FAIR VALUATION** ← |
| **4** | **Where the work cannot be measured — DAYWORK, at the contract's daywork rates** ← |

> **THE FIRST RULE CAN PRODUCE AN UNCOMFORTABLE RESULT AND IT IS WORTH ANTICIPATING: bill rates are binding even where they are demonstrably wrong.**

> **A contractor who priced an item very low, whether by error or as a tactical judgement, will have additional quantities of it valued at that low rate.**

> **One who priced an item very high will have additional quantities valued at the high rate, which is the basis of the practice of RATE LOADING — pricing items expected to increase in quantity at high rates and those expected to decrease at low ones.**

> **So the bill rates matter beyond the tender total, and an employer whose quantities are unreliable is exposed to that tactic — which is an argument for accurate quantities, and for scrutinising a tender whose individual rates look unbalanced even where its total is competitive.**

**THE SECOND ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES A CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT LIMITS THE POWER TO VARY:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A variation clause permits changes WITHIN the contract's scope** ← | ← |
| **It does not permit the employer to change the project into a different one** ← | ← |
| **Omitting a large part of the works to give it to another contractor is generally not permitted** ← | ← |
| **Nor is a change that alters the fundamental nature of the bargain** ← | ← |
| **Such a change requires the contractor's AGREEMENT, not merely an instruction** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A SPECIFIC AND WELL-ESTABLISHED LIMIT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: the power to omit work exists so the employer can decide not to have something built, not so they can have it built by somebody cheaper.**

> **An omission followed by the same work being let to another contractor deprives the original contractor of the profit they contracted for.**

> **Courts have generally held that this is outside the variation power, and that such an omission is a breach.**

> **So an employer dissatisfied with a contractor's price for a section of work cannot simply omit it and re-let it — and understanding that limit prevents a course of action that appears commercially attractive and is likely to produce a successful claim.**
tags: must be properly instructed in writing
limits on the power to omit

examTip.trick: **An instructed change under the variation clause** — the contractor must do it and is entitled to be paid for it.
examTip.trap: **Bill rates bind even when wrong** — which is the basis of rate loading, and why unbalanced tenders deserve scrutiny.
examTip.mnemonic: **Omitting work to give it to another contractor is generally a breach, not a variation** — the power exists to cancel work, not to re-let it.

questions.stem: In dispute resolution on construction contracts, the usual ESCALATION sequence, from least to most formal, is:
options: Litigation, arbitration, adjudication, negotiation
NEGOTIATION between the parties
Arbitration first in every case, as it is contractually required
Mediation only, as other methods are not permitted in construction
questions.solution:
**NEGOTIATION between the parties, then mediation or conciliation, then adjudication or a dispute board, then ARBITRATION, and finally litigation** — each step more formal, more costly and more damaging to the relationship.

**The methods and their character:**

| Method | Decision | Binding? |
|---|---|---|
| **NEGOTIATION** ← | **By the parties themselves** ← | **Only if agreed** ← |
| **MEDIATION / conciliation** ← | **The neutral FACILITATES; does not decide** ← | **Only if the parties settle** ← |
| **ADJUDICATION** ← | **A neutral decides, rapidly** ← | **Binding on an INTERIM basis — pending arbitration or litigation** ← |
| **DISPUTE BOARD** ← | **A standing panel, familiar with the project** ← | **Recommendation or decision, depending on the form** ← |
| **ARBITRATION** ← | **An arbitrator decides** ← | **Final and binding; enforceable; limited appeal** ← |
| **LITIGATION** ← | **A court decides** ← | **Final and binding, subject to appeal** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW'S INTERIM BINDING EFFECT IS ADJUDICATION'S DISTINCTIVE FEATURE AND IT IS DESIGNED TO SOLVE A SPECIFIC PROBLEM: 'pay now, argue later'.**

> **An adjudicator decides within a short period — often 28 days — and the decision must be complied with immediately, even if a party disagrees.**

> **The dissatisfied party may pursue arbitration or litigation afterwards, but meanwhile the money moves and the work continues.**

> **That prevents a dispute from starving a contractor of cash and halting a project, which is the practical damage that slow dispute resolution causes — and it is why adjudication has become the dominant mechanism in construction wherever it has been introduced.**

**THE DISPUTE BOARD IN THE FOURTH ROW DESERVES PARTICULAR ATTENTION FOR LARGE PROJECTS:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **Appointed at the START of the project, not when a dispute arises** ← | ← |
| **Visits the site regularly and follows progress** ← | ← |
| **So it understands the project before any dispute** ← | ← |
| **Available to give informal opinions early** ← | **Often preventing disputes rather than deciding them** ← |
| **And able to decide quickly when needed, from an informed position** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WHERE A DISPUTE BOARD DELIVERS MOST OF ITS VALUE AND IT IS EASILY OVERLOOKED: its greatest contribution is usually the disputes that never happen.**

> **Parties who know that a knowledgeable panel will examine their position tend to adopt more reasonable ones.**

> **And an informal early opinion on a brewing disagreement often settles it before positions harden.**

> **So the board's cost — a retainer plus site visits over the project's life — is justified by prevention rather than by resolution, which makes it hard to demonstrate and easy to cut, and the projects that cut it are generally the ones that later discover what it was for.**

**THE PRINCIPLE UNDERLYING THE WHOLE SEQUENCE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Each step up costs more in fees, time and management attention** ← | ← |
| **Each step damages the working relationship further** ← | ← |
| **And the parties must continue working together while it proceeds** ← | **Which distinguishes construction disputes from most commercial ones** ← |
| **So the strong incentive is to resolve at the lowest level possible** ← | ← |
| **And the best outcome is a dispute that never escalates beyond negotiation** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHAT MAKES CONSTRUCTION DISPUTES DISTINCTIVE AND IT SHOULD SHAPE HOW THEY ARE HANDLED: the parties are not finished with one another.**

> **A contractor in arbitration with an employer must still build the project, and an employer in dispute must still administer the contract and issue instructions.**

> **A relationship poisoned by an escalated dispute makes every subsequent interaction adversarial, and the project's cost rises accordingly through defensive behaviour on both sides.**

> **So resolving early is worth more than winning later, and an engineer administering a contract contributes most by addressing disagreements promptly and fairly while they are still small — which is unglamorous, is rarely recognised, and saves far more than any amount of skilful claim-handling afterwards.**
tags: the parties must keep working together

examTip.trick: **Negotiation → mediation → adjudication → arbitration → litigation** — increasing formality, cost and damage.
examTip.trap: **Adjudication is binding on an INTERIM basis** — pay now, argue later, so a dispute cannot starve the project of cash.
examTip.mnemonic: **A dispute board's value is the disputes that never happen** — which makes it hard to justify and easy to cut.

questions.stem: In construction SAFETY management, the HIERARCHY OF CONTROL ranks risk control measures in order of effectiveness. The correct order, from most to least effective, is:
options: Personal protective equipment, administrative controls, engineering controls, substitution, elimination
Engineering controls, elimination, personal protective equipment, substitution, administrative controls
Administrative controls, personal protective equipment, elimination, engineering controls, substitution
ELIMINATION, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment LAST
questions.solution:
**ELIMINATION, substitution, engineering controls, administrative controls, and personal protective equipment LAST.**

**The hierarchy and an example of each:**

| Rank | Control | Example |
|---|---|---|
| **1** | **ELIMINATE the hazard** ← | **Design out the need to work at height — assemble at ground level and lift into place** ← |
| **2** | **SUBSTITUTE something less hazardous** ← | **A less toxic solvent; a smaller, safer plant** ← |
| **3** | **ENGINEERING controls** ← | **Guard rails, edge protection, guarding, extraction, isolation** ← |
| **4** | **ADMINISTRATIVE controls** ← | **Permits to work, procedures, training, signage, rotation, exclusion zones** ← |
| **5** | **PERSONAL PROTECTIVE EQUIPMENT** ← | **Harness, helmet, boots, gloves, respirator** ← |

> **THE ORDERING PRINCIPLE IS WHETHER THE CONTROL DEPENDS ON HUMAN BEHAVIOUR, AND IT EXPLAINS THE WHOLE HIERARCHY: elimination removes the hazard, so nothing can go wrong.**

> **An engineering control protects everyone in the area whether or not they are paying attention.**

> **An administrative control works only if people follow it, every time.**

> **And PPE works only if it is provided, the right type, correctly fitted, worn, maintained and used properly — five conditions, each of which can fail, on each individual person.**

> **So the hierarchy ranks controls by how many opportunities there are for them to fail, and PPE is last because it has the most.**

**PPE'S POSITION AT THE BOTTOM IS THE MOST IMPORTANT PRACTICAL LESSON AND IT IS ROUTINELY INVERTED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **PPE protects ONE person — the wearer** ← | **An engineering control protects everyone present** ← |
| **It does nothing to reduce the hazard itself** ← | ← |
| **It depends entirely on correct and continuous use** ← | ← |
| **It is often uncomfortable, which undermines that use** ← | ← |
| **And it can create a false sense of security** ← | ← |
| **So it is the LAST resort, not the first response** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW STATES THE PRINCIPLE AND THE COMMON PRACTICE IS THE OPPOSITE: a site's response to a fall hazard is frequently to issue harnesses.**

> **That is the least effective available control, adopted because it is the cheapest and most visible.**

> **Edge protection — an engineering control — protects everyone who goes near the edge, needs no decision from anyone, and cannot be forgotten.**

> **And designing the work so nobody needs to go near the edge eliminates the hazard entirely, which is better still and costs least of all if it is thought of early enough.**

**THAT LAST OBSERVATION LEADS TO THE MOST IMPORTANT SAFETY PRINCIPLE AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE — SAFETY IN DESIGN:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The greatest opportunity to eliminate hazards is at the DESIGN stage** ← | ← |
| **A designer can specify a method that avoids work at height, confined space entry or heavy manual handling** ← | ← |
| **Once the design is fixed, the constructor can only manage the hazards it creates** ← | ← |
| **So the designer's decisions determine what risks the builder must face** ← | ← |
| **Which is why designers carry statutory safety duties in many jurisdictions** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE INSIGHT THAT CONNECTS THIS TO EVERYTHING ELSE IN THIS SUBCHAPTER: a structure designed with parapets cast into the units eliminates a fall hazard for every worker on the roof, for ever, at almost no cost.**

> **The same structure designed without them requires temporary edge protection during construction, during every subsequent maintenance visit, and for the building's whole life.**

> **The designer who thought about it for a minute saved more risk than any amount of site supervision can.**

> **So the hierarchy of control is not only a site tool — its top two levels belong to the designer, and a designer who never considers how their design will be built and maintained has passed every hazard down to people with far less power to remove them.**

examTip.trick: **Eliminate, Substitute, Engineering, Administrative, PPE** — most to least effective, PPE always last.
examTip.trap: **The ranking is by how much each depends on human behaviour** — elimination cannot fail; PPE has five conditions that each can.
examTip.mnemonic: **The top two levels belong to the DESIGNER** — designing out a hazard removes it for construction and for the whole life of the asset.

questions.stem: A JOB SAFETY ANALYSIS (JSA) or method statement prepared before a construction operation should:
options: Break the task into its constituent STEPS, identify the hazards associated with each step, and specify the control measures
Be prepared by the safety officer alone and issued to the workforce
Be a generic document reused for all similar operations without change
Be prepared after the work, as a record of what was done
questions.solution:
**Break the task into its constituent STEPS, identify the hazards associated with each step, and specify the control measures** — prepared with the involvement of those who will do the work, and briefed to them before they start.

**The structure of a job safety analysis:**

| Column | Content |
|---|---|
| **Step** | **A sequential breakdown of the task** ← |
| **HAZARDS at that step** | **What could cause harm** ← |
| **Who might be harmed** | **Operatives, others on site, the public** ← |
| **CONTROL measures** | **Applied through the hierarchy of control** ← |
| **Residual risk** | **What remains after the controls** ← |
| **Responsible person** | ← |

> **THE STEP-BY-STEP BREAKDOWN IN THE FIRST COLUMN IS WHAT MAKES THE METHOD EFFECTIVE AND IT IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES IT FROM A GENERIC RISK ASSESSMENT: hazards attach to specific operations rather than to a task in the abstract.**

> **'Erect scaffolding' identifies few hazards.**

> **'Unload materials — carry to position — erect first lift — install ties at the second lift — fit boards and guard rails — hand over' identifies the hazards of each, and they differ: manual handling at one step, fall from height at another, incomplete guard rails at a third.**

> **So the decomposition surfaces hazards that a holistic view misses, which is the same reason a work breakdown structure surfaces work that a summary misses.**

**THE INVOLVEMENT OF THE WORKFORCE IN PREPARING IT IS THE FEATURE MOST OFTEN NEGLECTED AND IT MATTERS FOR TWO DISTINCT REASONS:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They know how the work is ACTUALLY done** ← | **Which often differs from how it is imagined in an office** ← |
| **They will identify hazards a planner does not see** ← | ← |
| **And they are far more likely to follow a method they helped write** ← | ← |
| **A document imposed on them is complied with formally and ignored practically** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MORE IMPORTANT AND IT REFLECTS A GENERAL TRUTH ABOUT SAFETY DOCUMENTATION: there is always a gap between work-as-imagined and work-as-done.**

> **A method statement written without the crew describes the imagined work, and its controls address the imagined hazards.**

> **The real work has different steps, different constraints and different hazards, and the document does not reach them.**

> **So involving the crew is not a matter of engagement or morale but of accuracy — they are the only source of information about what will actually happen, and a method statement that does not reflect it is protecting nobody.**

**THE BRIEFING IN THE STEM IS THE FINAL AND ESSENTIAL STEP AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A method statement filed in an office protects nobody** ← | ← |
| **It must be BRIEFED to everyone doing the work, before they start** ← | ← |
| **In a language and manner they understand** ← | **Which matters greatly with a multilingual workforce** ← |
| **With the opportunity to raise questions and objections** ← | ← |
| **And re-briefed when the method, the conditions or the people change** ← | ← |
| **The briefing recorded, with those present signing** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE CONDITION MOST OFTEN MISSED AND IT IS WHERE ACCIDENTS OCCUR: a method statement briefed at the start of an operation covers the conditions then prevailing.**

> **When the weather changes, the crew changes, the plant is substituted or the sequence is altered, the assessment no longer describes the work.**

> **Continuing under the original briefing is proceeding on an assessment that has quietly become invalid.**

> **So a change of method, people or conditions should trigger a review and a re-brief — and building that trigger into the site routine, rather than relying on somebody noticing, is what makes it happen.**
tags: work as imagined versus work as done

examTip.trick: **Break the task into steps, identify each step's hazards, specify controls** — prepared with the crew and briefed before starting.
examTip.trap: **The crew know how the work is ACTUALLY done** — a statement written without them addresses imagined hazards and protects nobody.
examTip.mnemonic: **Re-brief when method, people or conditions change** — otherwise the assessment has quietly become invalid.

questions.stem: The PROJECT CHARTER (or project initiation document) is significant because it:
options: Contains the detailed design of the project
Lists the materials to be used
Formally AUTHORISES the project and appoints the project manager with defined authority
Is the contract between the employer and the contractor
questions.solution:
**It formally AUTHORISES the project and appoints the project manager with defined authority** — recording the objectives, the scope boundaries, the key stakeholders, the high-level budget and schedule, and the success criteria, against which the project will be judged.

**What the charter contains and why each element matters:**

| Element | Why |
|---|---|
| **The project's PURPOSE and objectives** ← | **Why it is being done, in terms of the benefit sought** ← |
| **SCOPE boundaries — what is included and, crucially, what is EXCLUDED** ← | **Exclusions prevent later disagreement** ← |
| **SUCCESS criteria** ← | **How it will be judged, agreed before it starts** ← |
| **Key STAKEHOLDERS** ← | ← |
| **High-level budget and schedule** ← | **Indicative, with their accuracy stated** ← |
| **Key assumptions and constraints** ← | ← |
| **Major risks identified at the outset** ← | ← |
| **The project manager's APPOINTMENT and AUTHORITY** ← | **What they may decide without referring upward** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE CHARTER'S MOST PRACTICALLY IMPORTANT FUNCTION AND IT IS THE ONE MOST OFTEN LEFT VAGUE: a project manager without defined authority must seek approval for everything, which is slow, or act without it, which is risky.**

> **Stating the financial limit within which they may commit, the variations they may approve, and the decisions reserved to the sponsor resolves that at the outset.**

> **It also protects the project manager, who can point to the document when their authority is questioned.**

> **So a charter that describes the project beautifully and says nothing about authority has omitted the part that makes it operational.**

**THE SECOND ROW'S EXCLUSIONS DESERVE PARTICULAR ATTENTION BECAUSE THEY PREVENT A SPECIFIC AND COMMON PROBLEM:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A scope statement listing what is included leaves everything else ambiguous** ← | ← |
| **Stakeholders assume their own requirement is included** ← | ← |
| **And discover late that it is not** ← | ← |
| **Explicit EXCLUSIONS make that discoverable at the start** ← | ← |
| **When it can be discussed and either added or accepted** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS DESCRIBE WHY EXCLUSIONS ARE WORTH THE DISCOMFORT OF WRITING THEM: stating that the project does not include landscaping, or external works, or the relocation of an existing service, invites an argument at the outset.**

> **That argument is far cheaper then than when the omission is discovered at commissioning.**

> **And the decision it forces — to add the item and its budget, or to confirm it is somebody else's responsibility — is one that has to be taken eventually.**

> **So exclusions bring forward a conversation that will otherwise happen at the worst possible time, which is the whole value of writing them down.**

**SCOPE CREEP IS WHAT THE CHARTER DEFENDS AGAINST AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **SCOPE CREEP is the gradual, uncontrolled expansion of scope** ← | ← |
| **Each addition is small and individually reasonable** ← | ← |
| **None triggers a formal change** ← | ← |
| **But cumulatively they consume the budget and the programme** ← | ← |
| **And the project fails against targets set for a smaller scope** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE MECHANISM AND THE DEFENCE FOLLOWS DIRECTLY FROM IT: every change, however small, is assessed against the charter's scope and put through the change control process.**

> **That does not mean refusing changes — most are worth making — it means that each is recorded, its cost and time effect assessed, and the budget and programme adjusted or the change declined.**

> **So the scope grows visibly and with its consequences acknowledged, rather than invisibly and at the project's expense.**

> **A project that has absorbed a hundred small additions without a single approved change has not been well managed by being accommodating; it has lost control of its own baseline, and it will be judged against a target that no longer relates to what it was asked to deliver.**
tags: authorises the project and the manager

examTip.trick: **Formally authorises the project and appoints the manager with defined authority** — plus objectives, scope, stakeholders and success criteria.
examTip.trap: **State the EXCLUSIONS explicitly** — they bring forward an argument that would otherwise surface at commissioning.
examTip.mnemonic: **A hundred accommodated small additions is lost control, not good service** — every change assessed, recorded, and the baseline adjusted.

questions.stem: STAKEHOLDER ANALYSIS on a project typically maps stakeholders on two axes. These are:
options: Their POWER (or influence) and their INTEREST in the project
Their age and their professional qualification
Their distance from the site and their income
Their support for the project and their political affiliation
questions.solution:
**Their POWER (or influence) and their INTEREST in the project** — producing four quadrants that indicate how each group should be engaged.

**The four quadrants and the strategy for each:**

| Power | Interest | Strategy |
|---|---|---|
| **HIGH** | **HIGH** | **MANAGE CLOSELY — full engagement, regular consultation, they can make or break the project** ← |
| **HIGH** | **Low** | **KEEP SATISFIED — do not let them become dissatisfied and engaged; enough information, not too much** ← |
| **Low** | **HIGH** | **KEEP INFORMED — they care deeply and cannot act directly; good communication prevents grievance** ← |
| **Low** | **Low** | **MONITOR — minimal effort, but watch for changes** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE QUADRANT MOST OFTEN MISHANDLED AND THE RISK IS SPECIFIC: a powerful stakeholder with low interest is not currently engaged, and if something arouses their interest they move immediately to the top-left quadrant with the power to disrupt the project.**

> **A regulator, a senior official, a neighbouring landowner who has not yet noticed — each is quiet until they are not.**

> **So the strategy is to keep them satisfied and unbothered, which means enough proactive information that they do not learn of a problem from someone else.**

> **Neglecting them entirely is the error, because their lack of interest is a temporary state rather than a characteristic.**

**THE THIRD QUADRANT IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST ETHICALLY AND IT DESERVES CAREFUL TREATMENT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **High interest and low power describes most AFFECTED COMMUNITIES** ← | ← |
| **They bear the project's impacts and have little formal influence** ← | ← |
| **A purely instrumental reading says 'keep informed' at minimum cost** ← | ← |
| **That reading is inadequate** ← | ← |
| **Their low power is a reason for greater care, not less** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE POINT WORTH MAKING EXPLICITLY BECAUSE THE TOOL, READ NAIVELY, SUGGESTS THE OPPOSITE: the matrix describes how much a stakeholder can AFFECT the project, and it says nothing about how much the project affects THEM.**

> **Used as a guide to where influence lies, it is accurate and useful.**

> **Used as a guide to where obligation lies, it is actively misleading, because it would direct attention away from precisely the people with least ability to protect themselves.**

> **So the matrix should be paired with an IMPACT assessment — who is affected, and how severely — and the engagement effort determined by both, which gives a different and better answer for the communities in the third quadrant.**

**THE PRACTICAL PROCESS OF STAKEHOLDER ENGAGEMENT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **IDENTIFY stakeholders comprehensively** ← | **Including those easily overlooked — tenants, women, informal users, downstream communities** ← |
| **ANALYSE power, interest and impact** ← | ← |
| **PLAN the engagement for each group** ← | **Method, frequency, who leads it** ← |
| **ENGAGE — and do so EARLY** ← | ← |
| **RECORD what was said and what was done about it** ← | ← |
| **And FEED BACK, so people see their input had an effect** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES GENUINE ENGAGEMENT FROM CONSULTATION THEATRE AND IT IS THE STEP MOST OFTEN OMITTED: people asked for their views and never told what happened conclude, correctly, that the exercise was a formality.**

> **They then disengage, and the next consultation is attended by nobody or by people who are already hostile.**

> **Telling participants which suggestions were adopted, which were not and why, costs little and is what builds the credibility that makes future engagement possible.**

> **And where nothing was changed as a result, saying so honestly is better than silence — because the alternative is that people discover it themselves and conclude that they were deceived rather than merely unpersuasive.**
tags: keep satisfied the powerful and uninterested
the matrix measures influence not obligation

examTip.trick: **Power and interest** — manage closely, keep satisfied, keep informed, monitor.
examTip.trap: **The matrix maps who can AFFECT the project, not whom the project affects** — pair it with an impact assessment for affected communities.
examTip.mnemonic: **Feed back what changed and what did not** — consultation without feedback teaches people it was a formality.

questions.stem: In a construction contract, RETENTION money is:
options: A payment retained by the contractor from its subcontractors only
The advance payment made at the start of the contract
The profit retained by the contractor on completion
A percentage — commonly 5 or 10 per cent
questions.solution:
**A percentage — commonly 5 or 10 per cent — DEDUCTED from each interim payment and held by the employer as security for the contractor's performance and for making good defects**, released in stages at completion and at the end of the defects liability period.

**How retention operates:**

| Stage | Note |
|---|---|
| **Deducted from each interim certificate** ← | **Commonly 10 per cent, up to a limit of 5 per cent of the contract sum** ← |
| **Accumulates as the work proceeds** ← | ← |
| **HALF released at practical completion** ← | **The works are usable; the remaining risk is defects** ← |
| **The balance released at the end of the DEFECTS LIABILITY period** ← | **Once defects have been made good** ← |
| **And it may be drawn on if the contractor fails to make good defects** ← | ← |

> **THE TWO-STAGE RELEASE IN THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS MATCHES THE SECURITY TO THE RISK REMAINING AND THAT IS ITS LOGIC: before completion the employer's risk is that the works are not finished, which needs the full retention.**

> **After completion the risk is only that defects appear and are not remedied, which is a smaller exposure and needs less security.**

> **So half is released at completion and half at the end of the defects period, and the retained sum tracks the risk down rather than sitting at its maximum until the very end.**

> **That staging is worth insisting on in a contract that does not provide it, because the difference in the contractor's financing cost is material and it is recovered in the price.**

**THE COST OF RETENTION TO THE CONTRACTOR IS SUBSTANTIAL AND IS OFTEN UNDERESTIMATED BY EMPLOYERS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The contractor has performed the work and paid for it** ← | ← |
| **And is paid 90 per cent of its value** ← | ← |
| **The remaining 10 per cent is held, often for years** ← | **Through construction and the defects period** ← |
| **On a project with a thin margin, the retention may exceed the whole profit** ← | ← |
| **So a contractor is funding the employer's security out of their own profit** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE OBSERVATION THAT EXPLAINS WHY RETENTION IS SO CONTENTIOUS AND IT IS OFTEN LITERALLY TRUE: construction margins of 3 to 5 per cent are common, and a 5 per cent retention therefore exceeds the profit on the job.**

> **The contractor's entire return is tied up until the retention is released, and if release is delayed or disputed, the job may never produce cash however profitable it was on paper.**

> **This effect cascades down the supply chain, since main contractors retain from subcontractors who retain from theirs.**

> **So the smallest firms at the bottom of the chain bear retention deducted at several levels, which is a well-recognised cause of difficulty in the construction industry and the reason retention reform is a recurring policy topic.**

**THE ALTERNATIVES ARE WORTH KNOWING SINCE THEY ADDRESS THE PROBLEM WITHOUT REMOVING THE SECURITY:**

| Alternative | Note |
|---|---|
| **RETENTION BOND** ← | **A bank guarantee replaces the cash, as discussed earlier** ← |
| **A retention TRUST account** ← | **The cash is held in trust, protected if the employer becomes insolvent** ← |
| **Reducing the percentage or the release period** ← | ← |
| **Project bank accounts** ← | **Payments held in a neutral account, released to the whole chain simultaneously** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW ADDRESSES A RISK THAT IS EASY TO OVERLOOK AND THAT CRYSTALLISES OCCASIONALLY: retention held by an employer who becomes insolvent is simply lost.**

> **The contractor is an unsecured creditor for money that was their own, earned and certified, and withheld only as security.**

> **Holding it in a trust account separates it from the employer's assets, so it survives the insolvency.**

> **That protection costs the employer nothing beyond the administration, and its absence means the contractor is bearing the employer's credit risk on top of everything else — which is a risk allocation nobody negotiated and few notice until it materialises.**
tags: two stage release matching residual risk

examTip.trick: **A percentage deducted from each interim payment as security** — half released at completion, half at the end of the defects period.
examTip.trap: **On a 3-5% margin, a 5% retention exceeds the whole profit** — the contractor funds the employer's security out of their return.
examTip.mnemonic: **Retention held by an insolvent employer is simply lost** — a trust account or a bond removes that unnegotiated credit risk.

questions.stem: A project is judged SUCCESSFUL if it meets its time, cost and quality targets. This definition is incomplete because:
options: Time, cost and quality cannot be measured objectively
Cost targets are always adjusted during the project
Quality is not a valid project objective
It measures PROJECT MANAGEMENT success rather than PROJECT success
questions.solution:
**It measures PROJECT MANAGEMENT success rather than PROJECT success** — a project can be delivered perfectly and still fail to produce the benefits that justified it, or be delivered late and over budget and still be a great success.

**The two levels of success:**

| Level | Question | Measured |
|---|---|---|
| **PROJECT MANAGEMENT success** ← | **Was it delivered to time, cost and quality?** ← | **At handover** ← |
| **PROJECT success** ← | **Did it produce the intended BENEFITS?** ← | **Years later, in operation** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE IN THE TIMING COLUMN IS WHY THE TWO ARE SO EASILY CONFUSED AND WHY THE SECOND IS SO OFTEN NEGLECTED: project management success is assessed when the team is still assembled, the records are fresh and somebody is accountable.**

> **Project success is assessed years later, by which time the team has dispersed, the sponsor has moved on and nobody is required to look.**

> **So the measurable, immediate criterion displaces the important, delayed one, and projects are judged on delivery rather than on whether they were worth delivering.**

> **The standard examples make the point: a road built on time and on budget that carries a fraction of the forecast traffic is a project management success and a project failure, and several famously late and overspent buildings have transformed their cities.**

**BENEFITS REALISATION IS THE DISCIPLINE THAT ADDRESSES THIS AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Define the BENEFITS sought, measurably, before the project starts** ← | **In the business case and the charter** ← |
| **Identify who is accountable for DELIVERING each benefit** ← | **Usually an operational manager, not the project manager** ← |
| **Establish the BASELINE against which improvement will be measured** ← | **Before the project changes anything** ← |
| **Plan the changes in operation needed to realise the benefits** ← | **A new asset rarely delivers benefits by existing** ← |
| **MEASURE after an appropriate interval** ← | ← |
| **And FEED BACK into future project appraisal** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS A PRACTICAL POINT THAT IS ROUTINELY MISSED AND IT IS IRRECOVERABLE ONCE LOST: measuring an improvement requires knowing the starting point.**

> **If the journey time, the accident rate, the water supply hours or the crop yield before the project was never recorded, no subsequent measurement can demonstrate the change.**

> **The baseline must be captured before construction begins, which is exactly when nobody is thinking about evaluation.**

> **So a modest baseline survey at the outset — a few days' work — is the precondition for ever being able to say whether the project worked, and its omission means the question can never be answered.**

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE STEP THAT WOULD IMPROVE PRACTICE MOST AND IT IS ALMOST NEVER TAKEN: if the traffic forecasts for completed roads were systematically compared with the outturn, the forecasting method's bias would be measurable and correctable.**

> **The same holds for cost estimates, benefit projections and programme durations.**

> **Each project makes its forecasts afresh, using methods whose historical accuracy is unknown, because nobody goes back and checks.**

> **So the industry repeats its systematic biases indefinitely — optimism bias in costs and benefits is well documented precisely where somebody has done this work — and the cheapest available improvement to appraisal is not a better method but a habit of checking the old ones against what actually happened.**

examTip.trick: **It measures delivery, not benefit** — a project can be delivered perfectly and still not be worth having.
examTip.trap: **Capture the BASELINE before construction** — journey times, yields, service hours. Without it, no improvement can ever be demonstrated.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compare outturns with forecasts** — nobody does, so the same optimism bias repeats indefinitely.

questions.stem: A project has a total float of zero on every path. This means that:
options: The project cannot be completed
The project has been planned with no slack anywhere
The project will certainly finish early
The programme contains an error and must be redrawn
questions.solution:
**The project has been planned with no slack anywhere — every activity is critical, so any delay to any activity delays the project, making the programme extremely fragile.**

**Why this is a warning rather than an achievement:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A critical activity has no margin for error** ← | ← |
| **If EVERY activity is critical, every activity must go exactly to plan** ← | ← |
| **The probability of that is very low** ← | **Even if each activity individually is likely to be on time** ← |
| **So the programme will be delayed almost certainly** ← | ← |
| **And management attention cannot be prioritised** ← | **Everything is equally critical, so nothing stands out** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW CONTAINS THE PROBABILISTIC POINT AND IT IS WORTH MAKING NUMERICALLY: if each of twenty activities independently has an 80 per cent chance of finishing on time, and all twenty are critical, the chance of the project finishing on time is 0.8²⁰, which is about 1 per cent.**

> **So a programme in which everything is critical is almost certain to be late, even though every individual activity is more likely than not to be on time.**

> **That multiplication of probabilities is the mechanism by which apparently reasonable programmes fail, and it is entirely invisible in a deterministic critical path calculation, which reports a single completion date with no indication of its likelihood.**

> **PERT's probabilistic treatment exists precisely to expose this, which is why it was developed for a project where the schedule mattered more than the cost.**

**THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MANAGEMENT CONSEQUENCE AND IT IS AS IMPORTANT AS THE PROBABILISTIC ONE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The critical path's value is that it tells a manager where to LOOK** ← | ← |
| **A programme with a clear critical path directs attention to perhaps 20 per cent of the activities** ← | ← |
| **One where everything is critical directs attention nowhere** ← | ← |
| **So the analysis, though correct, has become useless as a management tool** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL LOSS AND IT MATTERS BECAUSE MANAGEMENT ATTENTION IS THE SCARCEST RESOURCE ON A PROJECT: a manager can watch a limited number of things closely.**

> **The critical path tells them which ones, and that prioritisation is most of the technique's value.**

> **An all-critical programme returns them to watching everything, which means watching nothing properly.**

> **So the response to discovering that everything is critical is not to admire the efficiency of the plan but to ask whether the durations were compressed to fit a date, which is usually what has happened.**

**THE USUAL CAUSE AND THE APPROPRIATE RESPONSE DESERVE THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Cause | Response |
|---|---|
| **Durations compressed to make the programme fit a required date** ← | **Restore realistic durations and show the true completion date** ← |
| **Excessive or artificial logic links** ← | **Review whether each dependency is genuine** ← |
| **Genuinely tight programme with everything on the critical path** ← | **Add buffers explicitly, and accept a later date** ← |
| **Resource constraints encoded as logic** ← | **Separate them, as discussed earlier** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE HONEST RESPONSE WHERE THE PROGRAMME IS GENUINELY TIGHT AND IT IS WORTH STATING AS A TECHNIQUE: rather than distributing hidden contingency into every activity's duration, add an explicit BUFFER at the end of the critical chain.**

> **The activities then carry realistic, unpadded durations, and the project carries a visible contingency that can be managed.**

> **Consuming the buffer is measurable — how much is left, against how much of the project remains — which gives a far better early warning than watching individual activities slip.**

> **That is the central idea of critical chain scheduling, and its advantage over padding every activity is simply that a visible contingency can be monitored while a hidden one is silently consumed.**
tags: usually caused by compression to fit a date

examTip.trick: **No slack anywhere — every activity critical, so any delay delays the project.** A warning, not an achievement.
examTip.trap: **Twenty critical activities each 80% likely on time gives about 1% for the project** — probabilities multiply, invisibly in a deterministic CPM.
examTip.mnemonic: **Add a visible BUFFER rather than padding every duration** — a hidden contingency is consumed silently; a visible one can be monitored.

questions.stem: The LESSONS LEARNED exercise at the end of a project is valuable only if:
options: It identifies who was responsible for each failure
It is conducted by an external consultant
The lessons are CAPTURED in a form that is accessible to future projects
It is completed within one week of handover
questions.solution:
**The lessons are CAPTURED in a form that is accessible to future projects, and the organisation has a mechanism that actually brings them to the attention of the next project team** — otherwise the exercise produces a document that nobody reads.

**Why most lessons-learned exercises fail:**

| Failure | Note |
|---|---|
| **Held too late, when the team has dispersed** ← | ← |
| **Conducted as a blame exercise, so people are defensive** ← | ← |
| **Recorded as vague generalities** ← | **'Communication could have been better'** ← |
| **Filed where nobody will find them** ← | ← |
| **With no mechanism to surface them to the next project** ← | **The decisive failure** ← |
| **So the same mistakes recur indefinitely** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE ONE THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT IS AN ORGANISATIONAL DESIGN PROBLEM RATHER THAN A DOCUMENTATION ONE: a lesson recorded and never retrieved has not been learned.**

> **Learning requires the lesson to reach someone who can act on it, at the moment they need it.**

> **A repository that must be searched by someone who does not know what they are looking for will not deliver that.**

> **So the mechanism must be a PUSH rather than a pull — lessons relevant to a project type surfaced automatically at the corresponding stage, or incorporated into the checklists, standards and templates that the next project will use anyway.**

**THAT LAST POINT IS THE MOST EFFECTIVE APPROACH AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The most reliable way to transmit a lesson is to CHANGE something** ← | ← |
| **Amend the standard specification, the design guide, the checklist, the template** ← | ← |
| **Then the next project follows it without needing to know why** ← | ← |
| **The lesson is embedded in the process rather than in a document** ← | ← |
| **And it cannot be overlooked, because it is part of the normal route** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN KNOWLEDGE AND PRACTICE AND IT IS WHERE MOST ORGANISATIONS FALL SHORT: a lesson in a report requires someone to find it, read it, believe it and apply it.**

> **A lesson embedded in a checklist requires nothing of anybody.**

> **So the output of a lessons-learned exercise should be a list of CHANGES to standing documents, each with an owner and a date, rather than a narrative report.**

> **And the review of that exercise six months later should ask whether those changes were made, not whether the report was written — which is a very different question and the one that determines whether anything was learned.**

**THE BLAME PROBLEM IN THE SECOND ROW DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT DETERMINES WHETHER THE EXERCISE GETS HONEST INPUT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **People will not describe their mistakes if doing so is punished** ← | ← |
| **So a blame-oriented review gets a sanitised account** ← | ← |
| **From which nothing useful can be learned** ← | ← |
| **A no-blame review gets the real story** ← | ← |
| **Which is where the valuable lessons are** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW REQUIRES A GENUINE COMMITMENT RATHER THAN A STATED ONE AND PEOPLE JUDGE IT BY BEHAVIOUR RATHER THAN BY ASSURANCES: if one person is criticised for an honest admission, nobody admits anything again.**

> **The commitment must therefore be held even when what emerges is uncomfortable, which is harder than declaring it.**

> **The distinction worth drawing is between blame and ACCOUNTABILITY — a no-blame review does not mean nobody is responsible for anything, it means the review's purpose is understanding rather than attribution.**

> **Serious misconduct is handled separately and through a different process, and keeping the two apart is what allows the learning process to function at all — the same principle that underlies incident reporting in aviation and medicine, where it has demonstrably worked.**
tags: embed lessons in standards and checklists
output should be changes not a report

examTip.trick: **Captured accessibly AND actively brought to the next project** — otherwise it is a document nobody reads.
examTip.trap: **The output should be CHANGES to standards, checklists and templates** — not a narrative report. Then the next project follows it automatically.
examTip.mnemonic: **No blame ≠ no accountability** — the review's purpose is understanding; misconduct goes through a separate process.

questions.stem: PRACTICAL COMPLETION (or substantial completion) of construction works is the stage at which:
options: Every item of work, however minor, has been finished to perfection
The works are complete for all PRACTICAL PURPOSES and can be occupied or used for their intended purpose
The contractor leaves the site for the last time
The final account has been agreed and paid
questions.solution:
**The works are complete for all PRACTICAL PURPOSES and can be occupied or used for their intended purpose**, notwithstanding minor outstanding items and defects that do not prevent that use.

**What practical completion triggers:**

| Consequence | Note |
|---|---|
| **The employer takes POSSESSION and may use the works** ← | ← |
| **Liability for INSURING the works passes to the employer** ← | ← |
| **Liquidated damages CEASE to run** ← | ← |
| **The DEFECTS LIABILITY period begins** ← | ← |
| **Half the RETENTION is released** ← | ← |
| **And the contractor's obligation to proceed regularly and diligently ends** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHY THE DATE IS SO COMMERCIALLY SIGNIFICANT AND WHY IT IS OFTEN DISPUTED: every day before practical completion is certified is a day of liquidated damages.**

> **So a contractor presses for certification and an employer, particularly one dissatisfied with the works, may resist it.**

> **That tension means the definition matters, and the practical test is whether the employer can USE the works for their intended purpose.**

> **A building with a few doors to be adjusted and some paintwork to complete is practically complete; one whose lift does not work or whose fire alarm is uncommissioned is not, however small the remaining work may appear.**

**THE SNAGGING LIST AND ITS LIMITS DESERVE ATTENTION BECAUSE THEY ARE OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A list of minor outstanding items is prepared at practical completion** ← | **The snagging or punch list** ← |
| **Its existence does NOT prevent practical completion** ← | **Provided the items are minor** ← |
| **The contractor remains obliged to complete them** ← | ← |
| **And to remedy defects appearing during the defects period** ← | ← |
| **But a list so long that the works cannot be used means completion has NOT occurred** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND FIFTH ROWS TOGETHER DEFINE THE JUDGEMENT AND IT IS A JUDGEMENT RATHER THAN A RULE: the question is not how many items remain but whether they prevent use.**

> **Two hundred minor decorative items do not prevent occupation of a building; one uncommissioned fire safety system does.**

> **So the certifier must assess the character of what remains rather than count it, and a mechanical rule based on the number or value of outstanding items would give the wrong answer in both directions.**

> **That is why the certifier's judgement is central, and why the contract vests the decision in a named professional rather than in a formula.**

**PARTIAL POSSESSION AND SECTIONAL COMPLETION ARE RELATED DEVICES WORTH DISTINGUISHING:**

| Device | Note |
|---|---|
| **SECTIONAL completion** ← | **Planned from the outset — the contract divides the works into sections with separate dates and separate liquidated damages** ← |
| **PARTIAL possession** ← | **Agreed during the works — the employer takes over part of the works early, by agreement** ← |
| **The difference** ← | **Sectional is contractual and priced; partial possession is a later accommodation** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW MATTERS COMMERCIALLY AND IT IS WORTH GETTING RIGHT AT THE DRAFTING STAGE: if the employer knows they will need part of the works early, that should be a SECTION in the contract.**

> **The contractor then prices and programmes for it, and liquidated damages apply to that section's date.**

> **Taking partial possession later, without that provision, is an accommodation the contractor may reasonably resist or price, and it complicates the insurance, the retention and the defects liability for the part taken.**

> **So the requirement should be identified before tender and written in, which costs nothing at that stage and is awkward to arrange afterwards — a pattern that has recurred throughout this material, and one that reflects the general truth that foresight is cheap and retrofit is not.**
tags: the test is fitness for use
snagging lists do not prevent it

examTip.trick: **Complete for practical purposes and usable for its intended purpose** — minor outstanding items notwithstanding.
examTip.trap: **The test is character, not count** — 200 decorative items do not prevent occupation; one uncommissioned fire system does.
examTip.mnemonic: **If early use of part is foreseen, make it a SECTION at tender** — partial possession arranged later is awkward and may be resisted.

questions.stem: The engineer's PARAMOUNT professional obligation, taking precedence over duties to the client and to the employer, is to:
options: Maximise the client's return on investment
Protect the SAFETY, HEALTH and WELFARE of the PUBLIC
Complete the project within the agreed budget
Maintain the confidentiality of the client's information in all circumstances
questions.solution:
**Protect the SAFETY, HEALTH and WELFARE of the PUBLIC** — which is the first canon of virtually every engineering code of ethics, and which overrides the engineer's duty to a client or employer where the two conflict.

**Why this obligation ranks first:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **The public cannot assess the safety of what engineers build** ← | **They must rely on the profession** ← |
| **They have no choice about being exposed to it** ← | **One crosses a bridge without inspecting it** ← |
| **So the profession holds a trust that individuals cannot verify** ← | ← |
| **That trust is the basis of the profession's standing and its licensure** ← | ← |
| **And it is forfeited if commercial duties are allowed to override it** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS WHAT DISTINGUISHES ENGINEERING FROM AN ORDINARY COMMERCIAL SERVICE AND IT IS THE ETHICAL FOUNDATION OF THE WHOLE STRUCTURE: a person buying a product can inspect it, compare it and decline it.**

> **A person crossing a bridge, living beside a dam or working in a building has no practical ability to assess its safety and usually no choice about using it.**

> **So their protection depends entirely on the engineer having done the work properly, with no possibility of the user detecting otherwise.**

> **That asymmetry is why the obligation is paramount rather than merely important, and why it cannot be traded against the client's interest — the client is a party to the bargain and the public is not.**

**THE PRACTICAL SITUATIONS IN WHICH THE CONFLICT ARISES ARE WORTH NAMING:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A client instructs a reduction that compromises safety** ← | **The instruction must be refused** ← |
| **An employer pressures for a certificate that is not justified** ← | ← |
| **A defect is discovered that would be expensive to disclose** ← | ← |
| **A design is found to be deficient after construction has begun** ← | ← |
| **Cost pressure invites reducing testing or supervision** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE HARDEST IN PRACTICE AND IT DESERVES A DIRECT ANSWER: discovering an error in one's own work, after construction has begun, is professionally and personally difficult.**

> **Disclosure means admitting the error, bearing the consequences and possibly facing liability.**

> **Silence means allowing a structure to be completed that one knows to be deficient.**

> **The obligation admits no ambiguity — the error must be disclosed promptly to those who can act on it — and the practical observation is that disclosure early is always less damaging than discovery later, both to the public and to the engineer, which aligns the ethical and the prudent course more often than the difficulty of the moment suggests.**

**THE MECHANISM THAT MAKES THE OBLIGATION ENFORCEABLE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **A code of ETHICS stating the obligations** ← | ← |
| **LICENSURE, so that only qualified persons may practise** ← | ← |
| **A DISCIPLINARY process with real sanctions** ← | **Including removal from the register** ← |
| **And a professional body independent enough to use it** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHAT GIVES THE CODE FORCE AND WITHOUT IT THE CODE IS AN ASPIRATION: an obligation with no consequence for its breach is advice.**

> **The sanction that matters is removal from the register, because it removes the ability to practise — which is why licensure and discipline are two aspects of one system rather than separate arrangements.**

> **The fourth row is the condition most often absent, and it is the hardest to establish: a professional body closely tied to the industry it regulates, or to the government that employs most of its members, may be reluctant to discipline.**

> **So the credibility of a profession's ethical framework rests on whether its disciplinary process has visibly been used, and a register from which nobody has ever been removed tells the public something about the framework's reality.**
tags: the public cannot verify or choose

examTip.trick: **Public safety, health and welfare** — the first canon of every engineering code, overriding client and employer duties.
examTip.trap: **The public cannot inspect and cannot choose** — that asymmetry is why the duty is paramount rather than merely important.
examTip.mnemonic: **Disclose your own error promptly** — early disclosure is always less damaging than later discovery, to everyone including yourself.

questions.stem: An engineer is offered a consultancy commission in a field in which they have no experience or training. The professionally correct response is to:
options: DECLINE it, or accept only in association with someone competent in that field — since engineers must undertake work only in their areas of COMPETENCE
Accept it and learn the subject during the commission
Accept it, since an engineering degree qualifies one to work in any branch of engineering
Accept it and subcontract the entire work without informing the client
questions.solution:
**DECLINE it, or accept only in association with someone competent in that field** — since engineers must undertake work only in their areas of COMPETENCE.

**The competence obligation:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Every engineering code requires practice only within one's competence** ← | ← |
| **Competence comes from education, training AND experience** ← | **A degree alone is not competence in a specialty** ← |
| **It is specific to a FIELD, not general** ← | **A structural engineer is not thereby a geotechnical engineer** ← |
| **And the client usually cannot judge it** ← | **Which is why the obligation falls on the engineer** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE REASON THE OBLIGATION IS SELF-POLICING AND IT PARALLELS THE PUBLIC SAFETY ARGUMENT: a client engaging an engineer generally cannot assess whether that engineer is competent in the specialty required.**

> **They rely on the engineer's own judgement of their competence, and on the profession's assurance that its members will exercise that judgement honestly.**

> **So accepting work beyond one's competence is a breach of trust rather than merely an error of judgement, because the client had no means of detecting it.**

> **And the harm is compounded by the fact that incompetent work often looks entirely normal — the drawings are produced, the calculations are presented, and the deficiency appears only when the structure is loaded.**

**THE LEGITIMATE WAYS TO PROCEED ARE WORTH SETTING OUT, SINCE DECLINING IS NOT THE ONLY OPTION:**

| Option | Note |
|---|---|
| **DECLINE and refer the client to someone competent** ← | **Which serves the client and the profession** ← |
| **ASSOCIATE with a competent specialist, disclosed to the client** ← | **The commonest arrangement** ← |
| **Sub-consult the specialist element, with the client's knowledge** ← | ← |
| **Accept the work and obtain the competence FIRST** ← | **Where time and the nature of the work permit** ← |
| **Accept a limited role within one's competence** ← | **Coordinating, or handling the elements one can** ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS SHARE A CONDITION THAT IS ESSENTIAL AND IS SOMETIMES OMITTED: the client must KNOW.**

> **Engaging a specialist behind the client's back, and presenting the work as one's own, deceives the client about who is doing their work and about what they are paying for.**

> **It also leaves the client unable to assess the specialist's standing or to deal with them directly.**

> **So disclosure is what distinguishes a legitimate association from the improper arrangement in option (d), and the difference is entirely about the client's knowledge rather than about the quality of the work done.**

**THE CONTINUING NATURE OF COMPETENCE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN TREATED AS A FIXED ATTRIBUTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Competence DECAYS as practice moves on** ← | **Codes change, methods change, materials change** ← |
| **An engineer who has not practised in a field for a decade may no longer be competent in it** ← | ← |
| **Even though they once were, and their qualification says so** ← | ← |
| **So CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT is an ethical requirement, not an administrative one** ← | ← |
| **And it is why registration is periodically renewed rather than granted for life** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE UNCOMFORTABLE PART AND IT APPLIES BROADLY: a qualification records competence at a moment, and it does not certify it thereafter.**

> **An engineer designing to a code superseded twice since they last used it is working from knowledge that is no longer current, however sound it was.**

> **So the honest self-assessment is not 'am I qualified in this field' but 'am I currently competent in it', and those are different questions with sometimes different answers.**

> **That is the reasoning behind CPD requirements and periodic re-registration, and understanding it as a substantive protection rather than a bureaucratic hurdle changes how seriously the requirement is met.**

examTip.trick: **Decline, or associate with someone competent** — engineers practise only within their competence.
examTip.trap: **Association is legitimate only if the CLIENT KNOWS** — the difference from improper subcontracting is disclosure, not work quality.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ask 'am I CURRENTLY competent', not 'am I qualified'** — competence decays as codes and methods move on.

questions.stem: A CONFLICT OF INTEREST arises for an engineer when:
options: The engineer has an interest
The engineer disagrees with the client's instructions
Two clients disagree with each other about a technical matter
The engineer works on more than one project at a time
questions.solution:
**The engineer has an interest — financial, personal or professional — that could IMPROPERLY INFLUENCE, or reasonably appear to influence, their professional judgement on behalf of a client or employer.**

**Common situations:**

| Situation | Note |
|---|---|
| **A financial interest in a supplier or contractor being considered** ← | ← |
| **Acting for two clients whose interests conflict** ← | **Even on unrelated matters, where confidential information overlaps** ← |
| **A family or personal relationship with a tenderer** ← | ← |
| **Accepting gifts or hospitality from those seeking work** ← | ← |
| **Specifying a proprietary product in which one has an interest** ← | ← |
