| **Certifying one's own work** ← | **A structural conflict rather than a personal one** ← |

> **THE PHRASE 'OR REASONABLY APPEAR TO INFLUENCE' IN THE ANSWER IS THE PART THAT MATTERS MOST AND IT IS OFTEN RESISTED: a conflict exists if a reasonable observer would think the judgement might be affected, whether or not it actually is.**

> **An engineer confident of their own impartiality may argue that their shareholding makes no difference to their recommendation, and they may be entirely right.**

> **That does not resolve the conflict, because the client's confidence in the advice depends on there being no reason to doubt it.**

> **So the test is the APPEARANCE to a reasonable outsider, not the engineer's own assessment of their integrity — which is the only workable test, since everyone believes themselves impartial.**

**THE REQUIRED RESPONSE IS A SEQUENCE AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING IN ORDER:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. IDENTIFY the conflict** ← | **Which requires actively looking for it** ← |
| **2. DISCLOSE it fully and promptly to the affected parties** ← | **In writing** ← |
| **3. WITHDRAW from the matter, unless** ← | ← |
| **4. All affected parties, fully informed, consent to the engineer continuing** ← | ← |
| **5. And appropriate safeguards are put in place** ← | **Separation of duties, independent review** ← |

> **THE SECOND STEP IS THE PIVOTAL ONE AND ITS OMISSION IS WHAT CONVERTS A MANAGEABLE SITUATION INTO MISCONDUCT: a disclosed conflict can usually be managed.**

> **An undisclosed one, discovered later, destroys trust entirely and looks like concealment regardless of whether the judgement was actually affected.**

> **So the engineer's exposure comes far more from failing to disclose than from having the interest, and disclosure is almost always the cheaper course.**

> **The practical rule that follows is to disclose anything one would be uncomfortable about the client discovering from someone else — which is a test that can be applied in a moment and usually gives the right answer.**

**THE SIXTH ROW OF THE FIRST TABLE DESERVES SEPARATE TREATMENT SINCE IT IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN PERSONAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An engineer who designs, supervises and certifies their own work has a built-in conflict** ← | ← |
| **Certifying it as satisfactory is also certifying their own competence** ← | ← |
| **The pressure to find it satisfactory is real, and it is not dishonesty** ← | ← |
| **So independent checking and certification is required for significant works** ← | ← |
| **Which is the same independence principle as in drawing checks and safety audits** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE HONEST ACKNOWLEDGEMENT AND IT IS WHY THE SAFEGUARD IS STRUCTURAL RATHER THAN A MATTER OF CHARACTER: nobody examines their own work with the scepticism they would apply to someone else's.**

> **That is not a failing to be overcome by resolve; it is how people work.**

> **So the remedy is organisational — an independent checker, a separate certifier, a design review by another party — rather than an exhortation to be objective.**

> **And the recurrence of this principle across drawing checks, safety audits, design certification and financial audit suggests it is one of the more reliable lessons available: where a judgement matters and self-assessment is unreliable, build in a second pair of eyes rather than relying on the first pair trying harder.**

examTip.trick: **An interest that could, or could reasonably appear to, influence professional judgement** — appearance counts as much as reality.
examTip.trap: **Your own confidence in your impartiality does not resolve it** — the test is what a reasonable observer would think.
examTip.mnemonic: **Disclose anything you would not want the client hearing from someone else** — a one-moment test that usually gives the right answer.

questions.stem: PROFESSIONAL NEGLIGENCE by an engineer is established when it is shown that:
options: The project suffered a defect or a failure of any kind
The client is dissatisfied with the outcome
The engineer's fee was higher than another engineer would have charged
The engineer owed a DUTY OF CARE
questions.solution:
**The engineer owed a DUTY OF CARE, BREACHED it by falling below the standard of a reasonably competent engineer in that field, and that the breach CAUSED loss or damage that was reasonably foreseeable.**

**The four elements, all of which must be present:**

| Element | Note |
|---|---|
| **DUTY of care** ← | **A relationship giving rise to an obligation — contractual or in tort** ← |
| **BREACH** ← | **Falling below the standard of a reasonably competent practitioner in that field** ← |
| **CAUSATION** ← | **The breach must have CAUSED the loss — the 'but for' test** ← |
| **DAMAGE that was reasonably FORESEEABLE** ← | **Remote or unforeseeable consequences are not recoverable** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW CONTAINS THE STANDARD AGAINST WHICH THE ENGINEER IS JUDGED AND IT IS NOT PERFECTION, WHICH IS THE POINT OPTION (a) MISSES: the test is the reasonably competent practitioner, not the best in the field and not an infallible one.**

> **So an engineer who exercised reasonable skill and care is not negligent even if the outcome was poor, and one who fell below that standard is negligent even if by good fortune nothing went wrong — though in the latter case there would be no damage and therefore no claim.**

> **A defect or failure is therefore EVIDENCE that may suggest negligence and is not proof of it: materials fail, ground conditions surprise, and events exceed what was designed for, all without anyone having been negligent.**

> **Establishing negligence requires showing what a reasonably competent engineer would have done differently, which is why expert evidence is central to such claims.**

**THE STANDARD OF CARE DESERVES FURTHER DEFINITION BECAUSE IT HAS SEVERAL FEATURES:**

| Feature | Note |
|---|---|
| **It is judged by the standards of the engineer's OWN FIELD** ← | **A specialist is judged as a specialist** ← |
| **And at the TIME the work was done** ← | **Not by later knowledge — hindsight is excluded** ← |
| **Following accepted practice is strong evidence of reasonable care** ← | **Though not an absolute defence if the practice is itself unreasonable** ← |
| **Holding oneself out as a specialist raises the standard applied** ← | ← |
| **And an engineer who designs to a code is generally protected if the code is followed properly** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS A PROTECTION OF REAL IMPORTANCE AND IT IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: the engineer is judged by what was known and accepted when they did the work.**

> **A design that complied with the code of its day is not negligent because a later code is more demanding, and a hazard not recognised at the time cannot found a claim for having failed to address it.**

> **Without that rule, every engineer would be liable indefinitely as knowledge advanced, which would make practice impossible.**

> **It also places weight on RECORDS: demonstrating what was known and what was done at the time requires the calculations, the correspondence and the decisions to have been retained — which is why professional indemnity insurers press so hard on record-keeping.**

**PROFESSIONAL INDEMNITY INSURANCE IS THE PRACTICAL RESPONSE AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **PI insurance covers claims arising from professional negligence** ← | ← |
| **It is written on a CLAIMS MADE basis** ← | **It responds to claims made during the policy year, whatever when the work was done** ← |
| **So cover must be MAINTAINED after the work, and after retirement** ← | **Run-off cover** ← |
| **A firm that ceases to insure is exposed to claims on all its past work** ← | ← |
| **And limits should reflect the scale of the projects undertaken** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS DESCRIBE A FEATURE THAT SURPRISES PEOPLE AND HAS CAUGHT OUT MANY SMALL PRACTICES: unlike most insurance, PI does not cover the year in which the work was done.**

> **It covers the year in which the claim is made.**

> **So an engineer who designed a building in 2015, retired in 2025 and let their policy lapse has no cover for a claim arising in 2027 about that 2015 design.**

> **Run-off cover, maintained for the limitation period after ceasing practice, is what addresses this — and its cost at the point of retirement, when there is no fee income, is a genuine and frequently unanticipated burden.**
tags: judged at the time not with hindsight

examTip.trick: **Duty, breach, causation, foreseeable damage** — all four required.
examTip.trap: **The standard is the reasonably competent engineer, not perfection** — a defect is evidence of negligence, not proof of it.
examTip.mnemonic: **PI is CLAIMS MADE, not work done** — so cover must continue after retirement, which is why run-off cover exists.

questions.stem: An engineer employed by a contractor is instructed by a manager to conceal a defect in completed work. The professionally correct course of action is to:
options: Comply, since the engineer is an employee and must follow lawful instructions
Comply but record a private note of the objection
Resign immediately without raising the matter
Refuse to conceal the defect
questions.solution:
**Refuse to conceal the defect, explain the reasons in writing, and if the instruction is maintained, escalate it within the organisation and if necessary to the client or the regulatory body** — the duty to public safety and to professional integrity overriding the employment relationship.

**Why the employment relationship does not settle the question:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An employee must follow lawful and reasonable instructions** ← | ← |
| **An instruction to conceal a defect is neither** ← | ← |
| **A professional engineer's obligations attach to them personally** ← | **Not to their employer** ← |
| **Registration is held by the individual and can be lost by the individual** ← | ← |
| **So 'I was instructed to' is not a defence, professionally or generally** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE POINT THAT MAKES THE ANSWER CLEAR AND IT IS WORTH INTERNALISING BEFORE THE SITUATION ARISES: professional obligations are personal and non-delegable.**

> **The engineer who conceals the defect has committed the breach, whoever told them to.**

> **The manager's instruction may be a mitigating circumstance and it does not transfer the responsibility.**

> **So the calculation that treats compliance as the safe option is mistaken — compliance preserves the job in the short term and exposes the engineer personally to professional and possibly criminal consequences.**

**THE ESCALATION SEQUENCE IS WORTH FOLLOWING IN ORDER RATHER THAN JUMPING TO THE END:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. Raise it with the person giving the instruction, explaining why** ← | **Often it is resolved here, the instruction having been given without thought** ← |
| **2. Put the objection in WRITING** ← | **Creating a record, and making the matter formal** ← |
| **3. Escalate within the organisation** ← | **To a senior manager, a director, or a designated officer** ← |
| **4. Use the organisation's whistleblowing procedure if one exists** ← | ← |
| **5. Report externally — to the client, the regulator or the professional body** ← | **Where internal routes fail or are not safe to use** ← |
| **6. Seek advice from the professional body at any stage** ← | **Most provide confidential ethical guidance** ← |

> **THE SIXTH ROW IS THE MOST USEFUL PRACTICAL POINT AND IT IS THE LEAST WIDELY KNOWN: professional bodies generally offer confidential advice to members facing ethical difficulties.**

> **An engineer in this position is usually isolated, under pressure and uncertain whether their reading of the situation is proportionate.**

> **A confidential conversation with someone experienced in such matters, who has no stake in the outcome, is enormously valuable and costs nothing.**

> **So knowing that the service exists, before it is needed, is worth more than any amount of ethical theory — and it should be one of the first things sought rather than a last resort.**

**THE PERSONAL COST DESERVES HONEST ACKNOWLEDGEMENT RATHER THAN BEING GLOSSED OVER:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Refusing an instruction from one's employer carries real risk** ← | **To the job, the career and relationships** ← |
| **Whistleblowing protections exist in law in many jurisdictions and are imperfect** ← | ← |
| **The engineer who does the right thing may suffer for it** ← | ← |
| **This is a genuine cost and pretending otherwise helps nobody** ← | ← |
| **What makes it bearable is that the alternative cost is greater** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE HONEST BASIS ON WHICH THE DECISION RESTS AND IT IS WORTH STATING WITHOUT PIETY: concealing a defect exposes the engineer to professional sanction, to civil liability and, where harm results, to criminal liability.**

> **It also places them permanently in the position of having concealed something, which a colleague may later reveal.**

> **So the choice is not between a costly right course and a free wrong one; it is between a cost that is immediate and bounded and one that is delayed and potentially unbounded.**

> **Recognising that before the moment arrives is what allows the decision to be made clearly under pressure, which is the practical purpose of thinking about professional ethics in advance rather than discovering one's position in the middle of a crisis.**

examTip.trick: **Refuse, explain in writing, escalate internally, then externally if needed** — professional duty overrides the employment relationship.
examTip.trap: **'I was instructed to' is not a defence** — registration is personal, and the engineer who conceals has committed the breach.
examTip.mnemonic: **Professional bodies give confidential ethical advice** — know it exists before you need it, and use it early rather than last.

questions.stem: The principle of SUSTAINABLE DEVELOPMENT, as it applies to engineering practice, is best expressed as:
options: Using only renewable materials in every project
Reducing the cost of construction by using local materials
Maintaining structures so they last indefinitely
Meeting the needs of the present WITHOUT COMPROMISING the ability of future generations to meet their own needs
questions.solution:
**Meeting the needs of the present WITHOUT COMPROMISING the ability of future generations to meet their own needs** — requiring the engineer to weigh environmental, social and economic consequences together, over the full life of the works.

**The three dimensions, which must be weighed together:**

| Dimension | In engineering practice |
|---|---|
| **ENVIRONMENTAL** ← | **Resource use, emissions, ecology, land, water, waste** ← |
| **SOCIAL** ← | **Who benefits, who bears the costs, displacement, health, access, heritage** ← |
| **ECONOMIC** ← | **Whole-life cost, viability, and whether the benefits justify the resources** ← |

> **THE REQUIREMENT TO WEIGH THEM TOGETHER IS WHAT MAKES THE PRINCIPLE DEMANDING AND IT IS WHERE IT IS MOST OFTEN REDUCED TO SLOGANS: any one dimension considered alone gives a clear answer and usually the wrong one.**

> **The environmentally best option may be unaffordable; the cheapest may impose costs on people who were not consulted; the socially preferred may consume resources disproportionately.**

> **So sustainability is not a constraint added to a design but a method of evaluating it across three axes simultaneously, and the difficulty is that the three are measured in incommensurable units and there is no formula for trading them.**

> **That is why the principle requires judgement, transparency about the trade-offs made, and the involvement of those affected — rather than a checklist, which is how it is frequently operationalised and consequently emptied of content.**

**THE ENGINEER'S PRACTICAL LEVERS ARE WORTH LISTING BECAUSE THE PRINCIPLE OTHERWISE REMAINS ABSTRACT:**

| Lever | Note |
|---|---|
| **Question whether the project is NEEDED at all, and in that form** ← | **The largest lever, and the one most rarely used** ← |
| **Extend the asset's LIFE, and design it to be adaptable** ← | **The most sustainable structure is one that need not be rebuilt** ← |
| **Reduce material QUANTITIES through efficient design** ← | ← |
| **Choose lower-impact MATERIALS** ← | **Cement substitution, recycled aggregate, local sourcing** ← |
| **Reduce OPERATIONAL energy and water over the life** ← | **Usually larger than the embodied impact for a building** ← |
| **Design for DECONSTRUCTION and reuse at the end of life** ← | ← |
| **Minimise construction-stage impacts** ← | **Waste, spoil, emissions, disturbance** ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE ONE WITH THE LARGEST EFFECT AND THE LEAST ATTENTION, AND IT CONNECTS TO THE LIFE-CYCLE COSTING MATERIAL: a structure that lasts a hundred years rather than fifty halves its embodied impact per year of service.**

> **And one that can be ADAPTED to a different use, rather than demolished when its original purpose ends, may last far longer than its function does.**

> **Most buildings are demolished not because they have failed structurally but because they no longer suit any use — so adaptability, generous floor-to-floor heights, accessible services and a structure that permits internal change all extend an asset's real life far more than durability does.**

> **That reframing — designing for adaptability rather than merely for durability — is one of the more useful practical translations of the sustainability principle into a decision an engineer actually makes.**

> **THE FIRST ROW DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS THE MOST UNCOMFORTABLE: the most sustainable project is often the one not built.**

> **An engineer asked to design a road may be able to observe that the transport need could be met otherwise, or that the traffic forecast does not support it, or that a smaller intervention would suffice.**

> **Raising that is professionally difficult — it questions the commission that provides the fee — and it is within the engineer's obligation to give honest advice.**

> **So the sustainability principle, taken seriously, occasionally requires an engineer to argue against their own immediate interest, which is the same structure as every other genuine professional obligation in this subchapter and is the reason they are obligations rather than preferences.**

examTip.trick: **Meeting present needs without compromising future generations'** — weighing environmental, social and economic effects together.
examTip.trap: **The three are incommensurable, so there is no formula** — which is why it needs judgement and transparency, not a checklist.
examTip.mnemonic: **Design for ADAPTABILITY, not just durability** — most buildings are demolished because they suit no use, not because they failed.

questions.stem: When an engineer acts as the ENGINEER under a traditional construction contract (as in FIDIC), their role requires them to:
options: Act solely in the employer's interests at all times, since the employer pays the fee
Act solely in the contractor's interests when valuing their work
Act as the employer's AGENT in administering the contract
Take no decisions, referring all matters to the parties
questions.solution:
**Act as the employer's AGENT in administering the contract, but to act IMPARTIALLY and fairly when exercising the certifying and decision-making functions the contract confers** — a dual role that is the source of much of the position's difficulty.

**The two capacities:**

| Capacity | Examples | Standard |
|---|---|---|
| **AGENT of the employer** ← | **Issuing instructions, supervising, protecting the employer's interests** ← | **Act on the employer's behalf** ← |
| **Independent CERTIFIER and decision-maker** ← | **Certifying payment, valuing variations, granting extensions of time, deciding claims** ← | **Act FAIRLY and impartially between the parties** ← |

> **THE TENSION BETWEEN THE TWO ROWS IS REAL AND IT IS INHERENT RATHER THAN A DEFECT OF ANY PARTICULAR ARRANGEMENT: the same person is paid by one party and must decide impartially between that party and another.**

> **When certifying an extension of time, the engineer's decision costs the employer money, and the employer is their client.**

> **The contract nonetheless requires the decision to be made fairly, and the contractor's entitlement depends on it being so.**

> **So the engineer's professional integrity is the mechanism on which the contractor's rights rest, which is a considerable responsibility and is why the role is entrusted to a professional bound by an ethical code rather than to an employee of the employer.**

**THE PRESSURES ON THE ROLE ARE WORTH NAMING SINCE THEY ARE PREDICTABLE:**

| Pressure | Note |
|---|---|
| **The employer pays the fee and may appoint on future projects** ← | ← |
| **An extension of time granted costs the employer directly** ← | ← |
| **A certificate may cover work the engineer themselves designed** ← | **The structural conflict identified earlier** ← |
| **And the employer may express displeasure at decisions favouring the contractor** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRESSURE MOST COMMONLY APPLIED AND THE CORRECT RESPONSE IS WORTH STATING PLAINLY: the employer is entitled to make representations and is not entitled to direct the outcome.**

> **An engineer who decides a matter to please the employer has failed in the role, and the decision may be overturned later at the employer's cost.**

> **An engineer who decides fairly has done what the contract requires and what the employer, properly advised, actually wants — because a decision that will not survive review is worth nothing to them.**

> **So resisting the pressure serves the employer's real interest as well as the contractor's, which is a useful thing to be able to say when the pressure is applied.**

**THE MODERN TREND IS TO SEPARATE THE ROLES AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Development | Note |
|---|---|
| **Some forms replace 'the Engineer' with an 'Employer's Representative'** ← | **Openly partisan; no pretence of impartiality** ← |
| **With decisions referred instead to a DISPUTE BOARD or adjudicator** ← | **A genuinely independent third party** ← |
| **FIDIC's later editions strengthen the duty to act fairly and add a DAAB** ← | **Dispute Avoidance/Adjudication Board** ← |
| **NEC uses a Project Manager and a separate Adjudicator** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE CLEANER ARRANGEMENT IN PRINCIPLE AND THE TRADE IS WORTH UNDERSTANDING: separating the partisan and impartial functions removes the conflict entirely.**

> **The employer's representative advocates for the employer, and a genuinely independent body decides disputes.**

> **What is lost is the speed and the informed judgement of a decision-maker who is on the project daily and knows it intimately — a dispute board, however good, is not there every day.**

> **So the traditional engineer's role trades a structural conflict for immediacy and knowledge, and the modern separation trades immediacy for independence, and neither is obviously right — which is why both arrangements remain in use and the choice depends on the project's size, its dispute risk and the availability of an engineer whose impartiality both parties will accept.**
tags: the employer may represent not direct
fair decisions serve the employer too
separating the roles in modern forms

examTip.trick: **Agent of the employer in administration; IMPARTIAL when certifying and deciding** — a dual role held together by professional integrity.
examTip.trap: **The employer may make representations, not direct the outcome** — and a decision that will not survive review is worth nothing to them anyway.
examTip.mnemonic: **Modern forms separate the roles** — a partisan Employer's Representative plus an independent dispute board. Independence traded against daily knowledge.

questions.stem: An engineer's duty of CONFIDENTIALITY to a client:
options: Is absolute and can never be overridden in any circumstance
Applies only while the engagement continues, and ends at completion
Is a strong obligation that continues after the engagement ends
Applies only to written information, not to anything learned verbally
questions.solution:
**It is a strong obligation that continues after the engagement ends, but yields where DISCLOSURE IS NECESSARY to prevent danger to the public, or where disclosure is required by law.**

**The scope of the obligation:**

| Aspect | Note |
|---|---|
| **It covers information obtained IN CONFIDENCE during the engagement** ← | **Written and verbal alike** ← |
| **Commercial information, designs, methods, and the client's affairs** ← | ← |
| **It CONTINUES after the engagement ends** ← | **Indefinitely, for genuinely confidential information** ← |
| **It binds the engineer's staff and sub-consultants too** ← | ← |
| **And it prevents using the information for another client's benefit** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE ASPECT MOST OFTEN MISUNDERSTOOD AND IT MATTERS PRACTICALLY: the obligation does not expire with the contract.**

> **An engineer who worked for a client five years ago still may not disclose that client's confidential information, or use it to benefit a competitor.**

> **This becomes acute when an engineer moves between firms or takes on a client's competitor, and it is why such moves require care about what may be brought and what must be left behind.**

> **The fifth row is the related point: the obligation covers USE as well as disclosure, so an engineer who silently applies one client's confidential method to another's project has breached it without telling anybody anything.**

**THE EXCEPTIONS ARE NARROW AND THEY DESERVE PRECISE STATEMENT:**

| Exception | Note |
|---|---|
| **The client CONSENTS** ← | **The cleanest route; ask first wherever possible** ← |
| **Disclosure is required BY LAW** ← | **A court order, a statutory duty, a regulatory requirement** ← |
| **Necessary to prevent DANGER to the public** ← | **The public safety override** ← |
| **The information is already PUBLIC** ← | **Confidentiality attaches to confidential information only** ← |
| **Necessary for the engineer to defend themselves** ← | **In proceedings brought against them** ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE EXCEPTION THAT CONNECTS TO THE PARAMOUNT DUTY AND ITS LIMITS ARE WORTH UNDERSTANDING: it permits disclosure necessary to prevent danger, not disclosure of anything the engineer disapproves of.**

> **So the test is whether there is a genuine risk to public safety and whether disclosure is NECESSARY to address it — which means internal routes should be exhausted first, and the disclosure should go to those able to act rather than to the public at large.**

> **Disclosing to a regulator who can require action is proportionate; disclosing to the press when the regulator has not been approached generally is not.**

> **So the override is real and it is disciplined, and an engineer invoking it should be able to explain why the disclosure was necessary and why it was made to whom it was made.**

**THE PRACTICAL MANAGEMENT OF CONFIDENTIALITY DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Measure | Note |
|---|---|
| **A written confidentiality clause in the appointment** ← | **Defining what is confidential and for how long** ← |
| **Marking confidential documents as such** ← | **Which removes later argument about what was covered** ← |
| **Controlling circulation, and requiring the same of sub-consultants** ← | ← |
| **Secure storage and disposal** ← | ← |
| **And obtaining CONSENT before using a project in marketing** ← | **A common and easily avoided breach** ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS A BREACH THAT OCCURS CONSTANTLY WITHOUT ANY ILL INTENT AND IT IS WORTH FLAGGING: publishing a project on a website, in a brochure or in a conference paper discloses the client relationship, the project details and sometimes the design itself.**

> **Much of that may be perfectly acceptable to the client and some of it may not — a client may not wish its expansion plans, its costs or its security arrangements published.**

> **Asking takes a message and usually produces agreement, often with helpful suggestions about what may be said.**

> **Not asking risks a breach over something the client would readily have permitted, which is the most avoidable kind of professional failure there is.**
tags: covers use as well as disclosure
the public safety override is disciplined

examTip.trick: **Strong and continuing, but yielding to legal requirement and to necessary prevention of public danger.**
examTip.trap: **It continues after the engagement and covers USE as well as disclosure** — applying a past client's method silently is still a breach.
examTip.mnemonic: **Ask before publishing a project in marketing** — the most avoidable breach, over something usually readily permitted.

questions.stem: In relation to CORRUPTION in construction procurement, the most effective structural defences are:
options: Relying on the personal integrity of the individuals involved

TRANSPARENCY in procurement, separation of duties so no one person controls a process end to end, competitive and openly advertised tendering, independent audit, and effective protection for those who report wrongdoing
Increasing the penalties for those who are caught
Reducing the number of people involved in each decision
questions.solution:
**TRANSPARENCY in procurement, separation of duties so no one person controls a process end to end, competitive and openly advertised tendering, independent audit, and effective protection for those who report wrongdoing.**

**Why construction is particularly exposed:**

| Factor | Note |
|---|---|
| **Very large sums, in discrete transactions** ← | ← |
| **Every project is UNIQUE, so prices cannot be simply compared** ← | ← |
| **Long supply chains with many intermediaries** ← | ← |
| **Much of the work becomes CONCEALED once built** ← | **Substandard work is hard to detect afterwards** ← |
| **Many discretionary decisions — variations, extensions, valuations** ← | ← |
| **And close, repeated relationships between the same parties** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE FACTOR PECULIAR TO CONSTRUCTION AND IT IS THE MOST DANGEROUS: a substandard foundation, an omitted reinforcement bar, an under-thickness pavement layer becomes invisible the moment the next operation covers it.**

> **So corruption in construction can produce not merely financial loss but structures that fail, and the failure may occur years later with no obvious connection to its cause.**

> **That is why anti-corruption in this industry is a public safety matter and not only a financial one, and why the engineer's professional obligation engages directly with it.**

> **It also explains why independent inspection at the moment work is covered is so disproportionately valuable — it is the only opportunity to verify what will otherwise never be seen again.**

**THE STRUCTURAL DEFENCES WORK BECAUSE THEY DO NOT DEPEND ON INDIVIDUALS AND THAT IS THE POINT OPTION (a) MISSES:**

| Defence | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **SEPARATION of duties** ← | **Specification, tendering, evaluation, award, supervision and payment in different hands** ← |
| **TRANSPARENCY** ← | **Published tender notices, opened in public, results disclosed** ← |
| **Objective EVALUATION criteria, published in advance** ← | **Removing discretion from the award** ← |
| **Independent AUDIT and inspection** ← | ← |
| **Rotation of staff in vulnerable positions** ← | ← |
| **Protection for WHISTLEBLOWERS** ← | ← |
| **And integrity pacts, in which all bidders commit publicly** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE SINGLE MOST EFFECTIVE MEASURE AND THE REASON IS THAT IT RAISES THE NUMBER OF PEOPLE WHO MUST COLLUDE: one person controlling a process end to end can act alone.**

> **Splitting it among four means four people must agree to act corruptly, each of whom risks exposure by the others.**

> **The probability of successful collusion falls sharply with the number involved, and each additional participant is an additional point of possible disclosure.**

> **So separation of duties does not rely on any individual being honest — it relies on the difficulty of finding several people who are not, simultaneously, in the same place.**

**THE ENGINEER'S PERSONAL POSITION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS WHERE THE PRINCIPLE BECOMES CONCRETE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Offering, accepting or facilitating a bribe is misconduct and usually a crime** ← | ← |
| **The prohibition covers FACILITATION payments in most modern frameworks** ← | **Small payments to expedite routine actions** ← |
| **It covers gifts and hospitality beyond the modest and customary** ← | ← |
| **And it extends to acts by agents and intermediaries on one's behalf** ← | **One cannot outsource the offence** ← |
| **Refusing is easier where the position is known in advance and stated early** ← | ← |

> **THE LAST ROW IS THE PRACTICAL ADVICE THAT MAKES THE OTHERS ACTIONABLE AND IT IS WORTH TAKING: an engineer who has decided in advance where their line is, and who has said so early in a relationship, is rarely asked.**

> **The request comes to those whose position is unknown, and it comes in a form that allows retreat if refused.**

> **So making the position clear at the outset — declining the first small gift, stating the organisation's policy — prevents the situation from developing rather than requiring it to be resisted later under pressure.**

> **That is a far easier course than refusing a substantial request in a moment of difficulty, and it is the reason anti-corruption training concentrates on early signals and small beginnings rather than on the dramatic decision that rarely presents itself cleanly.**
tags: concealed work makes it a safety matter
separation of duties raises collusion cost

examTip.trick: **Transparency, separation of duties, open competition, independent audit, whistleblower protection** — structural, not personal.
examTip.trap: **Construction's work becomes CONCEALED** — so corruption here can produce failures, not merely losses. Inspection before covering is critical.
examTip.mnemonic: **Separation works by raising the number who must collude** — it does not rely on anyone being honest.

questions.stem: WHISTLEBLOWING by an engineer is generally considered justified when:
options: There is a serious and specific danger or wrongdoing
The engineer disagrees with a management decision on commercial grounds
The engineer has been passed over for promotion
Any time the engineer believes the organisation could operate better
questions.solution:
**There is a serious and specific danger or wrongdoing, the engineer has a reasonable and well-founded belief based on EVIDENCE, INTERNAL routes have been exhausted or are demonstrably unavailable, and the disclosure is made to a party able to act and is proportionate in its extent.**

**The conditions, all of which matter:**

| Condition | Note |
|---|---|
| **The matter is SERIOUS** ← | **Danger to people, substantial fraud, significant legal breach — not a disagreement** ← |
| **The belief is REASONABLE and evidence-based** ← | **Not a suspicion or an inference from resentment** ← |
| **INTERNAL channels have been tried, or are futile or unsafe** ← | **Giving the organisation the chance to put it right** ← |
| **The disclosure goes to someone ABLE TO ACT** ← | **A regulator, a client, an authority — escalating outward only as needed** ← |
| **It is PROPORTIONATE in extent** ← | **Disclosing what is necessary, not everything known** ← |
| **And the motive is the public interest, not personal grievance** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE CONDITION THAT MOST OFTEN DISTINGUISHES A JUSTIFIED DISCLOSURE FROM AN UNJUSTIFIED ONE AND IT IS FAIR TO THE ORGANISATION AS WELL AS SENSIBLE: most wrongdoing discovered by an employee is not organisational policy.**

> **It is an individual's decision, and the organisation's senior management would stop it if they knew.**

> **So raising it internally usually resolves it, quickly and without damage to anyone.**

> **Going straight outside denies the organisation that opportunity and escalates a situation that might have been settled in a conversation — which is why the internal route comes first, unless there is good reason to believe it is compromised or that using it would allow evidence to be destroyed or the discloser to be victimised.**

**THE SIXTH ROW DESERVES CAREFUL TREATMENT BECAUSE MOTIVE IS OFTEN MIXED AND THAT IS NORMAL:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A discloser often has grievances as well as concerns** ← | ← |
| **Mixed motives do not make a true disclosure false** ← | ← |
| **But they will be used to discredit the discloser** ← | ← |
| **So the disclosure should rest on EVIDENCE that stands independently** ← | ← |
| **And should be framed around the danger, not around the individuals** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE PRACTICAL PROTECTION AND IT IS WORTH ACTING ON BEFORE DISCLOSING: a disclosure supported by documents, records and dates survives an attack on the discloser's motives.**

> **One resting on the discloser's account alone does not, and the response to it will be an examination of the discloser rather than of the concern.**

> **So assembling the evidence, recording dates and keeping copies of relevant documents — obtained legitimately in the course of one's work — is the single most useful preparatory step.**

> **And framing the disclosure around what is unsafe rather than around who is to blame keeps the recipient's attention on the thing that matters and gives them something they can act on.**

**THE PROTECTIONS AND THEIR LIMITS DESERVE THE CLOSING NOTE, HONESTLY STATED:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Many jurisdictions provide legal protection against retaliation** ← | ← |
| **Protection typically depends on following a prescribed procedure** ← | **Disclosing to the wrong body may forfeit it** ← |
| **It protects against dismissal and detriment, in principle** ← | ← |
| **In practice it is slow, adversarial and does not undo the damage** ← | ← |
| **And careers are frequently harmed regardless of the law** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND FIFTH ROWS SHOULD NOT BE CONCEALED FROM ANYONE CONSIDERING THIS COURSE: legal protection is real and it is not equivalent to safety.**

> **A discloser may win a tribunal case years later and still have lost their position, their standing and their working relationships.**

> **Knowing that in advance is better than discovering it, and it argues for taking advice early, using internal and confidential routes where they exist, and documenting everything.**

> **It does not argue for silence where there is serious danger — the obligation stands regardless of the cost — and the honest position is that this is one of the few situations in professional life where doing the right thing may genuinely cost a great deal, which is precisely why it is a professional obligation rather than an expectation.**
tags: proportionate disclosure to those who can act

examTip.trick: **Serious danger, reasonable evidence-based belief, internal routes exhausted, disclosed proportionately to someone who can act.**
examTip.trap: **Try internal routes first** — most wrongdoing is an individual's act that senior management would stop if they knew.
examTip.mnemonic: **Assemble evidence that stands without you** — mixed motives will be used to discredit a disclosure resting on your account alone.

questions.stem: A CLIENT instructs an engineer to certify payment for work that the engineer knows has not been executed. The engineer should:
options: Certify it, since the client is entitled to direct the engineer's work
Certify it but note the discrepancy in a file record
REFUSE to certify
Certify a reduced amount as a compromise
questions.solution:
**REFUSE to certify, because a certificate is a professional statement of fact upon which others rely**, and certifying work that has not been done is a false statement regardless of who requested it.

**What a certificate is and why it cannot be negotiated:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A certificate is a professional STATEMENT OF FACT** ← | **That specified work has been done, to a specified standard, to a specified value** ← |
| **Others RELY on it** ← | **The employer pays on it; funders release money on it; auditors accept it** ← |
| **Its value depends entirely on its being TRUE** ← | ← |
| **So a certificate issued to accommodate anyone is worthless and is a false statement** ← | ← |
| **And the engineer signing it is personally responsible for its content** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW EXPLAINS WHY THIS IS NOT MERELY A MATTER BETWEEN THE ENGINEER AND THE CLIENT AND IT IS THE POINT THAT DISPOSES OF OPTION (a): a certificate is used by people who are not parties to the conversation.**

> **A lender advancing funds against certified progress, an auditor verifying expenditure, a government releasing a grant instalment — each relies on the certificate being accurate.**

> **So a false certificate deceives parties who never asked for it and never had the opportunity to question it.**

> **That takes it outside anything the client could properly authorise, because the client cannot consent on behalf of those third parties — which is why a client's instruction has no bearing on the answer.**

**THE PROPER RESPONSE IS A SEQUENCE AND IT IS WORTH HAVING IN MIND:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **Certify what HAS been done, accurately and promptly** ← | **The engineer's obligation is to certify correctly, not to withhold** ← |
| **Explain in writing why the balance is not certified** ← | **Which work is incomplete, and what would be needed** ← |
| **Offer to re-certify as soon as the work is executed** ← | ← |
| **If pressed, state the position clearly and in writing** ← | ← |
| **Escalate or resign the role if the pressure persists** ← | ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW MATTERS BECAUSE REFUSAL IS NOT THE SAME AS OBSTRUCTION, AND THE DISTINCTION PROTECTS THE ENGINEER'S POSITION: an engineer who certifies accurately and promptly, including everything genuinely done, is plainly acting properly.**

> **One who withholds certification of legitimate work, or delays it, is failing in the other direction and may be liable to the contractor for doing so.**

> **So the answer to an improper request is a correct certificate rather than no certificate, which leaves the engineer's conduct unimpeachable and makes the disagreement specifically about the disputed portion.**

> **That narrows the conflict to the actual issue and makes it far easier to resolve than a general breakdown over certification.**

**THE SAME PRINCIPLE EXTENDS TO EVERY PROFESSIONAL CERTIFICATE AND THE LIST IS WORTH HAVING:**

| Certificate | What is being stated |
|---|---|
| **Interim payment certificate** ← | **Work of this value has been properly executed** ← |
| **Practical completion certificate** ← | **The works are complete for practical purposes** ← |
| **Making good defects certificate** ← | **Defects have been remedied** ← |
| **Structural stability certificate** ← | **The structure is safe and complies** ← |
| **Test certificates and material approvals** ← | **The material or the work meets the specification** ← |
| **Completion certificates for regulatory purposes** ← | **Compliance with the building code or permit conditions** ← |

> **THE FOURTH AND SIXTH ROWS CARRY THE HEAVIEST CONSEQUENCES AND THEY DESERVE PARTICULAR CARE: a structural or regulatory certificate is relied upon by occupants and by authorities who have no other means of knowing.**

> **Issuing one without having verified its content — signing off a structure one has not inspected, or a test one did not witness — is a serious breach even where the work turns out to be sound.**

> **The breach is in certifying without knowledge, not in the outcome, because the certificate asserts knowledge that the engineer did not have.**

> **So the discipline is to certify only what one has personally verified or has a proper documented basis to accept — and where that basis does not exist, to obtain it before signing rather than to sign and hope, which is the habit that turns an isolated accommodation into a routine one.**
tags: a certificate is a statement of fact
certifying without knowledge is the breach

examTip.trick: **Refuse** — a certificate is a statement of fact relied upon by others, and its value depends on being true.
examTip.trap: **Third parties rely on it** — lenders, auditors, authorities. The client cannot consent on their behalf, so the instruction is irrelevant.
examTip.mnemonic: **Certify what HAS been done, promptly, and explain the balance** — a correct certificate, not no certificate.

questions.stem: The professional relationship between an engineer and a client is generally one of:
options: A FIDUCIARY-like relationship of trust and confidence
A simple commercial transaction in which each party pursues its own interest
An employment relationship in which the client directs the work
A partnership in which profits and losses are shared
questions.solution:
**A FIDUCIARY-like relationship of trust and confidence, in which the engineer must act in the client's best interests within the bounds of their wider professional obligations, disclose anything material, and not profit secretly from the engagement.**

**The duties that follow:**

| Duty | Note |
|---|---|
| **Act in the client's best interests** ← | **Subject to the paramount duty to the public and to the law** ← |
| **Exercise reasonable skill and care** ← | ← |
| **DISCLOSE anything material to the client's decisions** ← | **Including bad news and one's own errors** ← |
| **Not to make a SECRET PROFIT** ← | **No undisclosed commissions, discounts or benefits** ← |
| **Avoid or disclose conflicts of interest** ← | ← |
| **Keep the client's affairs confidential** ← | ← |
| **Give honest advice, including advice the client will not welcome** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DUTY MOST OFTEN BREACHED WITHOUT THE ENGINEER REGARDING IT AS A BREACH, AND THE RULE IS STRICTER THAN INTUITION SUGGESTS: any benefit received in connection with the engagement, from anyone other than the client, must be disclosed.**

> **A discount from a supplier, a commission on a specified product, a fee for a referral — each is a benefit arising from the engineer's position and belongs to the client unless they agree otherwise.**

> **Retaining it secretly is a breach even where the advice given was entirely sound, because the client is entitled to know what influences may bear on the advice they are paying for.**

> **So the rule is disclose and obtain consent, and a benefit the client agrees the engineer may keep is entirely proper — which makes compliance straightforward and makes concealment the only real offence.**

**THE SEVENTH ROW IS THE DUTY THAT MOST DISTINGUISHES A PROFESSIONAL FROM A SUPPLIER AND IT DESERVES EMPHASIS:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A supplier gives the customer what they ask for** ← | ← |
| **A professional gives the client their honest judgement** ← | ← |
| **Even where it is that the client's plan is unwise** ← | ← |
| **Or that the project is not viable** ← | ← |
| **Or that the engineer's own earlier advice was wrong** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD AND FOURTH ROWS DESCRIBE ADVICE THAT WORKS AGAINST THE ENGINEER'S IMMEDIATE INTEREST AND THAT IS PRECISELY WHY IT IS OWED: telling a client their proposed scheme should not proceed may end the commission.**

> **A supplier would not do it and a professional must.**

> **The client is paying for judgement, and judgement that is withheld when it is unwelcome is not judgement at all.**

> **This is the same structure as every other professional obligation examined here — the duty binds precisely where it is costly, because that is the only situation in which it has any content.**

**THE LIMITS OF THE DUTY TO THE CLIENT DESERVE THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE THEY ARE WHAT PREVENT IT BECOMING ADVOCACY:**

| Limit | Note |
|---|---|
| **The PUBLIC's safety comes first** ← | ← |
| **The law comes first** ← | ← |
| **The duty to act fairly when certifying comes first** ← | **Where the engineer holds that role** ← |
| **And honesty toward third parties is not suspended** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS WORTH STATING EXPLICITLY BECAUSE IT IS SOMETIMES ASSUMED OTHERWISE: acting in the client's interests does not permit misleading anyone else on the client's behalf.**

> **An engineer may advocate for their client's position, present it in its best light and decline to volunteer information that is not theirs to give.**

> **They may not state something they know to be untrue, to a contractor, a regulator, a neighbour or a tribunal.**

> **So the duty to the client is a duty of loyalty and diligence within honest bounds, and a client who expects it to extend further has misunderstood what they engaged — which is a conversation better had at the outset than at the moment the expectation surfaces.**
tags: limits preventing advocacy from becoming deception

examTip.trick: **A relationship of trust — best interests, full disclosure, no secret profit** — bounded by the wider professional obligations.
examTip.trap: **Any benefit from a third party must be disclosed** — a supplier's discount belongs to the client unless they agree otherwise.
examTip.mnemonic: **A supplier gives what is asked; a professional gives honest judgement** — including that the scheme should not proceed.

questions.stem: CONTINUING PROFESSIONAL DEVELOPMENT (CPD) requirements for registered engineers exist principally because:
options: Professional bodies need a source of income from training courses
Engineering knowledge, codes, materials and methods CHANGE continuously
CPD demonstrates loyalty to the professional body
It provides a means of ranking engineers against one another
questions.solution:
**Engineering knowledge, codes, materials and methods CHANGE continuously, so competence established at qualification decays unless it is actively maintained** — and the public relies on registration as an assurance of CURRENT competence.

**What changes over a career:**

| Area | Note |
|---|---|
| **CODES and standards are revised** ← | **Often substantially — a seismic code may change its whole basis** ← |
| **MATERIALS and products develop** ← | **New binders, admixtures, composites, systems** ← |
| **METHODS and technology change** ← | **Analysis software, survey equipment, construction techniques, BIM** ← |
| **REGULATION and law change** ← | **Environmental, safety, procurement, contract forms** ← |
| **And the state of KNOWLEDGE advances** ← | **Failures teach lessons; research changes understanding** ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE MOST IMPORTANT AND THE LEAST VISIBLE, AND IT IS WHERE CPD DELIVERS ITS REAL VALUE: the profession learns from failures, and an engineer who does not follow that learning repeats errors the profession has already understood.**

> **The lessons of a bridge collapse, a dam failure, a building fire or a tunnel inundation propagate through codes eventually, and they propagate through the professional literature and conferences first.**

> **An engineer who reads only the code they were taught is working from the state of knowledge as it was compiled some years before they qualified.**

> **So keeping current is not about accumulating hours; it is about not making mistakes that someone else has already made and documented.**

**WHAT COUNTS AS CPD IS BROADER THAN COURSES AND THAT IS WORTH KNOWING:**

| Activity | Note |
|---|---|
| **Structured courses, seminars and conferences** ← | **The most visible form** ← |
| **Reading journals, codes, technical publications** ← | ← |
| **Learning on the job from new types of work** ← | **Often the most valuable, and the hardest to evidence** ← |
| **Teaching, mentoring and presenting** ← | **Which requires understanding more deeply than doing** ← |
| **Research, committee work and standards development** ← | ← |
| **Site visits to unfamiliar types of work** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS WHERE MOST ENGINEERS ACTUALLY LEARN AND IT IS SYSTEMATICALLY UNDER-RECORDED BECAUSE IT PRODUCES NO CERTIFICATE: the first time one designs an unfamiliar structure, supervises a new technique or investigates a failure, a great deal is learned.**

> **A CPD system that counts only attendance at courses measures the least of it.**

> **Good schemes are therefore OUTPUT-based rather than hours-based — asking what the engineer learned and how their practice changed, rather than how many hours they sat in a room.**

> **The fourth row deserves its own note because it is under-appreciated: preparing to teach a subject exposes gaps in one's own understanding that using it daily never does, which makes teaching one of the more efficient forms of development available.**

**THE CONNECTION TO REGISTRATION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Registration tells the public that an engineer is competent** ← | ← |
| **If it were granted once for life, it would tell them only that they WERE competent** ← | ← |
| **Which is not what the public needs to know** ← | ← |
| **So registration is periodically renewed, conditional on CPD** ← | ← |
| **Making the register an assurance of CURRENT standing** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE POINT THAT JUSTIFIES THE WHOLE ARRANGEMENT AND IT FOLLOWS FROM THE PUBLIC-TRUST ARGUMENT MADE EARLIER: a member of the public who checks a register wants to know whether this engineer can be relied upon now.**

> **A lifetime registration answers a different and less useful question.**

> **So periodic renewal with a CPD condition is what makes the register mean what people take it to mean, and it is a requirement of the profession's credibility rather than an administrative imposition on its members.**

> **Seen that way, an engineer who treats CPD as a box to be ticked has misunderstood what their registration represents — and is relying on an assurance to the public that they are personally declining to maintain.**

examTip.trick: **Knowledge, codes and methods change, so competence decays** — and the register must assure CURRENT competence.
examTip.trap: **Most real learning is on the job and produces no certificate** — good CPD schemes are output-based, not hours-based.
examTip.mnemonic: **Lifetime registration would only certify that someone WAS competent** — which is not what the public needs to know.

questions.stem: In relation to INTELLECTUAL PROPERTY in engineering design, the general position under a standard consultancy appointment is that:
options: The client automatically owns the copyright in all drawings and documents produced
Copyright is jointly owned by the designer and the contractor
Copyright does not apply to engineering drawings
The designer retains COPYRIGHT in their drawings and documents, and the client is granted a LICENSE to use them for the purposes of the project
questions.solution:
**The designer retains COPYRIGHT in their drawings and documents, and the client is granted a LICENSE to use them for the purposes of the project** — with the precise position depending on what the appointment says, which is why it should say so explicitly.

**The default position and why it surprises clients:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Copyright arises automatically in an original work when it is created** ← | **No registration is required** ← |
| **It belongs to the AUTHOR, unless assigned or created as an employee** ← | ← |
| **So a consultant retains copyright in what they produce** ← | ← |
| **Paying for the work does NOT transfer copyright** ← | **The client has bought the service, not the intellectual property** ← |
| **What the client needs is a LICENSE to use it** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE POINT THAT CAUSES DISPUTES AND IT IS COUNTER-INTUITIVE TO CLIENTS: having paid for drawings, a client naturally assumes they own them.**

> **They own the physical or electronic copies and they do not own the copyright, in the same way that buying a book does not permit reprinting it.**

> **So their right to use the drawings comes from the license, and the license's terms determine what they may do — build the project, certainly, but perhaps not build a second identical one, and perhaps not give the drawings to another engineer to develop.**

> **This should be settled in the appointment, and the argument that follows from leaving it unstated is entirely avoidable.**

**THE LICENSE'S TERMS ARE WHAT MATTER IN PRACTICE AND THEY ARE WORTH ENUMERATING:**

| Term | Question it answers |
|---|---|
| **SCOPE — for what purpose** ← | **This project only, or any project?** ← |
| **EXTENT — construction, maintenance, extension, reconstruction?** ← | ← |
| **Whether it is IRREVOCABLE** ← | **Can the designer withdraw it?** ← |
| **Whether it survives non-payment** ← | **Commonly it does not — a real lever for the designer** ← |
| **Whether it is transferable to a purchaser of the asset** ← | ← |
| **Whether it permits use by ANOTHER designer** ← | **Which the original designer may resist, for liability reasons** ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE DESIGNER'S MOST EFFECTIVE PROTECTION AGAINST NON-PAYMENT AND IT IS WORTH KNOWING: an appointment commonly provides that the license is conditional on the fees being paid.**

> **A client who has not paid therefore has no right to use the drawings, and using them is an infringement.**

> **That is a considerably stronger position than suing for the fee, because it can stop the project rather than merely producing a claim.**

> **So the clause is worth having and worth understanding — and a client negotiating it away should understand that they are removing the designer's principal security, which will be reflected in the terms elsewhere.**

**THE LAST ROW OF THE LICENSE TABLE DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT INVOLVES LIABILITY RATHER THAN OWNERSHIP:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **A designer resists another engineer developing their design** ← | ← |
| **Not chiefly for commercial reasons** ← | ← |
| **But because they may be blamed for the result** ← | ← |
| **A design altered by someone else may fail, and the original name is on the drawings** ← | ← |
| **So licenses commonly exclude liability for use beyond the original purpose** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE STANDARD RESOLUTION AND IT IS A FAIR ONE: the client may use the material for other purposes, and the designer is not responsible for what results.**

> **That gives the client the flexibility they want and protects the designer from liability for work they did not control.**

> **It requires the exclusion to be clearly recorded, because a court will otherwise ask whether the designer ought to have foreseen the further use.**

> **And it reflects a general principle worth carrying: where one party wants freedom to act and the other fears the consequences, allocating the freedom and the risk to the same party resolves the conflict, whereas splitting them guarantees a dispute when something goes wrong.**
tags: liability for use beyond the original purpose

examTip.trick: **The designer keeps copyright; the client gets a license for the project** — subject to what the appointment actually says.
examTip.trap: **Paying for drawings does not buy the copyright** — the client owns the copies, as a book buyer owns the book but not the right to reprint it.
examTip.mnemonic: **A license conditional on payment can stop a project** — a far stronger remedy than suing for the fee.

questions.stem: An engineer discovers, after a structure has been completed and occupied, that a design error means it does not meet the required factor of safety, though it has not failed. The engineer should:
options: Say nothing, since the structure is standing and disclosure would damage their reputation
Wait to see whether any distress appears before taking action
IMMEDIATELY inform those who can act
Inform their professional indemnity insurer only, and take no other action
questions.solution:
**IMMEDIATELY inform those who can act — the owner, and where appropriate the regulatory authority — assess the actual risk, advise on interim measures, and arrange for the deficiency to be remedied.**

**Why immediate disclosure is required:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **People are occupying the structure now** ← | ← |
| **They are exposed to a risk they do not know about and did not accept** ← | ← |
| **Only the owner and the authority can act to protect them** ← | ← |
| **And they cannot act on information they do not have** ← | ← |
| **The engineer's discomfort is not a consideration that can weigh against this** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND ROW IS THE HEART OF THE OBLIGATION AND IT CONNECTS DIRECTLY TO THE PARAMOUNT DUTY: the occupants have no way of knowing and no means of protecting themselves.**

> **Their safety depends entirely on whoever holds the information acting on it.**

> **The structure standing today is not evidence that it is adequate — an inadequate factor of safety means reduced margin against the loads it has not yet seen, not certainty of collapse.**

> **So waiting for distress, as option (b) proposes, means waiting for the margin to be tested by an event, which is precisely what the factor of safety exists to prevent and is not a course any professional can defend.**

**THE SEQUENCE OF ACTION MATTERS AND IT IS WORTH SETTING OUT:**

| Step | Note |
|---|---|
| **1. ASSESS the actual risk urgently** ← | **How deficient, under what loading, with what likelihood and consequence** ← |
| **2. Inform the OWNER immediately, in writing** ← | ← |
| **3. Advise on INTERIM measures** ← | **Load restriction, propping, partial evacuation, monitoring** ← |
| **4. Notify the regulatory authority where required or where the risk warrants** ← | ← |
| **5. Notify the professional indemnity insurer** ← | **A condition of most policies, and it must not delay steps 1 to 4** ← |
| **6. Arrange and oversee the REMEDY** ← | ← |
| **7. Record everything contemporaneously** ← | ← |

> **THE ORDER OF STEPS 3 AND 5 IS THE POINT ON WHICH OPTION (d) FAILS AND IT IS WORTH BEING EXPLICIT: notifying the insurer is necessary and it is not a substitute for anything.**

> **Most policies require prompt notification of circumstances that may give rise to a claim, and failing to notify can void the cover.**

> **But an insurer's interest is in managing a financial claim, and the engineer's obligation is to protect people.**

> **So the insurer is told, and the people at risk are told first — and an engineer whose insurer or lawyer advises them to say nothing to the owner has received advice that conflicts with their professional obligation and must follow the obligation.**

**THE FIRST STEP DESERVES EMPHASIS BECAUSE PROPORTIONATE ACTION DEPENDS ON IT:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **'Does not meet the required factor of safety' covers a wide range** ← | ← |
| **A factor of 1.4 where 1.5 was required is a different matter from 0.9** ← | ← |
| **The response should be proportionate to the actual risk** ← | ← |
| **But the DISCLOSURE is required in either case** ← | ← |
| **Because the decision about what to do is the owner's and the authority's, not solely the engineer's** ← | ← |

> **THE FIFTH ROW IS THE PRINCIPLE THAT SETTLES ANY REMAINING HESITATION AND IT IS WORTH HOLDING: the engineer's role is to provide the information and the technical assessment, not to decide alone whether the risk is acceptable to others.**

> **An owner may decide to close a building, restrict its use, strengthen it or accept a monitored risk — and that is their decision to take, informed by the engineer's advice.**

> **An engineer who decides privately that the risk is tolerable and says nothing has taken a decision that was not theirs to take, on behalf of people who were never consulted.**

> **That is the same failure as concealment, arrived at through reasoning that feels responsible — and recognising it as the same failure is what prevents a professional from talking themselves into it.**
tags: discovering one's own error after completion
standing is not evidence of adequacy
the risk decision belongs to others

examTip.trick: **Inform immediately, assess the risk, advise interim measures, arrange the remedy** — and record everything.
examTip.trap: **Standing today is not evidence of adequacy** — a low factor of safety means reduced margin against loads not yet seen.
examTip.mnemonic: **Tell the insurer too, but never instead** — and advice to stay silent conflicts with the obligation, which prevails.

questions.stem: TENDER PRICE COLLUSION between contractors — such as cover pricing, bid rotation or market sharing — is damaging principally because it:
options: Makes the tender evaluation process take longer
Results in too many tenders being submitted
Is inconvenient for the contractors involved
DEFEATS the competition that the tendering process exists to create
questions.solution:
**DEFEATS the competition that the tendering process exists to create** — so the employer pays more than a competitive price, the appearance of competition conceals its absence, and public funds are wasted with no visible sign that anything is wrong.

**The common forms:**

| Form | Mechanism |
|---|---|
| **COVER PRICING** ← | **A contractor who does not want the work submits a deliberately high price supplied by a competitor, so as to appear to compete** ← |
| **BID ROTATION** ← | **Competitors take turns to win, each submitting high prices when it is not their turn** ← |
| **BID SUPPRESSION** ← | **A competitor agrees not to bid, or withdraws** ← |
| **MARKET SHARING** ← | **Competitors agree not to compete in one another's territories or sectors** ← |
| **Compensation payments** ← | **The winner pays the losers for their cooperation, recovered in the price** ← |

> **THE FIRST ROW IS THE MOST COMMON AND IT IS OFTEN REGARDED BY PARTICIPANTS AS HARMLESS, WHICH IS WHY IT DESERVES SPECIFIC ATTENTION: a contractor too busy to tender does not want to decline and lose their place on the list, so they obtain a high price from a competitor and submit it.**

> **They do not expect to win and they gain nothing directly.**

> **It nonetheless deceives the employer, who believes they received three competitive tenders and received two — and the absence of a genuine third bid may have allowed the other two to price higher.**

> **So the practice that feels like an administrative courtesy is a deception about the level of competition, and it is unlawful in most jurisdictions precisely because its harm is invisible to the person harmed.**

**THE SIGNS THAT MAY INDICATE COLLUSION ARE WORTH KNOWING SINCE DETECTION IS THE MAIN DEFENCE:**

| Sign | Note |
|---|---|
| **The same contractor always wins in a particular area or sector** ← | ← |
| **A regular pattern in who wins** ← | **Suggesting rotation** ← |
| **Losing bids clustered well above the winner, with the winner isolated below** ← | ← |
| **Identical arithmetic errors or wording in different tenders** ← | **A strong indicator of a common source** ← |
| **A bidder who withdraws late without explanation** ← | ← |
| **Prices that fall sharply when a new bidder enters** ← | ← |
| **Subcontracts awarded by the winner to the losing bidders** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS THE MOST DIRECT EVIDENCE AND IT IS SURPRISINGLY COMMON BECAUSE COVER PRICES ARE OFTEN PREPARED CARELESSLY: the same transposed digit, the same unusual phrasing or the same formatting in two supposedly independent tenders indicates a shared origin.**

> **Tender evaluations rarely look for it, because the evaluator is comparing totals rather than examining documents for common features.**

> **A deliberate check — comparing the losing bids with each other rather than only against the winner — costs little and occasionally finds something.**

> **The last row is similarly informative and similarly overlooked: a winner who subcontracts substantial packages to the firms that lost against them is a pattern worth noticing, though it has innocent explanations too.**

**THE ENGINEER'S POSITION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE BECAUSE IT IS OFTEN A PASSIVE ONE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **An engineer advising on tenders may see the indicators** ← | ← |
| **They are not usually the decision-maker on procurement** ← | ← |
| **But they are competent to recognise an implausible bid pattern** ← | ← |
| **And they have an obligation to report a reasonable suspicion** ← | ← |
| **To the client, and where appropriate to the competition authority** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW FOLLOWS FROM THE DUTIES ALREADY ESTABLISHED AND IT IS WORTH DRAWING OUT EXPLICITLY: the engineer's duty to act in the client's interests includes telling them when the price they are about to accept may not be a competitive one.**

> **That is uncomfortable, particularly where the contractors concerned are firms the engineer works with regularly.**

> **The discomfort is precisely the mechanism by which collusion persists in a small industry where everyone knows everyone.**

> **So the obligation is to raise a reasonable suspicion with the client and to let them decide what to do with it — which is a lower bar than proving anything, and is the contribution the engineer is actually in a position to make.**
tags: cover pricing bid rotation market sharing
harm is invisible to the victim
compare losing bids with each other
the engineer's duty to report suspicion

examTip.trick: **It defeats the competition the process exists to create** — while preserving its appearance, so nothing looks wrong.
examTip.trap: **Cover pricing feels like an administrative courtesy** — and it deceives the employer about how many genuine bids they received.
examTip.mnemonic: **Compare the LOSING bids with each other** — shared arithmetic errors or wording indicate a common source. Rarely checked.

questions.stem: An engineer is asked to review and comment on work carried out by another engineer. Professional practice requires that they:
options: Decline in all circumstances, as reviewing a colleague's work is unprofessional
Carry out the review objectively and confine comment to technical substance
Find fault wherever possible, to demonstrate the value of the review
Approve the work without detailed examination, out of professional courtesy
questions.solution:
**Carry out the review objectively and confine comment to technical substance, inform the other engineer where circumstances permit, and avoid gratuitous criticism** — while never allowing collegial consideration to suppress a genuine and material concern.

**The competing obligations that must be reconciled:**

| Obligation | Note |
|---|---|
| **To the client who commissioned the review — an honest, competent opinion** ← | ← |
| **To the PUBLIC — to identify anything unsafe** ← | ← |
| **To the other engineer — fairness, and not to injure their reputation unjustly** ← | ← |
| **To the profession — to maintain its standing** ← | ← |

> **THE SECOND AND THIRD ROWS ARE WHERE THE TENSION LIES AND THE PRIORITY IS SETTLED BY THE HIERARCHY ALREADY ESTABLISHED: where the review finds something genuinely unsafe, the duty to the public prevails absolutely and collegial consideration is irrelevant.**

> **Where the review finds matters of judgement on which reasonable engineers could differ, the other engineer's position deserves respect and the comment should reflect that there is more than one defensible approach.**

> **So the distinction to draw is between a DEFICIENCY and a DIFFERENCE OF OPINION, and a reviewer who presents the latter as the former does an injustice and misleads their client.**

> **Making that distinction explicit in the report — 'this does not comply' against 'I would have approached this differently' — is what allows both obligations to be met at once.**

**THE COURTESY OF INFORMING THE OTHER ENGINEER DESERVES EXPLANATION SINCE ITS PURPOSE IS PRACTICAL:**

| Reason | Note |
|---|---|
| **They may have information the reviewer lacks** ← | **A constraint, an instruction, a superseded assumption** ← |
| **What looks like an error may have a sound explanation** ← | ← |
| **So informing them improves the review's accuracy** ← | ← |
| **And it is fair, since their reputation is affected** ← | ← |
| **Though it is not always possible** ← | **In litigation, or where the client forbids it** ← |

> **THE FIRST AND SECOND ROWS MAKE THIS A MATTER OF QUALITY RATHER THAN MERELY OF ETIQUETTE, WHICH IS THE MORE PERSUASIVE ARGUMENT: a reviewer sees the output and not the constraints under which it was produced.**

> **An apparently over-conservative foundation may reflect a ground investigation the reviewer has not seen; an unusual detail may have been instructed by the client.**

> **So a review conducted without the opportunity to ask is a review of the documents rather than of the engineering, and its conclusions should be qualified accordingly.**

> **Where contact is genuinely impossible, the report should say so and should frame its findings as questions rather than as conclusions wherever an explanation might exist.**

**THE MANNER OF EXPRESSION MATTERS AND IT DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Comment on the WORK, not on the engineer** ← | ← |
| **State findings factually, with the basis for each** ← | ← |
| **Distinguish non-compliance from preference** ← | ← |
| **Acknowledge what is sound as well as what is not** ← | ← |
| **And avoid language that invites a conclusion beyond the evidence** ← | ← |

> **THE FOURTH ROW IS OFTEN OMITTED AND ITS OMISSION DISTORTS THE REPORT: a review listing only deficiencies gives the impression that the work was deficient throughout, even where most of it was competent.**

> **A reader who is not an engineer — a client, a lawyer, a tribunal — will draw exactly that inference.**

> **So recording that the work was generally sound, where it was, is not a courtesy but an accuracy, and its absence misleads.**

> **The fifth row follows: a report that is technically accurate and rhetorically loaded conveys more than its author can defend, and an engineer whose review is later tested will be asked to justify the impression it created as well as the statements it made — which is a good reason to write it as though it will be read aloud in front of the engineer whose work it concerns.**
tags: informing the other engineer improves accuracy
comment on the work not the person

examTip.trick: **Objective, technical, informing the other engineer where possible** — without letting collegiality suppress a genuine concern.
examTip.trap: **Distinguish a DEFICIENCY from a DIFFERENCE OF OPINION** — presenting the second as the first misleads the client and wrongs the engineer.
examTip.mnemonic: **Write it as if it will be read aloud in front of the engineer concerned** — and record what was sound, or the report misleads by omission.

questions.stem: The NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL (NEC) was established under the Nepal Engineering Council Act with the principal purpose of:
options: REGULATING the engineering profession
Employing engineers in government service
Carrying out engineering design work for public projects
Setting the fees that engineers may charge
questions.solution:
**REGULATING the engineering profession — registering qualified engineers, recognising and accrediting engineering qualifications, setting standards of professional conduct, and taking disciplinary action** — so that engineering is practised only by competent and accountable persons.

**The Council's principal functions:**

| Function | Note |
|---|---|
| **REGISTRATION of engineers** ← | **Maintaining the register of those entitled to practise** ← |
| **RECOGNITION of qualifications and accreditation of programmes** ← | **Both Nepali and foreign** ← |
| **Setting the CODE OF ETHICS and standards of professional conduct** ← | ← |
| **DISCIPLINARY action against registered engineers** ← | **Including suspension and removal from the register** ← |
| **Advising the Government on matters relating to the profession** ← | ← |
| **Determining the categories and scope of engineering practice** ← | ← |

> **THE COMBINATION OF THE FIRST AND FOURTH ROWS IS WHAT MAKES A REGULATOR EFFECTIVE AND IT IS THE STRUCTURE IDENTIFIED EARLIER: the power to admit to practice is meaningful only if it is paired with the power to remove.**

> **Registration without discipline is a directory; discipline without registration has no sanction to apply.**

> **Together they give the Council the means to require a standard of conduct, because the consequence of falling below it is the loss of the ability to practise.**

> **That is why these two functions sit in the same body rather than being separated, and why a regulator's credibility is judged by whether the disciplinary power has visibly been used.**

**THE DISTINCTION BETWEEN A REGULATOR AND A PROFESSIONAL ASSOCIATION IS WORTH MAKING CLEARLY:**

| Body | Role |
|---|---|
| **NEPAL ENGINEERING COUNCIL** ← | **STATUTORY REGULATOR — established by Act, protects the public, registration is mandatory to practise** ← |
| **NEPAL ENGINEERS' ASSOCIATION** ← | **A professional ASSOCIATION — represents members' interests, membership is voluntary** ← |

> **THE DIFFERENCE IN WHOSE INTERESTS EACH SERVES IS THE ESSENTIAL ONE AND IT IS FREQUENTLY CONFUSED: a regulator exists to protect the PUBLIC from the profession's failures.**

> **An association exists to advance the interests of its MEMBERS.**

> **Both are legitimate and they are not the same thing, and a body attempting both has a conflict at its centre.**

> **That is why the regulatory function was placed in a statutory council rather than left with the professional association, and it is the same separation found in medicine, law and accountancy in most countries.**

**THE PRACTICAL EFFECT OF REGISTRATION DESERVES THE CLOSING NOTE:**

| Point | Note |
|---|---|
| **Practising engineering without registration is prohibited** ← | ← |
| **Signing drawings, certifying work and holding professional positions require it** ← | ← |
| **Employers and clients may verify a person's registration** ← | ← |
| **Foreign engineers require registration to practise in Nepal** ← | **Subject to the Council's recognition procedures** ← |
| **And registration must be renewed periodically** ← | ← |

> **THE THIRD ROW IS THE FUNCTION THAT MAKES THE REGISTER USEFUL TO PEOPLE OUTSIDE THE PROFESSION AND IT IS WORTH ENCOURAGING: a client engaging an engineer, or an employer recruiting one, can check the register.**

> **That check verifies the qualification, the registration category and whether any disciplinary action has been taken.**

> **It costs nothing and it is rarely done, largely because people do not know it is possible.**

> **So the register's protective value depends partly on public awareness of it, which is why regulators publicise the register and encourage its use — a register nobody consults protects nobody, however well maintained it is.**

examTip.trick: **Regulating the profession — registration, qualification recognition, conduct standards and discipline.**
examTip.trap: **A regulator protects the PUBLIC; an association serves its MEMBERS** — NEC and the Nepal Engineers' Association are different things.
examTip.mnemonic: **Registration without discipline is a directory** — the power to admit means something only with the power to remove.

questions.stem: Under the Nepal Engineering Council's framework, a person registered as a PROFESSIONAL ENGINEER is distinguished from one registered in the general engineer category chiefly by:
options: Holding an additional EXPERIENCE requirement and having demonstrated professional competence
The university from which they graduated
